Band-family discrepancy at every ramp width

16 October 2026 · Working proof; against Lebesgue measure · Sub-scale layers. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort set by the session).

Where we stand. Unchanged: The entry adds a lemma toward the core statement; the goal's state in Where we stand is unchanged.

Question. The tube-localized discrepancy entry bounded disjoint band families whose ramps are at least the Leighton–Shor scale \(m=2^{-\ell_1}\), and left plateau bands with ramps between \(6\sqrt{\log N/N}\) and \(m\) and a large width ratio: its part (c) needs a mesh of at least \(m\), and its per-cell part (e) charges the width ratio. The missing implication is conj:conjugate-class-discrepancy at \((4,4)\); this entry closes the band families at every ramp width, by layers between the mesh \(m\) and the ramp width, and below \(6\sqrt{\log N/N}\) by a comparison.

Chosen. The queue head is sandpile-odometer-flow, a primal flow simulation; this entry continues entry-2026-10-16-fourth-route-review:2, the chaining lead, whose last entry named this attempt, because it bears directly on conjugate-class-discrepancy and bounds the tube part of the fourth route review's decisive test where that part consists of full-width bands of bounded slope.

General statement. lem:band-family-discrepancy, for every band along a graph of slope at most \(K\), every ramp width and every width ratio, and for every family of disjoint such bands inside the square under the class cost.

Band-family discrepancy

Statement. There is a universal \(L\) such that with probability tending to one, for \(X_1,\dots,X_N\) i.i.d. uniform on \([0,1]^2\), with \(s_0=3\sqrt{\log N/N}\) and \(w_0=2s_0\):

(a) for every \(i\) with \(2^{-i}\ge s_0\), every \(K\ge0\), and every set \(S\) of cells of mesh \(2^{-(i-1)}\) that meets each column of cells in an interval of at most \(K+4\) cells, the intervals of neighbouring columns starting at most \(K+1\) rows apart, \(\sum_Q|n_Q-n_{\pi(Q)}/4|\le L\big((K+4)\sqrt N+\sqrt{(K+4)N2^{-i}\log N}\big)\), at most \(2L(K+4)\sqrt N\) when \(2^{i}\ge\log N\), the sum over the children \(Q\) (mesh \(2^{-i}\)) of the cells of \(S\), \(\pi(Q)\) the parent;

(b) for a band \(G(x,y)=a\varphi(y-f(x))\) as in lem:tube-localized-discrepancy (c), \(|f'|\le K\), \(a>0\), ramp width \(w>0\) and band width \(W'\le1\), with \(w_*=\max(w,w_0)\), \[\Big|\sum_iG(X_i)-N\int G\Big|\le L(1+K)^2a\sqrt N\Big(\big(2\log_2(2+W'/w_*)+9\big)^{3/4}+\sqrt{\log N}\Big);\]

(c) for bands \(G_1,\dots,G_n\) as in (b), each inside the square (\(0\le f_r\), \(f_r+W'_r\le1\)), with disjoint supports, slopes at most \(K\), ramp gradients \(y_r=a_r/w_r\ge e^{16}\), any ramp widths, \(G=\sum_r\varepsilon_rG_r\) with signs \(\varepsilon_r=\pm1\), and \(\int\sum_i\psi_4^*(|\partial_iG|)\le2\): \(|\sum_iG(X_i)-N\int G|\le L(1+K)^2\sqrt{N\log N}\). No upper bound on the gradients \(y_r\) is needed.

Proof. The event: Bernstein's inequality and Chernoff's bound for every cell of every dyadic mesh of side at least \(s_0\) (at most \(2N\) cells per mesh, at most \(\log_2N\) meshes), so that \(|n_Q-N\lambda(Q)|\le L(\sqrt{N\lambda(Q)\log N}+\log N)\) and \(n_Q\le2N\lambda(Q)\); the event of lem:tube-localized-discrepancy (b) and (e), the latter including the cellwise event of lem:cellwise-lipschitz-split for those meshes; and the event of (a) below, which fails with probability at most \(N^{-1}\) (the union over \(S\), \(i\) and \(K\) in its proof).

(a) Condition on the counts of the cells of mesh \(2^{-(i-1)}\). Given them, the children's counts are independent across parents, and within a parent \(P\) with \(n_P\) points multinomial with four equal cells, so \(\xi_Q=n_Q-n_P/4\) is a centred binomial minus its mean, with \(|\xi_Q|\le n_P\) and \(\mathbb P(|\xi_Q|>u)\le2\exp(-u^2/(2(n_P/4+u/3)))\le2\exp(-3u^2/(8n_P))\) for \(u\le n_P\); so \(\xi_Q\), and \(|\xi_Q|-\mathbb E|\xi_Q|\), are sub-Gaussian with norm at most \(L\sqrt{n_P}\), and \(\mathbb E|\xi_Q|\le\sqrt{n_P}/2\). On the count event \(n_P\le2N4^{1-i}\). For a fixed \(S\) of \(|S|\le(K+4)2^{i-1}\) parents (at most \(K+4\) in each of the \(2^{i-1}\) columns), the sum over its at most \(4(K+4)2^{i-1}\) children has mean at most \(4(K+4)2^{i-1}\sqrt{2N4^{1-i}}/2\le3(K+4)\sqrt N\), and, since the four children of one parent are dependent (their counts are multinomial and sum to \(n_P\)), the summands are taken per parent: \(Y_P=\sum_{Q\subset P}(|\xi_Q|-\mathbb E|\xi_Q|)\) has sub-Gaussian norm at most \(4L\sqrt{n_P}\), and the \(Y_P\) are independent across parents given the parents' counts (the reviewer's correction); by Hoeffding's inequality for these independent sub-Gaussian summands, with variance proxy \(|S|\cdot16L^2\cdot2N4^{1-i}\) of the same order, the sum exceeds its mean by more than \(L\sqrt{2(K+4)2^{i}\cdot2N4^{1-i}\cdot t}=L'\sqrt{(K+4)N2^{-i}t}\) with probability at most \(e^{-t}\). The sets \(S\) of the statement are determined by the first column's interval and, column by column, the start (\(2K+3\) choices) and length (\(K+4\) choices) of the next interval: at most \(4^{i}(2K+3)^{2^{i-1}}(K+4)^{2^{i-1}}\le\exp(2^{i}\log(2K+5)+2i)\) of them. With \(t=2^{i}\log(2K+5)+2i+3\log N\), the union bound over \(S\), over the at most \(\log_2N\) values of \(i\) and over the integers \(K\le2^{i-1}\) (beyond them the family of sets saturates, and a non-integer \(K\) gives no set that \(\lceil K\rceil\) does not) fails with probability at most \(N^{-1}\), and the deviation is at most \(L'\sqrt{(K+4)N(2\log(2K+5)+(2i+3\log N)2^{-i})}\le L''\big((K+4)\sqrt N+\sqrt{(K+4)N2^{-i}\log N}\big)\), using \(\log(2K+5)\le K+4\) and \(2i\le3\log N\). Summing mean and deviation gives (a).

(b) Three cases; "cells of side \(s_0\)" below means the cells of the dyadic mesh whose side lies in \([s_0,2s_0)\), which changes only the constants. If \(W'<2w_0\): the band lies in the cells of side \(s_0\) meeting it, at most \(W'/s_0+K+2\le K+6\) per column of \(1/s_0\) columns, each holding at most \(2Ns_0^2\) points, so \(|\sum_iG(X_i)-N\int G|\le a(2(K+6)Ns_0+NW')\le L(K+6)a\sqrt{N\log N}\). If \(w<w_0\le W'/2\): let \(G'\) be the band with the same outer edges, \(f\) and \(a\), and ramps of width \(w_0\); \(G-G'\) vanishes off the two edge strips of vertical width \(w_0\) and \(|G-G'|\le a\); each strip meets at most \(w_0/s_0+K+2=K+4\) cells of side \(s_0\) per column, so the points in the strips are at most \(2(K+4)\cdot2Ns_0\) and their area is \(2w_0\), and \(|\operatorname{disc}(G-G')|\le a(4(K+4)Ns_0+2Nw_0)\le L(K+4)a\sqrt{N\log N}\); it remains to bound \(G'\), whose ramps are \(w_0=w_*\). So assume \(w\ge w_0\), and let \(j\) be the least integer with \(2^{-j}\le w\), so \(2^{-j}>w/2\ge s_0\). If \(j\le\ell_1\), that is \(w\ge m\), lem:tube-localized-discrepancy (c) gives the bound. Otherwise write \[G=E_{\ell_1}G+\sum_{i=\ell_1+1}^{j}D_i+(G-E_jG),\qquad D_i=E_iG-E_{i-1}G,\] \(E_i\) the averages on the cells of mesh \(2^{-i}\). Remainder: as in lem:tube-localized-discrepancy (e), \(|\operatorname{disc}(G-E_jG)|\le L\sqrt{N\log N}\Lambda_j(G)\le2L(K+4)(1+K)a\sqrt{N\log N}\). Layers: \(D_i\) has integral \(0\) on each cell \(P\) of mesh \(2^{-(i-1)}\), and on its four children, of equal area, \(\sum_{Q\subset P}D_i(Q)=0\), so \(\sum_kD_i(X_k)-N\int D_i=\sum_P\sum_{Q\subset P}D_i(Q)(n_Q-n_P/4)\); \(D_i=0\) on every parent on which \(G\) is constant, and the others meet one of the two ramp strips, of vertical width \(w\le2\cdot2^{-j}\le2^{-(i-1)}\), along a graph of slope at most \(K\): each strip meets each column of parents in an interval of at most \(K+3\) cells, neighbouring intervals starting at most \(K+1\) rows apart, a set as in (a); where the strip is clipped at the square's edge or misses a column, \(\sum_Q|\xi_Q|\) is monotone in \(S\), so a superset is bounded instead, whose interval in each column is the unclipped interval clamped to the rows, which keeps the start differences at most \(K+1\). With \(|D_i|\le a\) and \(2^{i}\ge2^{\ell_1}\ge\log N\), (a) gives \(|\operatorname{disc}(D_i)|\le4La(K+4)\sqrt N\). There are \(j-\ell_1\le\log_2(2m/w_0)\le\log_2(\frac23(\log N)^{1/4})\le\frac14\log_2\log N\) layers, so the layers give at most \(La(K+4)\sqrt N\log_2\log N\le La(K+4)\sqrt{N\log N}\). Coarse part: \(E_{\ell_1}G\) is constant on the cells of mesh \(m\); apply lem:tube-localized-discrepancy (b) with \(j=\ell_1\) and \(k\) the least of \(\ell_1\) and the largest integer with \(2^{-k}\ge W'\), \(W=2^{-k}\). The inner edges give \(V^0\le8\|\nabla G\|_1\le16(1+K)a\) (as in that lemma's (c)), the edges on \(\partial[0,1]^2\) at most \((6+2K)a\); a column of cells of side \(W\ge\max(W',m)\) meets the support of \(E_{\ell_1}G\) in a vertical extent at most \(W'+KW+2m\le(K+3)W\), so in at most \(K+5\) cells, and the cut term is at most \(4(K+5)a\); and \(\Phi_{\ell_1,k}\le(2\log_2(2W'/m)+5)^{3/4}+\sqrt{\log N}\) when \(k<\ell_1\) (then \(2^{\ell_1-k}<2W'/m\)), and \(5^{3/4}+\sqrt{\log N}\) when \(k=\ell_1\). Since \(m>w\), \(2W'/m\le2W'/w\le(2+W'/w)^{2}\) in both cases, and the coarse part is at most \(L(1+K)a\sqrt N((2\log_2(2+W'/w)+9)^{3/4}+\sqrt{\log N})\). The three parts give (b) with \(L(1+K)^2\).

(c) By linearity and (b), with \(x_r=W'_r/w_{*,r}\) and \(\tilde y_r=a_r/w_{*,r}\), so that \(\tilde y_r\le y_r\) and \(\tilde y_r\le a_r/w_0\le\sqrt N\), since \(a_r\le1\) by the cost bound below (\(a_r(\log y_r)^{1/4}\le2\) and \((\log y_r)^{1/4}\ge2\)): \(2+x_r\le(2+\tilde y_r)(1+W'_r/a_r)\), so \((2\log_2(2+x_r)+9)^{3/4}\le(2\log_2(2+\tilde y_r))^{3/4}+k(W'_r/a_r)\), \(k(x)=(2\log_2(1+x)+9)^{3/4}\) concave and increasing. Jensen's inequality with the weights \(a_r/B\), \(B=\sum_ra_r\), and \(\sum_rW'_r\le1\) (the bands are inside the square and disjoint) give \(\sum_ra_rk(W'_r/a_r)\le Bk(1/B)\), bounded for \(B\le1\). The cost: on the ramps of \(G_r\), \(|\partial_2G|=y_r\) on an area \(2w_r\), the supports are disjoint, and \(\psi_4^*(y)\ge\frac12y(\log y)^{1/4}\) for \(y\ge e^{16}\), so \(\sum_ra_r(\log y_r)^{1/4}\le2\) and \(B\le1\). Finally \((2\log_2(2+\tilde y_r))^{3/4}\le L(\log(2+\tilde y_r))^{3/4}\le L(\log y_r)^{1/4}(\log(2+\sqrt N))^{1/2}\) when \(\tilde y_r\ge e^{16}\) (using \(\tilde y_r\le y_r\)), and at most \(L\le L(\log y_r)^{1/4}\) otherwise; so \(\sum_ra_r(2\log_2(2+\tilde y_r))^{3/4}\le L\sqrt{\log N}\sum_ra_r(\log y_r)^{1/4}\le2L\sqrt{\log N}\), and \(\sum_ra_r\sqrt{\log N}\le\sqrt{\log N}\). \(\square\)

Hypotheses, each with its step. \(X_i\) i.i.d. uniform: the count event, the multinomial children in (a), and the events of lem:tube-localized-discrepancy. \(2^{-i}\ge s_0\) in (a): Chernoff's bound \(n_P\le2N4^{1-i}\) and the sub-Gaussian range; every such \(i\) is allowed, the second term mattering only for \(2^i<\log N\), and (b) uses \(\ell_1<i\le j\). The column-interval form of \(S\) in (a): the count of sets; it is what a strip along a graph of slope at most \(K\) meets. \(|f'|\le K\): the column counts in (b). \(W'\le1\): \(W\le1\) in the coarse part. Inside the square, disjoint supports, \(y_r\ge e^{16}\) and the cost in (c): the packing \(\sum_rW'_r\le1\), the ramp area, the additivity of the cost and the \(\psi_4^*\) lower bound. No bound on the ramp width from below is needed (the comparison with \(G'\)), and none on \(y_r\) from above. Conclusions: (a) for every such \(S\) and \(i\); (b) for every band; (c) for every such family; (b) and (c) against Lebesgue measure.

Baseline. The plainest bounds on a band are the per-cell count bound, lem:tube-localized-discrepancy (e), with the factor \(1+W'/w\), and for ramps of at least \(m\) that lemma's (c); per layer, the plainest bound on \(\sum_Q|\xi_Q|\) is the maximum count deviation times the number of children, \(L(K+4)2^{i}\cdot2^{-i}\sqrt{N\log N}\), which over the \(\frac14\log_2\log N\) layers would cost \(\log\log N\cdot\sqrt{N\log N}\); (a) removes the \(\sqrt{\log N}\) per layer by counting the sets instead of taking the worst cell.

Degenerate cases. \(w\ge m\): (b) is lem:tube-localized-discrepancy (c) with \(2+W'/w\) in place of \(W'/w\). \(W'\) of order \(w\): the first case or the per-cell bound, factor \(O(1)\). \(a\to0\): both sides vanish. \(w\to0\) at fixed \(W'\) (a sharp plateau): the comparison with \(G'\) costs \(L(K+4)a\sqrt{N\log N}\), and the factor stays \((\log(W'/w_0))^{3/4}\), which is the Leighton–Shor factor of the plateau's width over the grid side: a sharp plateau of height \(W'\) of order \(1\) gives \((\log\sqrt{N/\log N})^{3/4}\), the full one, and its amplitude decides. \(K=0\), and any one fixed shear: a function of one coordinate, already decided by the Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz inequality at \(O(a\sqrt N)\), stronger than the lemma.

Nonvacuity. On the curve's parameters at \((4,4)\), for (c) with ramps below \(m\), which lem:tube-localized-discrepancy (c) and (d) do not reach: \(y=(\log N)^4\), \(w=2w_0=12\sqrt{\log N/N}\), which is below \(m\ge(\log N)^{3/4}/\sqrt N\) when \((\log N)^{1/4}>12\), that is \(\log N>12^4\), \(a=yw\), \(W'=a\) (so \(W'/w=y\)), \(n=\lfloor(\log y)^{-1/4}/(4a)\rfloor\) bands along \(f_r(x)=\frac18+\frac{3(r-1)}{4n}+\frac1{16}\sin(2\pi x)\), \(K=1\). With \(a=12(\log N)^{4.5}/\sqrt N\), \(W'\le\frac1{16}\) and \(f_r\in[\frac1{16},\frac{15}{16}]\), so the bands lie inside the square; the vertical spacing \(\frac3{4n}\ge3a(\log y)^{1/4}\ge W'\), so they are disjoint; the cost is at most \(4na(\log(1+y))^{1/4}\le(\log(1+y)/\log y)^{1/4}\le2\), with \(|\partial_1G|\le y\) and \(\psi_4^*(x)\le x(\log(1+x))^{1/4}\); \(y\ge e^{16}\). Plainest bound. For this one fixed family, a bound for one function decides it: all \(f_r\) share one shear, \(G\) is a function of \(z=y-\sin(2\pi x)/16\), and the Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz inequality gives \(O(B\sqrt N)\); what the statement adds is uniformity over all graphs of slope at most \(K\). Among uniform bounds, the per-cell bound (e) gives the factor \(1+y=1+(\log N)^4\), and lem:tube-localized-discrepancy (c) needs \(w\ge m\), which fails here.

Architecture test

Architecture test. Not decided. The fourth route review's decisive test splits a single-level class function at its local spacing; this entry, like the tube-localized one, proves a lemma the test uses, so none of its outcomes (A), (B), (C) occurred. What it settles for the test: the tube part of the split, when it consists of disjoint bands inside the square along full-width graphs of bounded slope, is bounded at the conjectured order at every ramp width. The reviewer found that in general it does not: the tube part is made of level curves of any shape, nested and with ends, \(G-\rho_W*G\) is nonconstant on whole tubes, and neighbouring tubes overlap at scale \(W\). The next entry makes the test itself.

Record search. tools/search-claims.py "children counts parent cell multinomial union over traces column intervals layers below Leighton Shor scale" (the objects of the proof) returned lem:mesh-function-discrepancy, lem:local-factor-discrepancy, lem:two-mesh-partition-discrepancy and lem:cellwise-lipschitz-split, none below the Leighton–Shor scale; "band ramp narrower than grid side rounding strip points per cell sharp plateau" returned lem:tube-localized-discrepancy and claims of other notebooks. tools/claim_resemblance.py on the spec: lem:tube-localized-discrepancy (0.52), which this lemma refines (its (c) and (d) are the cases \(w\ge2^{-\ell_1}\) of (b) and (c) here, with \(W'/w\) for \(2+W'/w\)), lem:cellwise-lipschitz-split (0.30), a dependency, lem:dominant-level-split (0.25), not more general (it needs a bounded cellwise sum), lem:loglog-mesh-deviation (0.19), not used, and one claim of another notebook; none is more general than this one.

Follow-up

Owed attempt. The tube-localized entry named the layers between \(m\) and the ramp width, bounded by Bernstein's inequality and a union bound over traces, about \(C\sqrt N\) per layer: made, as (a) and (b); the per-layer bound came out \(L(K+4)\sqrt N\), the union over traces made with a sub-Gaussian bound for the children's deviations given the parents.

Follow-up. Continuing. The first draft closed the item as Developed; the reviewer found that the closure does not stand, since the decisive split's tube part is made of level curves of a class function, closed curves or arcs ending on the boundary, of any shape, nested and with ends, which are not full-width bands along graphs of bounded slope, so the item's translation still bears on conjugate-class-discrepancy. Next attempt: the reviewer's suggestion, unverified, a curve-trace version of (a): replace the column-interval sets by the cells met by a lattice path of \(P2^{i}\) steps around a rectifiable curve of length \(P\), at most \(4^{i}9^{\lceil P2^{i}\rceil}\) sets, giving about \(P\sqrt N+\sqrt{PN2^{-i}\log N}\) per layer, with the length \(P\) in place of \(1+K\), and then (b) for a function Lipschitz in a curve tube and nonconstant only on its traces. Smallest case. One closed level curve, a circle of radius \(r\), with ramps below \(m\). Plainest bound. For one fixed circle a bound for one function decides it: the variance bound gives \(O(a\sqrt N)\); the attempt's content is the uniformity over all curves of length \(P\), whose count \(C^{P2^i}\) the attempt must beat with the per-layer deviation, so the smallest instance decides nothing.

Suggestion checked. The counting step of the curve-trace suggestion, checked here and corrected by the reviewer's second pass: points at arc-length spacing \(2^{-i}\) along a curve of length \(P\), \(\lceil P2^{i}\rceil+1\) of them, lie in the same or king-adjacent cells of mesh \(2^{-(i-1)}\), so the cells the curve meets lie within one cell of a lattice path of \(\lceil P2^{i}\rceil\) steps of nine possible moves; there are at most \(4^{i}9^{\lceil P2^{i}\rceil}\) such sets, with at most \(9(\lceil P2^{i}\rceil+1)\) parents and four times as many children, so the mean of \(\sum_Q|\xi_Q|\) is at most of order \(P\sqrt N\), and Hoeffding's inequality with the per-parent summands of (a), variance proxy of order \(PN2^{-i}\), and \(t=\lceil P2^{i}\rceil\log9+2i+5\log N\), the union taken over \(i\) and over the integer step count \(\lceil P2^{i}\rceil\le4^{i}\) (counting steps, not \(P\)), gives a deviation at most \(L'(P\sqrt N+\sqrt{PN2^{-i}\log N})\) for all curves at once: the per-layer bound of the suggestion holds for curve traces. Not checked: how a general single-level function's layers \(D_i\) are supported on such traces with weights, which is the attempt's content.

New mathematics. lem:band-family-discrepancy: (a) over the children of the cells a strip along a graph of slope at most \(K\) meets, the summed absolute deviations from the parents' quarter counts are at most \(L(K+4)\sqrt N\) at every mesh of side at least \(3\sqrt{\log N/N}\); (b) every band, at every ramp width, has discrepancy at most \(L(1+K)^2a\sqrt N((2\log_2(2+W'/w_*)+9)^{3/4}+\sqrt{\log N})\); (c) disjoint bands inside the square at any ramp widths and gradients \(y_r\ge e^{16}\) are at most \(L(1+K)^2\sqrt{N\log N}\) under the class cost.

On the curve's parameters at \((4,4)\): every family of disjoint plateau or tent bands, each inside the square along a full-width graph of slope at most a constant \(K\), at any ramp widths and gradient levels at least \(e^{16}\), with class cost at most \(2\), has discrepancy against Lebesgue measure at most \(C\sqrt{N\log N}\), uniformly over the graphs. Verification gate. Dependencies re-read: the full entries of lem:tube-localized-discrepancy (parts (b) to (e) and its extended cellwise event) and lem:cellwise-lipschitz-split. One fresh-context medium reviewer read the draft, spec, commit message and those entries and found (a), (b) and (c) correct in substance, checking the constants (mean \(2\sqrt2(K+4)\sqrt N\), the set count, the layer count) and every hypothesis on the Nonvacuity witness, with no unused hypothesis. It required: per-parent summands in the Hoeffding step, the children of a parent being dependent; a union over \(K\) and one failure probability; the clamped superset where a strip is clipped at the square's edge; dyadic cells for \(s_0\); the follow-up Continuing instead of Developed; the Stakes and Meta sentences; the \(K=0\) degenerate case; the condition \(\log N>12^4\) on the witness. All were made, the proof corrections in its wording. The same reviewer read the corrections and the new Suggestion checked paragraph, and passed that paragraph after asking for the covering step (points at arc-length spacing \(2^{-i}\), nine moves) and a union over the integer step count, now in. Process audit. It proposed the title "Band-family discrepancy at every ramp width", which the title follows; strength count 4 (the Chosen paragraph's "completes the tube part", the spec rationale's dropped qualifiers, the Follow-up's "no application left", the Meta's "no mistake escaped"), all corrected, and 1 on the second pass (the gate's first sentence saying no second pass was made); it found unasked whether the decisive split's tube part has the form the lemma needs, which it does not in general, and the commit message missing \(y_r\ge e^{16}\) and the full-width graph.

Process assessment. The first draft of (a) carried the constant \((K+4)^{3/2}\), stated (a) only where its use needed it, and gave a wrong reason for \(a_r\le1\); the recheck before the brief found these. It did not find two gaps the reviewer found: the four children of a parent were summed as independent summands, though their counts are multinomial, and the statement quantified over every \(K\) with no union over \(K\) in the proof; nor the clipping at the square's edge. The Follow-up first closed the item as Developed while the entry's own Not covered list named what the decisive split produces, and the Chosen and spec rationale said the lemma completes the split's tube part without the condition that this part be full-width bands of bounded slope. Prevention. AGENTS.md now asks a statement holding with high probability for every value of a parameter to name the union bound covering it, and each concentration inequality to name the independence it rests on, a rule where no check can read a proof's independence; the same omission recurred minutes later in the Suggestion checked paragraph (a union over the curve length), so the build union-parameter-check is queued in this notebook, a finisher check listing each quantified parameter beside its union bound, not built now because it needs a parser of quantified parameters that no tool here has, and CLAUDE.md asks that a rule written for a mistake be applied at once to the next text written; the overstated closure and summaries were rewritten under AGENTS.md's rule of rereading summaries with each correction.

Meta. The habit behind the two gaps is rechecking a proof's numbers and not its tools' preconditions: every constant of the concentration step was right while the inequality did not apply as used. The change, in CLAUDE.md, is that a recheck reads each step's preconditions (independence, quantifier ranges, domains) as well as its arithmetic.

Mollified smooth part; the spacing split fails on a staircase

16 October 2026 · Working proof; against Lebesgue measure · Spacing split. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort set by the session).

Where we stand. Unchanged: The entry decides the review's test and adds a reduction; the goal's state in Where we stand is unchanged.

Question. The fourth route review's decisive test splits a single-level class function \(G\) at \((4,4)\) at its local spacing \(W(x)\), bounds the smooth part \(\rho_W*G\) by lem:local-factor-discrepancy (b) on the partition by \(W\) and the tube part by the band lemmas, and asks whether the summed charges fit the class cost. The missing implication is the single-level case of conj:conjugate-class-discrepancy at \((4,4)\); this entry makes the test, finds the operation failing on a constant-spacing staircase for a reason of its own, and repairs the split.

General statement. lem:mollified-smooth-part, for every Lipschitz function on the square and every mesh \(2^{-j}\), \(j\le\ell_1\), with its corollary for the functions whose larger partial is at least \(y\) where their gradient is nonzero.

Mollified smooth part

Statement. Fix a bounded measurable \(\rho\ge0\) supported in the unit disc with \(\int\rho=1\) (smoothness is not used), and write \(\rho_h(z)=h^{-2}\rho(z/h)\). There is \(L\) depending only on \(\|\rho\|_\infty\) such that, on the event of lem:cellwise-lipschitz-split (probability tending to one), for every \(j\) with \(1\le j\le\ell_1\), \(h=2^{-j}\), and every Lipschitz \(G\) on \([0,1]^2\), with \(\hat G\) the even reflection of \(G\) to \([-1,2]^2\) and \(S=(\rho_h*\hat G)|_{[0,1]^2}\):

(a) \(\big|\sum_iS(X_i)-N\int S\big|\le L\sqrt N\big(j^{3/4}+\sqrt{\log N}\big)\|\nabla G\|_1\);

(b) if \(\int\sum_i\psi_4^*(|\partial_iG|)\le2\) and the larger partial of \(G\) is at least \(y\ge e^{16}\) where \(\nabla G\ne0\), then for every \(j\le j^*(y)=\min(\ell_1,\lfloor(\log N)^{2/3}(\log y)^{1/3}\rfloor)\), \(|\sum_iS(X_i)-N\int S|\le L'\sqrt{N\log N}\), and so \[\Big|\sum_iG(X_i)-N\int G\Big|\le L'\sqrt{N\log N}+\Big|\sum_iR(X_i)-N\int R\Big|,\qquad R=G-S:\] the single-level case of the class bound at \((4,4)\) is the same, up to \(L'\sqrt{N\log N}\), as the bound for the high-frequency remainder \(R\) at the scale \(2^{-j^*(y)}\).

Proof. (a) \(\hat G\) is Lipschitz on \([-1,2]^2\), and on \([-h,1+h]^2\) it consists of \(G\) and its reflections across the sides and corners, each the image of a part of the square, so \(\int_{[-h,1+h]^2}|\nabla\hat G|_1\le9\|\nabla G\|_1\). \(S\) is smooth, \(\nabla S=\rho_h*\nabla\hat G\), so \(|\nabla S|_1\le\rho_h*|\nabla\hat G|_1\) and \(\|\nabla S\|_{L^1([0,1]^2)}\le9\|\nabla G\|_1\). By lem:cellwise-lipschitz-split for the Lipschitz \(S\), \(|\sum_iS(X_i)-N\int S|\le L\sqrt N(j^{3/4}+\sqrt{\log N})\cdot8\|\nabla S\|_1+L\sqrt{N\log N}\Lambda_j(S)\). For \(x\) in a cell \(Q\) of side \(h\), \(|\nabla S(x)|\le\|\rho\|_\infty h^{-2}\int_{B(x,h)}|\nabla\hat G|\le\|\rho\|_\infty h^{-2}\int_{Q^+}|\nabla\hat G|\), \(Q^+\) the block of nine cells around \(Q\), so \(\Lambda_j(S)\le\sum_Q4^{-j}\sup_Q|\nabla S|\le\|\rho\|_\infty\sum_Q\int_{Q^+}|\nabla\hat G|\le9\|\rho\|_\infty\int_{[-h,1+h]^2}|\nabla\hat G|\le81\|\rho\|_\infty\|\nabla G\|_1\). Both terms are at most the display.

(b) Where \(\nabla G\ne0\) the larger partial \(t\ge y\ge e^{16}\), so, as in lem:dominant-level-split, \(|\partial_1G|+|\partial_2G|\le4\psi_4^*(t)(\log y)^{-1/4}\) and \(\|\nabla G\|_1\le8(\log y)^{-1/4}\); for \(j\le j^*(y)\), \(j^{3/4}(\log y)^{-1/4}\le\sqrt{\log N}\), so (a) gives \(L'\sqrt{N\log N}\). The display is linearity, \(G=S+R\). \(\square\)

Hypotheses, each with its step. \(G\) Lipschitz on the square: the reflection, \(\nabla S=\rho_h*\nabla\hat G\), and lem:cellwise-lipschitz-split for \(S\). \(1\le j\le\ell_1\): that lemma's range. \(\rho\) bounded, supported in the unit disc: the pointwise gradient bound and \(B(x,h)\subset Q^+\). In (b), the cost and the larger partial at least \(y\ge e^{16}\): the bound on \(\|\nabla G\|_1\); \(j\le j^*(y)\): the comparison with \(\sqrt{\log N}\). Conclusions: (a) for every Lipschitz \(G\) and every such \(j\); (b) for every function of the dominant-level class; both against Lebesgue measure.

Baseline. The plainest bound on a function of the dominant-level class is lem:dominant-level-split, \(L\sqrt{N\log N}(1+\Lambda_j(G))\), whose cellwise sum \(\Lambda_j(G)\) is unbounded for thin supports; (a) shows that after mollifying at the cell side the cellwise sum is at most \(81\|\rho\|_\infty\|\nabla G\|_1\) for every \(G\), so the smooth part never pays a thickness ratio, and what (b) leaves is the remainder \(R\) alone.

Degenerate cases. \(G\) constant: \(S=G\), both sides vanish. \(G\) affine and \(\rho\) even (or of mean zero): \(S=G\) away from the boundary strip of width \(h\) (the even reflection keeps affine functions affine only up to the reflection's kink), and \(R\) is supported in that strip; without that, \(S\) is \(G\) shifted by \(h\) times the mean of \(\rho\). \(j=\ell_1\): \(h\) is the Leighton–Shor scale and (a) is the cellwise split at its finest mesh. A thick single-level function, of bounded \(\Lambda_j(G)\) at some \(j\le j^*\): lem:dominant-level-split already bounds \(G\), and (b) bounds \(S\) and hence \(R\).

Nonvacuity. On the curve's parameters at \((4,4)\), for (b) with a function whose own cellwise sum is unbounded at every mesh up to \(j^*\), in coordinates \((x_1,x_2)\): the staircase \(G(x_1,x_2)=A\sum_{k=1}^{n}\min\{1,\max\{0,(x_2-kW)/w\}\}\) with level \(y_0=(\log N)^4\), \(W=1/(n+1)\), \(n=2^{\lfloor\ell_1/2\rfloor}\), \(A=W/(4(\log(1+y_0))^{1/4})\) and \(w=A/y_0\) (the reviewer's choice); its ramps have \(|\partial_2G|=y_0\), \(\partial_1G=0\), on area \(nw\), so the cost is at most \(nw\,y_0(\log(1+y_0))^{1/4}=nA(\log(1+y_0))^{1/4}\le\frac14\) for every \(N\); the larger partial is \(y_0\ge e^{16}\) on the ramps for large \(N\). \(j^*(y_0)\) is about \((\log N)^{2/3}(4\log\log N)^{1/3}\), far below \(\ell_1/2\), so every cell of side \(2^{-j}\), \(j\le j^*\), meets a ramp and \(\Lambda_j(G)=y_0\), unbounded, while (a) bounds \(\Lambda_j(S)\le81\|\rho\|_\infty\|\nabla G\|_1\le81\|\rho\|_\infty\cdot8(\log y_0)^{-1/4}\). Plainest bound. \(G\) depends only on \(x_2\) and is monotone in it, so the Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz inequality bounds every such staircase, uniformly over all of them, at \(O(\|G\|_\infty\sqrt N)\): the witness shows the hypotheses hold together and exercises (a)'s bound on \(\Lambda_j(S)\), but not the class's two-dimensional difficulty, which a staircase along curved graphs (the Sub-ideas) would; among the uniform two-dimensional bounds, lem:dominant-level-split pays \(\Lambda_j(G)=(\log N)^4\) on it.

Architecture test

Architecture test. Decided. None of the fourth route review's outcomes (A), (B), (C) occurred, so its outcome list was not exhaustive: the operation as posed (its smooth part charged by lem:local-factor-discrepancy (b) "on that partition") fails on a constant-spacing staircase, for a reason of its own, not of the class, and the review's Trivial cases sentence deciding the constant-spacing staircase in favour of (A) is refuted. On the staircase of the Nonvacuity paragraph with \(y_0=e^{16}\) instead, \(A=(\log(1+e^{16}))^{-1/4}/n\) and \(w=A/y_0\) (so \(nA=(\log(1+e^{16}))^{-1/4}\approx0.5\) and the cost is at most \(nA(\log(1+y_0))^{1/4}=1\)), the spacing is \(W(x)=W\) up to a constant factor (each ramp's width plus the distance to the next, the Lipschitz envelope adding at most \(cW\)), the partition by \(W\) has cells of level \(i=\log_2(1/W)\approx\lfloor\ell_1/2\rfloor\), and \(\rho_W*G\) rises from at most \(A\) at \(x_2=0\) to at least \(nA-A\) at \(x_2=1\) on every vertical line, so \(\int|\nabla(\rho_W*G)|\ge(n-2)A\), and the operation's charge \(\sum_QF(i(Q))\int_Q|\nabla(\rho_W*G)|\ge i^{3/4}(n-2)A\) is of order \((\log N)^{3/4}\), a factor about \((\log N)^{1/4}\) above the target's \(\sqrt{\log N}\); yet the smooth part is a ramp of slope below \(1\), which lem:cellwise-lipschitz-split at mesh \(2^{-1}\) bounds by \(O(\sqrt{N\log N})\), and the staircase as a fixed function has discrepancy \(O(\sqrt N)\). The structural reason: lem:local-factor-discrepancy charges every edge of the partition from scale \(1\) down, with no cancellation for a function that is smooth above the partition's scale, so charging the smooth part on the partition by the spacing overcharges every function whose spacing is finer than its smoothness. The replacement is (b): mollify at \(2^{-j^*(y)}\), not at \(W(x)\), and charge the smooth part on the mesh of that side, where its cellwise sum is bounded by its gradient mass for every function, so the test's cancellation inequality is not needed for the smooth part. It is not like for like: the operation localized its remainder to tubes of width about \(W\), while at \(h=2^{-j^*}\gg W\) the staircase's remainder is a sawtooth filling the square, and for a band thinner than \(h\) the remainder is about \(G\) itself, so the reduction removes nothing there; it trades the tube localization for a bounded smooth part, and the single-level case is the remainder's.

New mathematics. lem:mollified-smooth-part: for every Lipschitz \(G\), the mollification at the cell side \(2^{-j}\) has cellwise sum at most \(81\|\rho\|_\infty\|\nabla G\|_1\), so its discrepancy is at most \(L\sqrt N(j^{3/4}+\sqrt{\log N})\|\nabla G\|_1\); for the dominant-level class at \(j\le j^*(y)\) this is \(O(\sqrt{N\log N})\), and the single-level class bound reduces to the remainder \(G-\rho_h*\hat G\), which for features thinner than \(h\) is about \(G\) itself, so the reduction trades the operation's tube localization for a bounded smooth part. The fourth review's operation fails on a constant-spacing staircase by a factor about \((\log N)^{1/4}\), from charging a smooth part on a fine partition.

Sample-point pyramids refute the Lebesgue class bound

16 October 2026 · Working proof; every point set · Remainder target. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort set by the session).

Where we stand. Unchanged: The entry refutes a convenience form and reduces the smeared form to a discrete class; the goal's state in Where we stand is unchanged.

Question. The mollified split reduced the single-level case of conj:conjugate-class-discrepancy at \((4,4)\), against Lebesgue measure, to the remainder \(R=G-\rho_h*\hat G\) below \(h=2^{-j^*(y)}\), and named a curve-trace bound on \(R\) as the next attempt. The missing implication is the single-level case; before bounding the remainder, this entry tests the target itself, the class bound against Lebesgue measure, on the plainest instance that separates it from the smeared form the conjecture uses: functions concentrated at the sample points.

Chosen. The chaining lead entry-2026-10-16-fourth-route-review:2, not the queue head sandpile-odometer-flow: it bears directly on conjugate-class-discrepancy, the core open statement, whose single-level case the mollified split reduced to a remainder, and its owed attempt needs its target checked first; the head, a flow simulation, bears on the primal form only.

General statement. lem:sample-point-pyramids, for every exponent pair in \([1,\infty]^2\), every \(N\), every level \(y\ge2\) (at most \(N\) when an exponent is infinite) and every set of \(N\) points.

Sample-point pyramids

Statement. Let \(\alpha\in[1,\infty]^2\), \(\beta=\max_j1/\alpha_j\le1\), \(\psi_\alpha(t)=e^{t^\alpha}-1\) for finite \(\alpha\) and \(\psi_\infty(t)=N(t-1)_+\) (the reduction's costs, in units of \(s\)), \(\psi^*\) their conjugates. Let \(N\ge1\), \(y\ge2\), with \(y\le N\) if some \(\alpha_j=\infty\), and let \(x_1,\dots,x_N\in[0,1]^2\) be any points. Put \(r=(2Ny(\log(1+y))^{\beta})^{-1/2}\), \(a=yr\), \(P_i(z)=\max\{0,a-y|z-x_i|_\infty\}\) and \(G=\max_iP_i\) on \([0,1]^2\). Then \(G\) is Lipschitz; almost everywhere on \(\{\nabla G\ne0\}\) one partial of \(G\) is \(\pm y\) and the other is \(0\); \(\int_{[0,1]^2}\sum_j\psi^*_{\alpha_j}(|\partial_jG|)\le2\); and \[\sum_{i\le N}G(x_i)-N\int_{[0,1]^2}G\;\ge\;\tfrac23Na\;=\;\tfrac{\sqrt2}3\sqrt{Ny}\,(\log(1+y))^{-\beta/2}.\] Consequently, for every \(N\) and every point set, the supremum of \(\sum_iG(x_i)-N\int G\) over the class \(\int\sum_j\psi^*_{\alpha_j}(|\partial_jG|)\le2\) is infinite when both exponents are finite (let \(y\to\infty\)), and at least \(\frac{\sqrt2}3N(\log(1+N))^{-\beta/2}\) when an exponent is infinite (take \(y=N\)), in both cases far above \(\sqrt{N\log N}\); and at \((4,4)\) a bound \(L'\sqrt{N\log N}\) for the functions whose larger partial is at least \(y\) where their gradient is nonzero, against Lebesgue measure, fails for every point set as soon as \(\frac{\sqrt2}3\sqrt y(\log(1+y))^{-1/8}>L'\sqrt{\log N}\), for instance at \(y=(\log N)^2\) for all large \(N\).

Proof. Conjugate bound: for finite \(\alpha\ge1\) and \(y\ge2\) let \(t_0=(\log(1+y))^{1/\alpha}\ge1\); then \(\psi_\alpha'(t_0)=\alpha t_0^{\alpha-1}e^{t_0^\alpha}\ge1+y>y\), and as \(\psi_\alpha'\) increases, \(ty-\psi_\alpha(t)\) decreases on \([t_0,\infty)\), so \(\psi^*_\alpha(y)=\sup_{0\le t\le t_0}(ty-\psi_\alpha(t))\le t_0y=y(\log(1+y))^{1/\alpha}\); for \(\alpha=\infty\) and \(y\le N\), \(\psi^*_\infty(y)=\sup_t(ty-N(t-1)_+)=y\). Since \(\log(1+y)\ge1\), \(\psi^*_{\alpha_j}(y)\le y(\log(1+y))^{\beta}\) for both \(j\). Gradient: \(|\cdot|_\infty\) has gradient \((\pm1,0)\) or \((0,\pm1)\) almost everywhere, so each \(P_i\) has, almost everywhere on \(\{P_i>0\}\), one partial \(\pm y\) and the other \(0\). For Lipschitz \(f,g\), \(\nabla\max(f,g)=\nabla f\) almost everywhere on \(\{f\ge g\}\) (on \(\{f=g\}\), \(\nabla(f-g)=0\) almost everywhere), so by induction almost everywhere \(\nabla G=\nabla P_k\) for an index \(k\) with \(P_k=G\), and \(\nabla G=0\) almost everywhere on \(\{G=0\}\): the gradient claim. Cost: \(\{\nabla G\ne0\}\) lies in the union of the squares \(|z-x_i|_\infty<r\), of area at most \(4Nr^2\), and \(\psi^*(0)=0\), so the cost is at most \(4Nr^2y(\log(1+y))^{\beta}=2\). Discrepancy: \(G(x_i)\ge P_i(x_i)=a\), so \(\sum_iG(x_i)\ge Na\); \(G\le\sum_iP_i\) and \(\int P_i\le\frac43r^2a\) (a square pyramid of base \(4r^2\) and height \(a\)), so \(N\int G\le\frac43N^2r^2a=\frac43Na\cdot\frac1{2y(\log(1+y))^{\beta}}\le\frac13Na\) for \(y\ge2\). Hence the difference is at least \(\frac23Na\), and \(Na=Nyr=\sqrt{Ny/2}\,(\log(1+y))^{-\beta/2}\). The consequences: let \(y\to\infty\) (or \(y=N\)); at \((4,4)\), \(\beta=\frac14\), and at \(y=(\log N)^2\) the ratio \(\frac{\sqrt2}3\log N(\log(1+(\log N)^2))^{-1/8}/(L'\sqrt{\log N})\) tends to infinity. \(\square\)

Hypotheses, each with its step. \(\alpha_j\ge1\): \(\psi_\alpha'(t_0)\ge1+y\) and the convexity of \(\psi_\alpha\); the curve's pairs, in \([2,\infty]^2\), are covered with \(\beta\le\frac12\). \(y\ge2\): \(\log(1+y)\ge1\), used for \(t_0\ge1\), for comparing the two conjugates, and for \(N\int G\le\frac13Na\). \(y\le N\) when an exponent is infinite: \(\psi^*_\infty(y)\) finite. Points in the square: \(G(x_i)\) is defined and at least \(a\). No randomness is used: the conclusion holds for every point set, against Lebesgue measure.

Baseline. The plainest bound for one function is \(|\sum_iG(x_i)-N\int G|\le N\|G\|_\infty\), which is \(Na\) here: the pyramids attain it up to the factor \(\frac23\), so nothing is lost to cancellation; and the plainest lower bound for the class is lem:lipschitz-class-lower-bound's \(\sqrt{N\log N}\) order, which needs random points. The plainest construction is one spike at one point, of radius \((2y(\log(1+y))^{\beta})^{-1/2}\): its discrepancy is at least \(a(1-\frac23N/(y(\log(1+y))^{\beta}))\), unbounded as \(y\to\infty\) for finite exponents but only once \(y\gg N\). What the \(N\) pyramids add is reaching levels of order \(\log N(\log\log N)^{1/4}\) at \((4,4)\). What the lemma adds: against Lebesgue measure the class is unbounded for every point set when both exponents are finite, and at \((4,4)\) the single-level form fails from levels of order \(\log N\,(\log\log N)^{1/4}\) on.

Degenerate cases. \(N=1\): one pyramid, difference at least \(\frac{\sqrt2}3\sqrt y(\log(1+y))^{-\beta/2}\), unbounded in \(y\). Coinciding points: the maximum takes one pyramid, \(G(x_i)\ge a\) still holds and the cost only drops. Points at the boundary: the pyramid is cut by the square, which lowers \(\int G\) and the cost. \(y<2\): excluded; there the cost bound needs \((\log(1+y))^{\beta}\) replaced by \(1\), and the difference \(\sqrt{Ny/2}\) is below \(\sqrt N\), within the conjectured order.

Nonvacuity. On the curve's parameters at \((4,4)\), \(\beta=\frac14\), level \(y=(\log N)^2\) (at least \(2\) for \(N\ge5\), finite exponents so no cap): \(r=(2N(\log N)^2(\log(1+(\log N)^2))^{1/4})^{-1/2}\), \(a=yr\), cost at most \(2\), the larger partial exactly \(y\) where the gradient is nonzero, and difference at least \(\frac{\sqrt2}3\sqrt N\log N\,(\log(1+(\log N)^2))^{-1/8}\), which divided by \(\sqrt{N\log N}\) is \(\frac{\sqrt2}3\sqrt{\log N}(\log(1+(\log N)^2))^{-1/8}\to\infty\) as \(N\) grows. Plainest bound. For this fixed function the trivial bound \(N\|G\|_\infty=Na\) already holds, and is attained up to the factor \(\frac23\); the lemma's content is that \(Na\) is unbounded over the class at fixed cost, for every point set.

Consequences for the route

Correction to the fourth route review. Its decisive test's outcome (A), the single-level case closed against Lebesgue measure for every single-level class function at \((4,4)\), cannot occur at levels \(y\) of order \((\log N)^2\) or more, for any operation and any point set, by the lemma. The pyramids realize the conclusion of its outcome (C), a counterexample refuting only the sufficient statement, here its Lebesgue form, by a mechanism (C) did not name (functions concentrated at the points, not varying spacing); and the mollified split found an outcome the review did not list, the operation failing for a reason of its own.

Smeared form. The conjecture's class bound is for the cell-smeared \(\mu_X-\mu_Y\), each point spread over its cell of side \(\delta=1/\lceil32/s\rceil\) of the reduction's grid; since \(\int G\,d\mu_X=\sum_i(E_\delta G)(X_i)\), \(E_\delta G\) the cell averages, and \(\int E_\delta G=\int G\), the \(X\)-term of the smeared discrepancy is the Lebesgue discrepancy of \(E_\delta G\), a function constant on the cells. The pyramids are harmless after smearing: \(r\le(4N)^{-1/2}<\delta\) for \(L\ge132\) and \(N\ge2\), so \(P_k\) meets the cell \(Q(X_i)\) only if \(X_k\) lies in the block \(Q(X_i)^+\) of nine cells around it, and \(\int G\,d\mu_X\le\delta^{-2}\frac43r^2a\,\#\{(i,k):X_k\in Q(X_i)^+\}\le\frac43Na\,r^2n^+/\delta^2\), \(n^+\) the largest count of a nine-cell block; with \(r^2=1/(2Ny(\log(1+y))^{\beta})\) and \(m=N\delta^2\) this is \(\frac23Na\,(n^+/m)/(y(\log(1+y))^{\beta})=\frac{\sqrt2}3\sqrt{N/y}\,(\log(1+y))^{-3\beta/2}\,n^+/m\), and the \(Y\)-term is nonnegative and bounded the same way with the counts of \(Y\), so the pyramids' smeared discrepancy is \(O(\sqrt{N/y}\,n^+/m)\), of order \(\sqrt{N/y}\) on the event that the block counts are of order \(m\) (conditional here; for uniform points it holds with probability tending to one by a Chernoff bound, \(m\asymp\log N\), not written out). Smearing removes structure below \(\delta\); it does not cap levels: a slope \(y\) across whole cells survives averaging. The reduction to the grid (the reviewer's computation, checked here): for neighbouring cells \(Q,Q'=Q+\delta e_j\), \(|E_QG-E_{Q'}G|\le\delta^{-2}\int_Q\int_0^\delta|\partial_jG(z+te_j)|\,dt\,dz\le\delta^{-1}\int_{Q\cup Q'}|\partial_jG|\), so with \(g=E_\delta G\) and \(D_jg\) its increment divided by \(\delta\), \(|D_jg|/2\) is at most the average of \(|\partial_jG|\) over \(Q\cup Q'\), and by Jensen's inequality and each cell lying in at most two edges of each direction, \(\sum_{\text{edges}}\delta^2\psi^*_{\alpha_j}(|D_jg|/2)\le\int\psi^*_{\alpha_j}(|\partial_jG|)\). So the smeared \(X\)-term is at most the supremum of \(\sum_Q(n_Q-m)g_Q\) over grid functions with \(\sum\delta^2\sum_j\psi^*_{\alpha_j}(|D_jg|/2)\le2\), a discrete class with about \(m\asymp\log N\) points per cell; the remainder below \(2^{-j^*(y)}\) is to be bounded there.

Fine-grid Leighton–Shor bound for unions of cells

16 October 2026 · Working proof; dyadic grids · Discrete class. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort set by the session).

Where we stand. Unchanged: The entry adds a bound in the discrete class; the goal's state in Where we stand is unchanged.

Question. The sample-point pyramids entry reduced the smeared \(X\)-term of conj:conjugate-class-discrepancy to a discrete class: grid functions \(g\) on the cells of side \(\delta\) against the centred counts \(n_Q-m\), with \(\sum_{\text{edges}}\delta^2\sum_j\psi^*_{\alpha_j}(|D_jg|/2)\le2\). The missing implication is the class bound; this entry asks what the Leighton–Shor bound gives in that class, below the Leighton–Shor mesh, where the recorded mesh lemmas stop, and at which increment levels it already reaches the conjectured order.

Target form. The goal's form is the class bound for the cell-smeared \(\mu_X-\mu_Y\); the working form is its \(X\)-term, the discrete class on a dyadic grid, against Lebesgue measure through the cell counts; it adds the restriction to a dyadic grid side (the reduction's side \(1/\lceil32/s\rceil\) is not dyadic) and leaves the \(Y\)-term aside.

Chosen. The chaining lead entry-2026-10-16-fourth-route-review:2, not the queue head sandpile-odometer-flow: it bears directly on conjugate-class-discrepancy, whose smeared form the previous entry reduced to the discrete class, and this is the item's last entry before its spell boundary.

General statement. lem:fine-grid-leighton-shor, for every fixed \(\kappa>0\), every dyadic grid side between \(\kappa\sqrt{\log N/N}\) and the Leighton–Shor mesh, every union of cells, and every function constant on the cells.

Fine-grid Leighton–Shor bound

Statement. Let \(X_1,\dots,X_N\) be i.i.d. uniform on \([0,1]^2\), \(\ell_1\) the Leighton–Shor scale (\(2^{-\ell_1}\ge(\log N)^{3/4}/\sqrt N\), \(\ell_1\) largest), \(\kappa>0\) fixed and \(s_0=\kappa\sqrt{\log N/N}\). There is \(L\) depending only on \(\kappa\) such that with probability tending to one, for every dyadic \(\delta_0=2^{-k}\) with \(s_0\le\delta_0\le2^{-\ell_1}\): (a) every union \(A\) of cells of side \(\delta_0\) has \[\Big|\#\{i:X_i\in A\}-N\lambda(A)\Big|\le L\sqrt N\,(\log N)^{3/4}\,P(A),\] \(P(A)\) the total length of the inner edges of the grid separating a cell of \(A\) from a cell outside \(A\); (b) every \(g\) constant on the cells has \(|\sum_ig(X_i)-N\int g|\le L\sqrt N(\log N)^{3/4}\,\mathrm{TV}(g)\), \(\mathrm{TV}(g)=\sum_e\delta_0|\Delta_eg|\) over the inner edges; (c) at \((4,4)\), if every increment satisfies \(|\Delta_eg|/\delta_0\in\{0\}\cup[y,\infty)\) with \(y\ge2e^{16}\) and \(\sum_e\delta_0^2\psi^*_4(|\Delta_eg|/(2\delta_0))\le2\), then \(\mathrm{TV}(g)\le8(\log(y/2))^{-1/4}\) and \(|\sum_ig(X_i)-N\int g|\le8L\sqrt N(\log N)^{3/4}(\log(y/2))^{-1/4}\); in particular for \(y\ge N^c\), \(0<c\le1\), this is at most \(8\cdot3^{1/4}c^{-1/4}L\sqrt{N\log N}\) for \(N\) large.

Proof. Events. (E1) The event of lem:mesh-function-discrepancy at \(j=\ell_1\). (E2) Every cell \(C\) of side \(2^{-\ell_1}\) has \(n_C\le2\mu\), \(\mu=N4^{-\ell_1}\): \(\mu\ge(\log N)^{3/2}\), so by the Chernoff bound \(\Pr(n_C>2\mu)\le e^{-\mu/3}\), and a union over at most \(4^{\ell_1}\le N\) cells. (E3) Conditionally on the counts \((n_C)\), the points of different coarse cells are independent and uniform in their cells (the multinomial's conditional law); for each coarse cell \(C\) and each union \(B\) of fine cells inside \(C\), \(p=\lambda(B)/\lambda(C)\), the count \(\#(X\cap B)\) is binomial \((n_C,p)\), and Bernstein's inequality gives \(|\#(X\cap B)-n_Cp|\le\sqrt{2n_Ct}+t\) except with probability \(2e^{-t}\). A coarse cell holds \(q=(2^{-\ell_1}/\delta_0)^2\le\frac4{\kappa^2}\sqrt{\log N}\) fine cells (as \(2^{-\ell_1}<2(\log N)^{3/4}/\sqrt N\) and \(\delta_0\ge s_0\)), so the union over the dyadic \(\delta_0\) (at most \(\log_2N\)), the coarse cells (at most \(N\)) and the \(2^q\) sets \(B\) has at most \(N^{1+o(1)}\) members; take \(t=4\log N\), so the failure probability is \(O(N^{-3+o(1)})\). On (E2) and (E3), \(|\#(X\cap B)-n_Cp|\le\sqrt{16\mu\log N}+4\log N\le8\sqrt{\mu\log N}\le16(\log N)^{5/4}\), using \(\log N\le\mu\le4(\log N)^{3/2}\).

(a) Let \(H=E_{\ell_1}1_A\), the averages of \(1_A\) on the coarse cells, \(p_C=H_C\). Then \(1_A-H\) has, on each coarse cell, discrepancy \(\#(X\cap A\cap C)-N\lambda(A\cap C)-p_C(n_C-N\lambda(C))=\#(X\cap A\cap C)-n_Cp_C\), which vanishes unless \(0<p_C<1\). Such a cut cell contains fine cells of \(A\) and of its complement, so an edge of \(\partial A\) between two of its fine cells, inside it; these edges are distinct for distinct cells, so there are at most \(P(A)/\delta_0\) cut cells, and by (E3) \(|\sum_i(1_A-H)(X_i)-N\int(1_A-H)|\le16(\log N)^{5/4}P(A)/\delta_0\le\frac{16}\kappa\sqrt N(\log N)^{3/4}P(A)\), as \(\delta_0\ge\kappa\sqrt{\log N/N}\). For \(H\): by lem:mesh-function-discrepancy (b) and (c), \(|\sum_iH(X_i)-N\int H|\le L\sqrt N(\ell_1^{3/4}+\sqrt{\log N})\cdot4V^{\mathrm{in}}_{\ell_1}(H)\). For coarse cells \(C,C'=C+we\) side by side, \(w=2^{-\ell_1}\), \(|H_C-H_{C'}|=w^{-2}|\int_C(1_A(z)-1_A(z+we))\,dz|\le w^{-2}\cdot w\cdot\ell_\perp\), so \(w|H_C-H_{C'}|\le w^{-1}\int_C|1_A(z)-1_A(z+we)|\,dz\). Summing over all pairs of direction \(e\), the sets \(C\) are disjoint, and by Fubini along the lines parallel to \(e\), each segment \([z,z+we]\) with \(1_A(z)\ne1_A(z+we)\) crossing an edge of \(\partial A\) perpendicular to \(e\), the total is at most \(w^{-1}\cdot w\cdot\ell_e\), \(\ell_e\) the length of those edges (the reviewer's global count, which replaces a per-pair count that miscounted edges on coarse-cell sides); over both directions \(V^{\mathrm{in}}_{\ell_1}(H)\le P(A)\). With \(\ell_1\le\log_2N\), (a) follows. (b) With \(c=\min g\), \(g-c=\int_c^\infty1_{\{g>t\}}dt\), constants have no discrepancy, each \(\{g>t\}\) is a union of cells, and \(\int P(\{g>t\})\,dt=\sum_e\delta_0|\Delta_eg|\); apply (a) under the integral. (c) Where \(\Delta_eg\ne0\), \(u=|\Delta_eg|/(2\delta_0)\ge y/2\ge e^{16}\), and the recorded lower bound \(\psi^*_4(u)\ge\frac12u(\log u)^{1/4}\) for \(u\ge e^{16}\) gives \(\delta_0|\Delta_eg|=2\delta_0^2u\le4\delta_0^2\psi^*_4(u)(\log(y/2))^{-1/4}\); summing, \(\mathrm{TV}(g)\le8(\log(y/2))^{-1/4}\), and (b). For \(y\ge N^c\), \(\log(y/2)\ge\frac c3\log N\) for \(N\) large. \(\square\)

Hypotheses, each with its step. \(\delta_0\ge\kappa\sqrt{\log N/N}\), any fixed \(\kappa>0\) (more general than the first draft's \(\kappa=3\); the reviewer's observation): at most \(\frac4{\kappa^2}\sqrt{\log N}\) fine cells per coarse cell, so the union over their subsets is affordable, and the conversion of \(P/\delta_0\) cut cells into \(\frac{16}\kappa\sqrt N(\log N)^{3/4}P\); \(L\) depends on \(\kappa\). The reduction's grid side \(1/\lceil32/s\rceil\), \(s=L_{\mathrm{red}}\sqrt{\log N/N}\) with the reduction's constant \(L_{\mathrm{red}}\ge132\) (cor:exponential-matching-discrepancy-reduction), is at least \(4\sqrt{\log N/N}\) and below \(2^{-\ell_1}\) for large \(N\), so it satisfies the side bound with \(\kappa=4\), but it is not dyadic. \(\delta_0\le2^{-\ell_1}\): the fine cells nest in the coarse ones. Dyadic \(\delta_0\): the nesting. Independence: the points i.i.d. uniform, used through the multinomial counts' conditional law in (E3) and through lem:mesh-function-discrepancy. \(y\ge2e^{16}\) in (c): the range of the recorded lower bound of \(\psi^*_4\). Conclusions: (a) and (b) for every union and every grid function at every such \(\delta_0\) simultaneously; (c) for the grid functions of increment level at least \(y\) under the discrete cost at \((4,4)\).

Baseline. The plainest recorded bound for unions of cells is lem:tube-localized-discrepancy (a), at meshes up to the Leighton–Shor scale; below it, the plainest bound approximates \(A\) by its coarse averages \(H\) and charges each coarse cell met by \(\partial A\) its whole count, at most \(3\mu\le6\sqrt N(\log N)^{3/4}2^{-\ell_1}\) per cell. For a set whose boundary has few components this is \(O(\sqrt N(\log N)^{3/4}P)\), the standard Leighton–Shor bound plus a coarse approximation; for a boundary with \(K\) components it costs \(\sqrt N(\log N)^{3/4}(P+K2^{-\ell_1})\), and as each component has length at least \(4\delta_0\), \(K2^{-\ell_1}\) can reach \(P(\log N)^{1/4}/6\) (for \(\kappa=3\)): the plainest bound loses a factor \((\log N)^{1/4}\) on sets made of many small components. The lemma's new content is that many-component case: the union over the subsets of the at most \(\frac4{\kappa^2}\sqrt{\log N}\) fine cells of a coarse cell, the conditional multinomial mechanism of lem:band-family-discrepancy (a) applied to all subsets, costs only \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log N})}\) and charges a cut cell \((\log N)^{5/4}\) instead of \((\log N)^{3/2}\).

Degenerate cases. \(A\) empty or the whole square: \(P(A)=0\) and both sides vanish. \(\delta_0=2^{-\ell_1}\): no cut cells, and (a) is lem:mesh-function-discrepancy (b) for an indicator. \(g\) constant: \(\mathrm{TV}=0\), no discrepancy. In (c) a grid function with no nonzero increment is constant; with exactly one cell raised, its four increments carry the whole cost.

Nonvacuity. On the curve's parameters at \((4,4)\), for (c) with \(c=\frac12\): \(\delta_0\) the dyadic number in \([s_0,2s_0)\), which is at most \(2^{-\ell_1}\) once \((\log N)^{1/4}>12\), true for all large \(N\); \(y=\sqrt N\ge2e^{16}\); \(A\) a square block of fine cells of side \(b\) (a multiple of \(\delta_0\)) with \(4b=P\), \(P=2/(\delta_0\psi^*_4(y/2))\) rounded down to a multiple of \(4\delta_0\), and \(g=y\delta_0\,1_A\): every increment is \(0\) or \(y\delta_0\), so \(|\Delta_eg|/\delta_0\in\{0,y\}\), and the cost is \((P/\delta_0)\delta_0^2\psi^*_4(y/2)\le2\). Here \(\psi^*_4(\sqrt N/2)\le\frac{\sqrt N}2(\log(1+\sqrt N/2))^{1/4}\), so \(P\ge4/(\delta_0\sqrt N(\log N)^{1/4})-4\delta_0\), which is at least \(4\delta_0\) (so \(A\) is nonempty) because \(\delta_0^2\sqrt N(\log N)^{1/4}\le36(\log N)^{5/4}/\sqrt N\to0\). (c) gives \(|\sum_ig(X_i)-N\int g|\le8\cdot6^{1/4}L\sqrt{N\log N}\). Plainest bound. For this one fixed block the variance bound gives \(y\delta_0\sqrt{N\lambda(A)}\), far smaller; uniformly over blocks and all sets of the same perimeter the plainest bound is the coarse-mesh one of the Baseline, which on a set of \(P/(4\delta_0)\) separated fine cells costs \((\log N)^{1/4}\) more than (a); and a bound by the counts alone, \(y\delta_0\sum_{Q\in A}|n_Q-m|\le y\delta_0(b^2/\delta_0^2)\,C\log N\), is with \(b\approx1/(3(\log N)^{3/4})\) and \(\delta_0\approx3\sqrt{\log N/N}\) of order \(N/(27\log N)\), far above \(\sqrt{N\log N}\), while (a) gives \(y\delta_0L\sqrt N(\log N)^{3/4}P\approx4L\sqrt{N\log N}\); the lemma's content is the uniformity over all unions of cells.

What the bound reaches

Levels. Balanced sandpile flow is electrical

16 October 2026 · Working proof; stabilizing odometers · Sandpile flow. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort set by the session).

Where we stand. Unchanged: The entry decides the premise of a queued item; the goal's state in Where we stand is unchanged.

Question. The queue head sandpile-odometer-flow asks to simulate the divisible-sandpile odometer flow of the excess of \(X\) over the background and compare its per-point tails with the dyadic flow's, as "a nonlinear flow that moves mass only where needed", a candidate against the Gaussian per-point obstacle of thm:dyadic-flow-obstruction. The missing implication is a flow whose per-point values have lighter than Gaussian tails at the scale \(\sqrt{N\log N}\), which lem:flow-matching-bound would turn into the conjecture's conclusion at a pair of the curve. Before any simulation, this entry asks whether the odometer flow is nonlinear at all in the balanced setting a perfect matching needs.

Target form. The goal's form is the primal form of conj:conjugate-class-discrepancy: a field \(\Phi\) with the divergence of \(\nu_X-\nu_Y\) and \(\int\sum_k\psi_{\alpha_k}(|\Phi_k|/(\lambda's))\) of order one per point (lem:flow-matching-bound); the working form is a flow on the graph of grid cells carrying the cell counts to a uniform background, which adds the discretization to cells and leaves the within-cell field aside.

General statement. lem:balanced-sandpile-flow, for every finite set with a reversible irreducible splitting rule and every balanced initial mass and thresholds.

Balanced sandpile flow

Statement. Let \(V\) be finite, \(P=(p(x,y))\) a stochastic matrix on \(V\), irreducible and reversible with respect to \(\pi>0\) (\(\pi(x)p(x,y)=\pi(y)p(y,x)\)), and \(c(x,y)=\pi(x)p(x,y)\) the conductances; let \(\eta,t:V\to\mathbb R\) with \(\sum_xt(x)=\sum_x\eta(x)\) (balanced). Call an odometer any \(v:V\to[0,\infty)\) whose final configuration \(\eta'(x)=\eta(x)-v(x)+\sum_yv(y)p(y,x)\) satisfies \(\eta'\le t\): the divisible sandpile in which site \(x\) emits mass \(v(x)\) in total, split by \(p(x,\cdot)\), ends stable below the thresholds \(t\). Then (a) every odometer has \(\eta'\equiv t\); (b) its net flow \(\theta(x,y)=v(x)p(x,y)-v(y)p(y,x)\) equals \(c(x,y)(u(x)-u(y))\) for any solution \(u\) of \(\sum_yc(x,y)(u(x)-u(y))=\eta(x)-t(x)\), so it is the same for every odometer, linear in \(\eta-t\), and it is the electrical flow with conductances \(c\), the least-energy flow \(\sum\theta^2/c\) carrying \(\eta\) to \(t\); (c) odometers exist: \(v=\pi\,(u-\min u)\). Equal splitting on a connected graph (\(p(x,y)=1/\deg x\), \(\pi\propto\deg\), constant conductances) with \(t\equiv1\) and \(\sum\eta=|V|\) is the case the item names. The conclusion holds for every odometer whose final configuration is stable; whether a given sequence of legal topplings converges to one (as Levine and Peres's odometer, the limit of legal topplings, does when it is finite; not read in this cycle) is not used.

Proof. (a) \(\sum_x\sum_yv(y)p(y,x)=\sum_yv(y)\) since \(P\) is stochastic, so \(\sum\eta'=\sum\eta=\sum t\); with \(\eta'\le t\) at every site, \(\eta'\equiv t\). (b) By (a), \(v(x)-\sum_yv(y)p(y,x)=\eta(x)-t(x)\). With \(u=v/\pi\): \(v(y)p(y,x)=u(y)c(y,x)=u(y)c(x,y)\) by reversibility, and \(v(x)=u(x)\pi(x)=u(x)\sum_yc(x,y)\); so \(\sum_yc(x,y)(u(x)-u(y))=\eta(x)-t(x)\), the weighted Laplacian equation. Its kernel is the constants, since \(P\) is irreducible, so the graph of positive conductances is connected; it is solvable since \(\sum(\eta-t)=0\) and the weighted Laplacian is symmetric. So \(u\) is determined up to a constant, and \(\theta(x,y)=u(x)\pi(x)p(x,y)-u(y)\pi(y)p(y,x)=c(x,y)(u(x)-u(y))\) is determined. Least energy: another flow from \(\eta\) to \(t\) is \(\theta+\gamma\), \(\gamma\) antisymmetric and divergence-free, and \(\sum_{\{x,y\}}\theta\gamma/c=\sum_{\{x,y\}}(u(x)-u(y))\gamma(x,y)=\sum_xu(x)\sum_y\gamma(x,y)=0\), so its energy is \(\sum\theta^2/c+\sum\gamma^2/c\). (c) \(u-\min u\ge0\) solves the same equation, and \(v=\pi(u-\min u)\) gives \(\eta'=t\). \(\square\)

Hypotheses, each with its step. \(\sum t=\sum\eta\) (balanced): (a), where a stable configuration of the same total is forced to equal \(t\); with slack, \(\sum t>\sum\eta\), the final configuration has free sites and the odometer solves an obstacle problem, which is nonlinear. Reversibility: \(v(y)p(y,x)=u(y)c(x,y)\) in (b); for a non-reversible \(P\) the odometers differ by multiples of the stationary vector, and the net flows by the divergence-free circulation \(\pi(x)p(x,y)-\pi(y)p(y,x)\) times a constant, so the flow is unique only up to that circulation. Irreducibility: uniqueness of \(u\) up to a constant. With a non-reversible rule the least odometer adds the multiple \(-\min(v_0/\pi)\) of \(\pi\), which is not linear in \(\eta\), so even an equal-mass fixed rule with drift gives a flow nonlinear in the data: the electrical part plus a nonlinear multiple of a fixed circulation (the reviewer's observation). \(\eta\ge0\): not used; (a)–(c) hold for every real \(\eta\) and \(t\) with equal sums. Conclusion for every balanced initial mass and every reversible irreducible splitting rule on a finite set, deterministic. More general than the first draft's equal splitting with threshold \(1\) (the reviewer's observation, with reversibility added as the step (b) needs).

Baseline. The plainest reading of the item takes the odometer flow as a new nonlinear flow to be simulated; the plainest bound on any flow from the record is thm:dyadic-flow-obstruction, which concerns the dyadic flow only (its assessment: "for a general fixed kernel the concentration over points is not proved"). What the lemma adds: in the balanced setting the odometer flow is no new object; it is the electrical flow, a linear flow with a fixed kernel, so the item becomes the question whether that one linear flow's per-point values have lighter than Gaussian tails, and the simulation it asked for is not needed to see that it does not move mass "only where needed".

Degenerate cases. \(\eta=t\): \(u\) constant, no flow, the odometers are the multiples of \(\pi\). One site: no edges, \(\eta=t\). A reducible \(P\): (b) fails across classes unless each closed class carries its own balance, and then holds on each.

Nonvacuity. On the curve's parameters, at every pair: \(G\) the 4-neighbour graph of the cells of side \(\delta=1/\lceil32/s\rceil\) of the reduction's grid, \(M=\delta^{-2}\) cells, \(\eta(Q)=n_Q/m\) with \(m=N/M\), so \(\sum\eta=M\) for every \(N\); (c) gives an odometer for every sample, and (a), (b) apply. Plainest bound. For one fixed sample the flow is one explicit vector, decided by solving one linear system; the lemma's content is that the flow is linear for every sample and every toppling order, so the per-point law of the item's flow is that of a fixed linear kernel applied to the centred counts.

What it decides

The item's premise. The item's source, the first route review's Levine–Peres bridge, read the odometer as solving an obstacle problem, "a flow nonlinear in the data"; in Levine and Peres's setting the nonlinearity comes from an unbounded domain, mass on \(\mathbb Z^d\) spreading into free space, which gives a free boundary and not a transport onto the square's uniform measure, so it cannot give a perfect matching. On the square, with the counts as mass and the uniform measure as thresholds, the sandpile is balanced, and by the lemma its flow is the electrical flow, a linear functional of \(n_Q-m\), fixed for each reversible splitting rule (each rule has its own conductances) and the same for every stabilizing odometer; a signed reading (holes as negative mass) is balanced too and gives the same flow. Nonlinearity needs slack (thresholds above \(m\)), followed by a second transport filling the deficit, or a splitting rule that depends on the state (mass sent only to neighbours below their threshold). Every balanced transport flow, linear or not, is the electrical flow plus a divergence-free circulation (the lemma's least-energy step), which is the class ex:greedy-circulation-tails probed for the dyadic flow.

The claim search does not read review text: the reviewer found, and this cycle then read, the first route review's Levine–Peres bridge (the item's source) and Holtsmark bridge, and the fourth route review's Holtsmark item (falsified: linear flows Gaussian per point by Lindeberg) and the third route review's Ambrosio–Stra–Trevisan lead (a linear heat-regularized Poisson flow). tools/claim_resemblance.py on the spec: nearest scores 0.12 and below, claims of other notebooks (charged expanders, cube ideals), none a version of this one.

New mathematics. lem:balanced-sandpile-flow: for every balanced initial mass and every reversible irreducible splitting rule on a finite set, every divisible-sandpile odometer whose final configuration is stable ends at the thresholds, and its net flow is the electrical flow with the rule's conductances, the same for every such odometer and linear in the mass; so the queued candidate, on the square with the uniform thresholds, is a fixed linear flow, and every balanced transport flow is that flow plus a divergence-free circulation.

Follow-up

Follow-up. Continuing. For the linear flow, the record already holds the per-point argument: the fourth route review's Holtsmark bridge, falsified, found a flow linear in the data with per-point variance of order \(N\log N\) Gaussian at bounded \(u\) by the Lindeberg theorem ("a primal route needs an adaptive flow"), a sketch whose concentration over points, as for thm:dyadic-flow-obstruction, is not proved. So the item's translation bears on conjugate-class-discrepancy only through its nonlinear versions. Next attempt: the state-dependent sandpile on the cells, mass sent only to neighbours below their threshold, written by the lemma's (a) and least-energy step as the electrical flow plus a divergence-free circulation, and the question whether that circulation lightens the per-point tails, as the greedy circulation of ex:greedy-circulation-tails did not at reachable sizes. Smallest case. In one dimension every flow from \(\eta\) to \(t\) is the cumulative excess, so every rule gives the same flow; the smallest case where they differ is the one checked in the Suggestion checked paragraph, a cycle of four cells, where the state-dependent rule's flow is the electrical one plus a circulation of \(0.75\); the attempt's question, whether such circulations lighten per-point tails on the grid, starts from there. Plainest bound. By the least-energy step, every balanced flow has energy at least the electrical flow's, whose per-point variance in cell-mass units is \(m^{-1}\sum_QK(x,Q)^2\), of order \(\log M/m\), bounded at the reduction's grid where \(m\) is of order \(\log N\); a circulation can only add energy, so it can lighten tails only by moving variance between points, which the attempt must show.

Suggestion checked. The reviewer's state-dependent rule, checked here on the smallest case where it can differ from the electrical flow: a cycle of cells \(1,2,3,4\) with masses \((3,1,0,0)\) and thresholds \(1\), excesses \((2,0,-1,-1)\). Every flow carrying them has \(f_{12}+f_{14}=2\), \(f_{23}=f_{12}\), \(f_{43}=f_{14}-1\); the electrical flow minimizes \(2f_{12}^2+f_{14}^2+(f_{14}-1)^2\), giving \(f_{14}=1.25\), \(f_{12}=0.75\); the state-dependent rule sends cell \(1\)'s excess only to cell \(4\), below its threshold (cell \(2\) is at it), so \(f_{14}=2\), then cell \(4\)'s excess \(1\) to cell \(3\), \(f_{12}=0\). Both end at the thresholds, as the lemma's (a) gives for every mass-conserving rule, and they differ by the divergence-free circulation \(0.75\) around the cycle, as the premise paragraph says. One instance does not show that the rule is nonlinear (a linear flow can be the electrical one plus a linear circulation), and the rule is not yet fully specified: the order of topplings, and what a site does when no neighbour is below its threshold (with masses \((2,1,0,1)\) cell \(1\) has none), are left to the next attempt, which must define them and exhibit a failure of additivity before calling the rule nonlinear.

Fifth route review: nested layers and their gaps

16 October 2026 · Route review · Fifth review. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort set by the session).

Where we stand. Unchanged: A route review; the goal's state in Where we stand is unchanged.

Where we stand. Open statements: conj:ultimate-matching and its sufficient form conj:conjugate-class-discrepancy, both open, with the two special-case statements of the list unchanged. The six entries since the fourth route review worked on the class bound's single-level case and on one flow candidate; none changed an implication toward the goal.

The line's general claim. conj:conjugate-class-discrepancy at \((4,4)\) and on the curve: with probability tending to one, every Lipschitz \(G\) with \(\int\sum_j\psi^*_{\alpha_j}(|\partial_jG|)\le2\) has \(\int G\,d(\mu_X-\mu_Y)\le\frac L2\sqrt{N\log N}\), \(\mu\) the cell-smeared measures; by cor:exponential-matching-discrepancy-reduction it gives the conjecture at every pair of the curve.

What the goal needs. The class bound in its smeared form at every pair of the curve, or a matching built directly; the period confirmed that the smearing is not cosmetic (lem:sample-point-pyramids: against Lebesgue measure the class is unbounded for every point set), so every working form must end in the smeared one.

The six entries

  • Tube-localized Leighton–Shor bound (lem:tube-localized-discrepancy): unions of cells localized to tubes at a coarser scale, disjoint band families against Lebesgue measure.
  • Band-family discrepancy (lem:band-family-discrepancy): bands along graphs of bounded slope at every ramp width, against Lebesgue measure.
  • Mollified smooth part (lem:mollified-smooth-part): the review's spacing split fails on a staircase; the smooth part mollified at \(2^{-j^*(y)}\) is bounded, leaving the remainder.
  • Sample-point pyramids (lem:sample-point-pyramids): the Lebesgue form is false; the smeared \(X\)-term reduces to a discrete class on the cells.
  • Fine-grid Leighton–Shor bound (lem:fine-grid-leighton-shor): unions of fine cells and grid functions by total variation; the discrete class at increment levels from \(N^c\) on is bounded at the conjectured order.
  • Balanced sandpile flow (lem:balanced-sandpile-flow): the queued sandpile candidate is the electrical flow, a linear flow.

Falsification attempt. Against the class bound in its discrete form at \((4,4)\), at level \(y=(\log N)^2\), with \(g=y\delta h\), \(h\) integer valued with increments \(1\) or \(2\) (so the cost is that of level \(y\)) and \(\mathrm{TV}(g)\le8(\log(y/2))^{-1/4}\). Three constructions were computed. (i) One union of cells \(A\): its perimeter is \(P=\mathrm{TV}(g)/(y\delta)\gg1\); tiling constructs \(P^2\) Leighton–Shor sets in squares of side \(1/P\) with discrepancy \(\sqrt NP(\log(N/P^2))^{3/4}\), and lem:tube-localized-discrepancy (a) with \(W\) about \(1/P\) bounds every union of perimeter \(P\) at \(L\sqrt N((2\log_2(1/(P\delta))+5)^{3/4}+\sqrt{\log N})\cdot5P\) (the \(W\)-cell term \(4W\#\{W\text{-cells met}\}\) at most \(4P\) here, as the stage-two reviewer computed), a factor of order \((\log y)^{3/4}\) at this level: \(g\)'s discrepancy is of order \(\sqrt N\,\mathrm{TV}(g)((\log y+\log\log N)^{3/4}+\sqrt{\log N})\), below the target. (ii) Nested copies of one Leighton–Shor set shifted cell by cell, \(K=\mathrm{TV}/(y\delta P(A))\) layers within a band of width about \(1/y\) for \(P(A)\) of order one: the copies share the scales above their spacing and lose their optimized fine scales below, so the sum is of order \(\sqrt N\,\mathrm{TV}(g)(\log y)^{3/4}\), below the target. (iii) What would refute: nested layers each keeping independently optimized wiggles at enough scales to carry the full factor \((\log N)^{3/4}\) while spending the whole budget \(K\approx\mathrm{TV}/(y\delta P)\); nesting forbids wiggles larger than the local gap between consecutive boundaries, and the stage-two reviewer showed that layers spread apart (a few nested sets in disjoint annuli) do each carry the full factor, but with a negligible budget. Not decided: (iii) with the full budget is the decisive test below.

Assessment of this line. The period sharpened the line's setting: the smeared form reduces to a discrete class on the cells (a computation in the pyramids entry, not registered), the high levels from \(N^c\) are bounded there, and the Lebesgue lemmas of the earlier periods remain true but serve only through cell averages. The obstacle is the same as at the fourth review, restated in the discrete class: at levels with \(\log y=o(\log N)\) the coarea bound loses \((\log N/\log y)^{1/4}\). Two reviews in a row end on it. The mechanism that would remove it, Leighton–Shor truncated at a scale set by the function, was the fourth review's spacing split, which failed as posed on a staircase because it charged the smooth part on a fine partition; the stage-two reviewer's correction of this review's test names the scale that nesting sets, the local gap between consecutive layers, so the same mechanism is posed again with that scale, its smooth-part charge still the open cancellation inequality.

Obstacle

The line is stuck on nested level sets at one gradient level in the discrete class: for an integer-valued \(h\) whose layers \(\{h>t\}\) are unions of cells, the coarea bound charges each layer the full Leighton–Shor factor \((\log N)^{3/4}\), while the full-budget constructions computed achieve only about \((\log y)^{3/4}\) because nesting forces neighbouring layers to share their wiggles above the local gap between them; no bound yet charges a chain by those gaps.

Outside leads

  • The ellipsoid theorem (Talagrand's [T4] treatment of the Ajtai–Komlós–Tusnády bound through Fourier ellipsoids, read in the monograph reading; the Fourier proof of the matching bound). Targets conj:conjugate-class-discrepancy: if the class lay in an ellipsoid \(\{\sum_kw_k|\hat G(k)|^2\le1\}\) with \(\sum_k1/w_k\) of order \(\log N\) over \(|k|\le\sqrt N\), the class bound would follow with no chaining. Answers. It would bound all nested layers at once, through Fourier coefficients, with no per-layer charge. Test. Falsified. A band of amplitude \(a\), ramp width \(w\) and length one, in the class at level \(y=a/w\) with \(a\le(\log y)^{-1/4}\), has \(\|G\|_{\dot H^s}^2\) of order \(a^2w^{1-2s}\); in the discrete class \(w\ge\delta\), and at \(w=\delta\) this is of order \(\delta^{1-2s}\), unbounded for \(s>\frac12\), so the class lies in no \(\dot H^s\) ball of bounded radius with \(s>\frac12\) (for \(s=1\), the Lipschitz ellipsoid, \(\int|\nabla G|^2=a^2/w\)); scaling the ball to contain the class, or taking \(s\le\frac12\), gives an ellipsoid bound of at least \(\sqrt N\,N^{1/4}\) up to logarithms, far above the target; and \(\sum_{|k|\le\sqrt N}1/w_k\le\log N\) forces weights of order \(|k|^2\), the \(s=1\) case. So no weight sequence does both.
  • García Trillos and Slepčev, "On the rate of convergence of empirical measures in \(\infty\)-transportation distance" (arXiv:1407.1157, Theorems 1.1, 1.2 and the dimension-two theorem read in this cycle): \(d_\infty(\nu,\nu_n)\le C(\ln n)^{3/4}n^{-1/2}\) in dimension two for densities bounded above and below, and a stability bound \(d_\infty(\nu_1,\nu_2)\le C\|\rho_1-\rho_2\|_{L^\infty}\). Targets conj:ultimate-matching through an adaptive transport built by adjusting densities. Answers. A density-adjusting construction is adaptive, the kind the primal obstacle needs. Test. Not run: the computation made tests the stability theorem alone (applied to the empirical measure smoothed at scale \(h\), density error of order \(1/(h\sqrt N)\) plus transport \(h\), it gives at best \(h\approx N^{-1/4}\), far above the scale \(\sqrt{\log N/N}\)), not the translation; the paper's dimension-two proof adapts Talagrand's generic-chaining proof of the Leighton–Shor bound to general densities ("a more subtle approach is needed", its Section 1.2, which credits the constant-density case to Leighton and Shor), and its bound is the maximum-displacement order that thm:maximum-displacement-curve-threshold already gives on the curve; whether its density-adjusting chaining controls per-point tails was not examined. Retrieval. tools/arxiv_source.py 1407.1157 fetched the source, title and authors identified.
  • Goldman, Huesmann and Otto, "A large-scale regularity theory for the Monge–Ampère equation with rough data and application to the optimal matching problem" (arXiv:1808.09250, Theorems 1.1 and 1.3 read in this cycle): in dimension two, for a Poisson process on \(Q_L\), the optimal quadratic map is, on every ball of radius \(\ell\ge2r_*\), close in averaged \(L^2\) to a shift \(x_L\) with \(|x_L|^2\lesssim r_*^2\log^3(L/r_*)\), and \(r_*\) has tails \(\exp(-cr_*^2/\log r_*)\). Targets conj:ultimate-matching through the quadratic-optimal matching. Answers. A large-scale regularity theory controls one matching at all scales at once, which the obstacle of coupled levels asks for. Test. Not run: the theorem is an upper bound in averaged \(L^2\) on balls, and its shift can be of order \((\log N)^{3/2}\) at \(L=\sqrt N\); it neither gives the per-point tails the curve needs nor, being an upper bound, rules them out; that the quadratic map linearizes to the electrical flow and that linear flows are Gaussian per point are the fourth review's sketch and unproved, so no outcome is drawn for the translation. Retrieval. tools/arxiv_source.py 1808.09250 fetched the source, title and authors identified.

Absurd bridges

  • Coulomb gases and screening (statistical mechanics; Serfaty's local laws for two-dimensional Coulomb gases, recalled): the counts of a Coulomb gas in a square of side \(\ell\) fluctuate like the perimeter, not the area. Translation: match \(X\) first to a Coulomb-gas configuration (an intermediate, hyperuniform point set), then the gas to the grid, where hyperuniformity makes the second matching short. Answers. The obstacle's fluctuations would be absorbed in a two-stage matching through a screened configuration. Test. Falsified by the triangle inequality, with no property of the gas beyond its short matching to the grid: the cost from \(X\) to the gas is at least the cost from \(X\) to the grid minus the gas-to-grid cost, so the first stage carries the whole Poisson fluctuation and the obstacle with it.
  • Random coverage (geometric probability; Janson's coverage theorem, recalled): the largest empty disc among \(N\) uniform points has radius about \(\sqrt{\log N/(\pi N)}\), the conjecture's scale. Translation: at level \(t\), a grid point with no sample within \(st^{\beta_j}\) is a point that cannot be matched there. Answers. It would locate the level counts' obstruction in voids. Test. Falsified as a restatement: the void probability \(\exp(-\pi Ns^2t^{2\beta})=N^{-\pi L^2t^{2\beta}}\) is negligible at every level, which is the easy direction of thm:per-level-count-matchings; coverage is per point, and the obstacle is the coupling of levels in one injective matching (lem:per-level-gluing-fails), which coverage does not see.

Picks: no lead and no bridge passed, so none joins the queue.
