Chosen. The chaining lead entry-2026-10-16-fourth-route-review:2, not the queue head sandpile-odometer-flow: its latest follow-up named the attempt this entry makes, it bears directly on conjugate-class-discrepancy, and this is its fourth entry in the spell, after which it rotates.

General statement. lem:guided-chain-bound: part (a) for every union of fine cells, every union of coarse cells as guide and every tube of dyadic cells of side between \(2^{-\ell_1}\) and \(1\) holding their difference; part (b) for every family of at most \(N^c\) unions of coarse cells fixed in advance, every \(c>0\); part (c) for every weighted sum of layers with such guides and tubes; part (d) for every nested chain at \((4,4)\) of such layers, whatever its number of layers, at every level \(y\ge2e^{16}\); all on dyadic grids of side between \(\kappa\sqrt{\log N/N}\) and \(2^{-\ell_1}\).

Guided chains

Setting. As in the cut-cell variance entry: \(X_1,\dots,X_N\) i.i.d. uniform on \([0,1]^2\), \(\ell_1\) the Leighton–Shor scale, \(\kappa>0\) fixed, \(\delta_0\) dyadic with \(\kappa\sqrt{\log N/N}\le\delta_0\le2^{-\ell_1}\), \(D(g)=\sum_ig(X_i)-N\int g\), \(P\) the inner perimeter of a union of cells, \(c_\kappa=\sqrt{10+20/\kappa^2}+\frac5{3\kappa}\), \(L\) the constant of lem:tube-localized-discrepancy, \(\Phi_k=(2(\ell_1-k)+5)^{3/4}+\sqrt{\log N}\). Fine cells have side \(\delta_0\), coarse cells side \(2^{-\ell_1}\), \(W\)-cells side \(W=2^{-k}\), \(0\le k\le\ell_1\). A nested chain at level \(y\) is \(g=y\delta_0\sum_{k\le K}1_{A_k}\), \(A_1\supseteq\dots\supseteq A_K\) unions of fine cells, \(P_k=P(A_k)\); its discrete cost at \((4,4)\) is \(\sum_e\delta_0^2\psi_4^*(|\Delta_eg|/(2\delta_0))\), and \(T=8(\log(y/2))^{-1/4}\).

Statement. Fix \(c>0\) and, for each \(N\), a family \(\mathcal F_N\) of at most \(N^c\) unions of coarse cells, chosen before the points are drawn. With probability tending to one, for every such \(\delta_0\): (a) every union \(A\) of fine cells, every union \(S\) of coarse cells, every \(W=2^{-k}\in[2^{-\ell_1},1]\) and every set \(\mathcal T\) of \(W\)-cells whose union contains \(A\triangle S\) have \[|D(1_A)-D(1_S)|\le c_\kappa\sqrt{N\log N}\,P(A)+L\sqrt N\,\Phi_k\big(P(A)+P(S)+12W\#\mathcal T\big);\] (b) every \(S\in\mathcal F_N\) has \(|D(1_S)|\le P(S)\sqrt{(c+3)N\log N}+(c+3)\log N\); more generally, for every family of \(M_N\ge1\) unions of coarse cells fixed before the points are drawn, with probability tending to one each member has \(|D(1_S)|\le P(S)\sqrt{N(\log M_N+3\log N)}+\log M_N+3\log N\); (c) for every \(\beta>0\), every \(w\in[2^{-\ell_1},1]\) and every finite collection of unions \(A_k\) of fine cells with \(P(A_k)>0\), each with a guide \(S_k\in\mathcal F_N\), a dyadic \(W_k\in[2^{-\ell_1},w]\) and a set \(\mathcal T_k\) of \(W_k\)-cells containing \(A_k\triangle S_k\) such that \(P(S_k)+12W_k\#\mathcal T_k\le\beta P(A_k)\), and all real \(a_k\), \[\Big|D\Big(\sum_ka_k1_{A_k}\Big)\Big|\le C\sqrt N\big((2\log_2(w2^{\ell_1})+5)^{3/4}+\sqrt{\log N}\big)\sum_k|a_k|P(A_k),\qquad C=c_\kappa+L(1+\beta)+\beta\sqrt{c+3}+(c+3)/\kappa;\] (d) at \((4,4)\), a nested chain \(g=y\delta_0\sum_k1_{A_k}\) of such layers at level \(y\ge2e^{16}\) with discrete cost at most \(2\) has \(|D(g)|\le C\sqrt N\,T\big((2\log_2(w2^{\ell_1})+5)^{3/4}+\sqrt{\log N}\big)\), whatever its number of layers, and so \(|D(g)|\le23C\sqrt{N\log N}\) for \(N\) large when moreover \(\log(w2^{\ell_1})\le(\log N)^{2/3}(\log(y/2))^{1/3}\).

Proof. Events: those of lem:cut-cell-variance-bound (its (a) at the coarse mesh, allowed for \(N\) large as \((2^{-\ell_1}/\delta_0)^2\le4\sqrt{\log N}/\kappa^2\le\log N\)), of lem:tube-localized-discrepancy and lem:fine-grid-leighton-shor, and, for (b), the event below. (a) With \(H=E_{2^{-\ell_1}}1_A\), lem:cut-cell-variance-bound (a) gives \(|D(1_A)-D(H)|\le c_\kappa\sqrt{N\log N}\,P(A)\). The coarse cell function \(F=H-1_S\) takes values in \([-1,1]\) and vanishes on every coarse cell \(Q\) outside the union of \(\mathcal T\): such a \(Q\) lies in a \(W\)-cell not in \(\mathcal T\) (the \(W\)-cells are unions of coarse cells), so \(Q\cap(A\triangle S)=\emptyset\), and as \(S\cap Q\) is \(Q\) or empty, \(H_Q=1_S(Q)\). lem:tube-localized-discrepancy (b) with \(j=\ell_1\) gives \(|D(F)|\le L\sqrt N\,\Phi_k\big(V^0_{\ell_1}(F)+4W\sum_{Q\in\mathcal G_k}(\max_QF^++\max_QF^-)\big)\). The inner part of \(V^0_{\ell_1}(F)\) is at most \(V^{\mathrm{in}}(H)+V^{\mathrm{in}}(1_S)\le P(A)+P(S)\), the first by the global Fubini count in the proof of lem:fine-grid-leighton-shor; its boundary ring counts \(|F|\le1\) along the edges on \(\partial[0,1]^2\) of coarse cells inside the union of \(\mathcal T\), at most \(4W\) of such edges per \(W\)-cell (exactly \(4W\) for the one cell at \(W=1\), at most \(2W\) otherwise), so at most \(4W\#\mathcal T\); and the extra term is at most \(4W\cdot2\#\mathcal T\). So \(|D(F)|\le L\sqrt N\,\Phi_k(P(A)+P(S)+12W\#\mathcal T)\), and \(D(1_A)-D(1_S)=(D(1_A)-D(H))+D(F)\). (b) \(\#(X\cap S)\) is binomial \((N,p)\), \(p=\lambda(S)\). The relative isoperimetry of the cut-cell variance entry, applied to the unit square cut into coarse cells, gives \(p(1-p)\le\min(p,1-p)\le P(S)^2/2\), so the variance is at most \(NP(S)^2/2\); Bernstein's inequality with \(t=\log M_N+3\log N\) gives \(|D(1_S)|\le P(S)\sqrt{Nt}+t/3\) except with probability \(2e^{-t}=2N^{-3}/M_N\), and the union over the \(M_N\) members, fixed before the points, fails with probability at most \(2N^{-3}\); \(M_N\le N^c\) gives the first form (no union over \(\delta_0\) is needed, as \(S\) does not depend on it). (c) By linearity \(D(\sum_ka_k1_{A_k})=\sum_ka_kD(1_{A_k})\). For each layer, (a) with \(W_k=2^{-k_k}\le w\), so \(\ell_1-k_k\le\log_2(w2^{\ell_1})\), and (b) give \(|D(1_{A_k})|\le c_\kappa\sqrt{N\log N}\,P_k+L(1+\beta)\sqrt N\,\Phi_wP_k+\beta\sqrt{(c+3)N\log N}\,P_k+(c+3)\log N\), with \(P_k=P(A_k)\) and \(\Phi_w=(2\log_2(w2^{\ell_1})+5)^{3/4}+\sqrt{\log N}\); as \(P_k>0\) forces \(P_k\ge\delta_0\), \((c+3)\log N\le\frac{c+3}\kappa\sqrt{N\log N}\,P_k\). Summing with the weights \(|a_k|\), and \(\sqrt{\log N}\le\Phi_w\), gives (c). (d) Layers with \(P_k=0\) are empty or the whole square and contribute \(0\). As in lem:cut-cell-variance-bound (c), nesting gives \(\mathrm{TV}(g)=y\delta_0\sum_kP_k\), and lem:fine-grid-leighton-shor (c) gives \(\mathrm{TV}(g)\le T\); (c) with \(a_k=y\delta_0\) gives the first bound. For the second, with \(x=\log(w2^{\ell_1})\le(\log N)^{2/3}(\log(y/2))^{1/3}\), \(2\log_2(w2^{\ell_1})=2.885x\), and \((a+b)^{3/4}\le a^{3/4}+b^{3/4}\): \(T(2.885x+5)^{3/4}\le8(\log(y/2))^{-1/4}\big(2.22(\log N)^{1/2}(\log(y/2))^{1/4}+5^{3/4}\big)\le17.8\sqrt{\log N}+13.4\), as \((\log(y/2))^{-1/4}\le\frac12\); with \(T\sqrt{\log N}\le4\sqrt{\log N}\) and \(13.4\le\sqrt{\log N}\) for \(\log N\ge180\), the bracket times \(T\) is at most \(23\sqrt{\log N}\). \(\square\)

Hypotheses, each with its step. Independence and uniformity of the points: the binomial count in (b) and the events of the cited lemmas. \(\delta_0\) dyadic between \(\kappa\sqrt{\log N/N}\) and \(2^{-\ell_1}\): lem:cut-cell-variance-bound (a) at the coarse mesh and lem:fine-grid-leighton-shor (c). \(S\) a union of coarse cells: \(F\) is a cell function of the coarse mesh, as the tube lemma needs, and the relative isoperimetry in (b); \(W\ge2^{-\ell_1}\) dyadic: the tube lemma's \(k\le j=\ell_1\) and the \(W\)-cells as unions of coarse cells. \(\mathcal F_N\) fixed before the points are drawn and of at most \(N^c\) members: the union bound in (b), whose event depends on the family, so the family is fixed before the event; a guide chosen after the points from a larger family is not covered, and (c) uses (b) only through its bound, so any guide satisfying that bound would serve. In (c), \(P(S_k)+12W_k\#\mathcal T_k\le\beta P_k\): to charge the guide and tube terms to the layer's own perimeter; \(W_k\le w\): the factor; \(P(A_k)>0\): the additive \(\log N\) charged to \(P_k\ge\delta_0\); (c) uses neither nesting, nor a level, nor the pair (the reviewer's observation; the first draft stated it for nested chains at \((4,4)\) only, less general than its proof). In (d), the pair \((4,4)\), the cost and \(y\ge2e^{16}\): lem:fine-grid-leighton-shor (c); nesting: \(\mathrm{TV}(g)=y\delta_0\sum_kP_k\); and for the second bound the condition on \(w\) and \(\log N\ge180\). Conclusions: (a) for every union and every guide and tube; (b) for every member of the family; (c) for every weighted sum of guided layers; (d) for every guided nested chain at \((4,4)\), of any number of layers, against Lebesgue measure.

Baseline. For a chain of \(K\) layers the plainest recorded bounds are lem:fine-grid-leighton-shor (b), \(L_f\sqrt N(\log N)^{3/4}T\), the full factor, and lem:cut-cell-variance-bound (c), \(C_b\sqrt NT(2\log_2(Ky^2)+5)^{3/4}\), which is the full factor once \(K\) is polynomial in \(N\); lem:discrete-flow-bound (c) charges chains of multiplicity \(m\) at \(C\sqrt{N\log N}(1+(\log(my))^{1/4})\). For the difference between a layer and its guide, the count that needs no idea is Bernstein in each tube cell with a union over the \(2^{(W/\delta_0)^2}\) unions of its fine cells: \(C\sqrt{N\log N}\,W\#\mathcal T\) when \(W2^{\ell_1}\) is bounded, which with (b) already decides chains with \(w2^{\ell_1}=O(1)\), and a loss of a factor of order \(W2^{\ell_1}\) beyond, where (a) loses \((\log(W2^{\ell_1}))^{3/4}\). Part (c) charges a guided chain by the tube width alone, whatever \(K\): the guides carry the large scales, which (b) charges at \(\sqrt{\log N}\) through a union bound over the family, and the layers' departures from their guides carry only the scales below \(w\).

Degenerate cases. (a) with \(A=S\) a union of coarse cells and \(\mathcal T\) empty: \(D(1_A)-D(1_S)=0\), while the bound is \(c_\kappa\sqrt{N\log N}\,P(S)+2L\sqrt N\Phi_kP(S)\), true and weaker; with \(W=1\), one \(W\)-cell with \(4W\) of the square's boundary: \(\Phi_0\) is the full factor and the bound adds \(12\) to the perimeters, the plainest coarse bound. (b) with \(S\) empty or the square: \(P(S)=0\) and \(D(1_S)=0\le(c+3)\log N\). (c) with \(K=0\): \(g=0\); with every guide equal to its layer (layers unions of coarse cells, \(\mathcal T_k\) empty, \(\beta=1\)): the chain is charged at \(\sqrt{\log N}\) per unit of variation when the layers lie in the family, and \(w=2^{-\ell_1}\) gives the factor \(5^{3/4}+\sqrt{\log N}\).

Nonvacuity. On the curve's parameters at \((4,4)\): \(\kappa=1\), \(\delta_0=2^{-\ell_1-1}\) (in range once \(\log N\ge16\)), \(y=y_N=e^{\sqrt{\log N}}\) (at least \(2e^{16}\) once \(\log N\ge281\)), \(\mathcal F_N\) the rectangles that are unions of coarse cells (at most \(2^{4\ell_1}\le N^2\), so \(c=2\)), and the tube side \(w=W_k=2^{r-\ell_1}\) with \(r=\lceil\log_2\log N\rceil\), so \(\log N\le w2^{\ell_1}<2\log N\). Guides \(S_k=[a_k,1-a_k]^2\), \(a_k=3kw\), unions of coarse cells, side \(s_k=1-2a_k\ge\frac12\) for \(k\le1/(12w)\); \(A_k=S_k\cup R_k\), where \(R_k\) is the union of the fine cells of the ring \(\{x\notin S_k:\mathrm{dist}_\infty(x,S_k)<w\}\) that lie within \(\infty\)-distance \(h_k\) of \(S_k\), \(h_k\) a fine-grid staircase along \(\partial S_k\) rising and falling between \(\delta_0\) and \(w-\delta_0\) with slope one; \(\mathcal T_k\) the \(w\)-cells of the ring, \(\#\mathcal T_k=4s_k/w+4\). The outer boundary of \(R_k\) is a staircase of slope one, of length \(2\) per unit along \(\partial S_k\) up to the corners, so \(7s_k\le8s_k-16w\le P_k\le8s_k+16w\) for \(N\) large; \(P(S_k)+12w\#\mathcal T_k=52s_k+48w\le53s_k\le8P_k\), \(\beta=8\). The ring of \(S_{k+1}\) lies in \([a_k+2w,1-a_k-2w]^2\subset S_k\), so \(A_{k+1}\subseteq S_k\subseteq A_k\), and the boundaries lie in disjoint rings, one through each edge. The cost is \(\delta_0\psi_4^*(y/2)\sum_kP_k\le9K\delta_0\psi_4^*(y/2)\), at most \(2\) for \(K\le K_N=\min(\lfloor2/(9\delta_0\psi_4^*(y/2))\rfloor,\lfloor1/(12w)\rfloor)\); with \(\psi_4^*(y/2)\le e^{\sqrt{\log N}}(\log N)^{1/8}\) and \(1/(12w)\ge2^{\ell_1}/(24\log N)\), \(K_N\) is of order \(N^{1/2-o(1)}\), so \(\log K_N>(\log N)^{2/3}(\log(y/2))^{1/3}=(\log N)^{5/6}\) and \(K_N>N^{1/7}\) for \(N\) large, while \(\log(w2^{\ell_1})\le\log\log N+1\) meets (d)'s condition. At this chain lem:cut-cell-variance-bound (d) does not apply and its (c) gives the factor \((2\log_2(K_Ny^2)+5)^{3/4}\), of order \((\log N)^{3/4}\); lem:discrete-flow-bound (c) (multiplicity one, from \(\log N\ge4096\)) gives \(C\sqrt{N\log N}(\log N)^{1/8}\); (d) gives \(C\sqrt NT((2r+5)^{3/4}+\sqrt{\log N})=O(\sqrt{N\log N}(\log N)^{-1/8})\), and here the tube factor \((2r+5)^{3/4}\) is of order \((\log\log N)^{3/4}\). Plainest bound. For one fixed chain, Bernstein's inequality for \(D(g)\), with variance at most \(N(y\delta_0K_N)^2\) and \(y\delta_0K_N\le\frac{2y}{9\psi_4^*(y/2)}\le\frac T9\) (as \(\psi_4^*(u)\ge\frac12u(\log u)^{1/4}\)), gives at most \(T\sqrt{N\log N}/6\): a fixed witness is decided by a bound for one function, and the statement's content is its uniformity, over every guided chain with these tubes (at most \(\exp(O(\sum_kP_k/\delta_0))\) of them) and over every guided collection. The plainest uniform bound for the tube terms, Bernstein in each \(w\)-cell of \(\mathcal T_k\) with a union over the \(2^{(w/\delta_0)^2}\) unions of its fine cells, charges about \(\sqrt N\,w/\delta_0\approx2\sqrt N\log N\) per unit of tube length, as \((w/\delta_0)^2\approx4(\log N)^2\) exceeds \(\log N\): above the conjectured order, where (a) charges \((\log\log N)^{3/4}\sqrt N\); at \(w=2^{-\ell_1}\), the first draft's witness, that count already decides the tube terms (the reviewer's observation), and (a) adds nothing there.

Architecture test

Architecture test. Not decided. Outcome (A)'s order of the fifth review's test holds for guided chains, on dyadic grids against Lebesgue measure, by (d): nested chains of any number of layers whose layers lie within tubes of width \(w\le2^{-\ell_1}\exp((\log N)^{2/3}(\log(y/2))^{1/3})\) of guides from a family of at most \(N^c\) sets fixed in advance, with guide and tube lengths at most \(\beta\) times each layer's perimeter; the layers' wiggles below \(w\) cost \((\log(w2^{\ell_1}))^{3/4}\) per unit of variation and the guides \(\sqrt{\log N}\). The test's operation, the gap-charged bound for every nested chain, is neither proved nor refuted, and outcome (B) is neither excluded nor exhibited for chains near no such guide.

New mathematics. lem:guided-chain-bound: with probability tending to one, on dyadic grids of side between \(\kappa\sqrt{\log N/N}\) and \(2^{-\ell_1}\), against Lebesgue measure, a union \(A\) of fine cells differing from a union \(S\) of coarse cells only inside a set \(\mathcal T\) of dyadic cells of side \(W\) has discrepancy within \(c_\kappa\sqrt{N\log N}\,P(A)+L\sqrt N((2\log_2(W2^{\ell_1})+5)^{3/4}+\sqrt{\log N})(P(A)+P(S)+12W\#\mathcal T)\) of the guide's; for a family of at most \(N^c\) unions of coarse cells fixed before the points are drawn, each member has discrepancy at most \(P(S)\sqrt{(c+3)N\log N}+(c+3)\log N\); every weighted sum of layers lying within tubes of side at most \(w\) of such guides, with guide and tube lengths at most \(\beta\) times each layer's perimeter, has discrepancy at most \(C\sqrt N((2\log_2(w2^{\ell_1})+5)^{3/4}+\sqrt{\log N})\) times the weighted sum of the perimeters; and at \((4,4)\) such nested chains at level \(y\ge2e^{16}\) and cost at most \(2\), of any number of layers, are at most \(23C\sqrt{N\log N}\) when \(\log(w2^{\ell_1})\le(\log N)^{2/3}(\log(y/2))^{1/3}\).

Follow-up

Reversible sandpile stages are electrical

17 October 2026 · Working proof and an explicit counterexample · Sandpile stages and a deficit-first rule. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort set by the session).

Question. The queue drains, and its head, sandpile-odometer-flow, asks whether a nonlinear sandpile flow that "moves mass only where needed" lightens the per-point tails of the flow carrying the cell counts to the background; the balanced sandpile entry showed every balanced odometer of a fixed splitting kernel gives the electrical flow, and named as next attempt a state-dependent rule, fully defined, with a failure of additivity exhibited before calling it nonlinear; its sub-idea asks whether the slack sandpile, thresholds \((1+\varepsilon)m\), followed by a second transport, beats the electrical flow's per-point tails. The missing implication is conj:conjugate-class-discrepancy, through the primal route of lem:flow-matching-bound: a flow with light per-point tails would give the goal at \((4,4)\).

Target form. The goal's form is the class bound for the cell-smeared \(\mu_X-\mu_Y\) on the reduction's grid; this entry works on flows carrying the cell counts of \(X\) to the uniform background on that grid, the primal side of lem:flow-matching-bound, and bounds nothing in the goal's form itself.

General statement. lem:idle-slack-sandpile: part (a) for every finite set, every reversible splitting rule and every finite sequence of divisible-sandpile stages with any thresholds; part (b) an explicit counterexample to additivity for the deficit-first rule; part (c) for every grid of square cells with \(1/\delta\) an integer and every slack.

Sandpile stages and the deficit-first rule

Setting. As in lem:balanced-sandpile-flow: \(V\) finite, \(P\) a stochastic matrix on \(V\), irreducible and reversible with respect to \(\pi>0\), conductances \(c(x,y)=\pi(x)p(x,y)\). A stage is a divisible-sandpile odometer \(v\ge0\) for some thresholds: site \(x\) emits mass \(v(x)\) in total, split by \(p(x,\cdot)\); its net flow is \(\theta(x,y)=v(x)p(x,y)-v(y)p(y,x)\), and it carries the initial configuration to the final one \(\eta-v+vP\). The deficit-first rule, on any finite graph with thresholds \(t\) and initial \(\eta\) with \(\sum(\eta-t)\le0\): scan the sites in index order; the first site \(x\) with \(\eta(x)>t(x)\) has excess \(e\), and \(D\) is its set of neighbours below their thresholds, with deficits \(d(y)\); if \(D\) is nonempty and \(e\le\sum d\), \(x\) sends \(e\,d(y)/\sum d\) to each \(y\in D\); if \(e>\sum d\) it fills each \(y\in D\) and splits the rest equally among all its neighbours; if \(D\) is empty it splits \(e\) equally among all neighbours; repeat until stable, the flow being defined when this ends in finitely many steps (in general it may converge only in the limit, which (b) does not need). For cells: \(X_1,\dots,X_N\) i.i.d. uniform, \(M=\delta^{-2}\) square cells of side \(\delta\), counts \(n_Q\), \(\mu=N\delta^2\), \(h(\varepsilon)=(1+\varepsilon)\log(1+\varepsilon)-\varepsilon\).

Statement. (a) The net flow of every finite sequence of stages with one reversible rule \(P\), whatever their thresholds, carrying \(\eta\) to \(\eta'\), is the electrical flow from \(\eta\) to \(\eta'\) with conductances \(c\) (the proof uses neither the thresholds, nor stability, nor the sign of the odometers, so this holds for any emission vectors): in particular the slack sandpile followed by the balanced sandpile to the background, for every slack \(\varepsilon\ge0\) and every odometer of each stage, has exactly the electrical flow, with probability one. (b) The deficit-first rule's net flow \(F\) is not additive in the excess: on the cycle of four cells with thresholds \(0\), \(F((2,0,-1,-1))+F((-1,-1,2,0))=(0,-1,0,-1)\) on the edges \(1\)-\(2\), \(2\)-\(3\), \(3\)-\(4\), \(4\)-\(1\) (positive in the written direction), while \(F((1,-1,1,-1))=(\frac12,-\frac12,\frac12,-\frac12)\). (c) With probability at least \(1-M\exp(-\mu h(\varepsilon))\), no cell holds more than \((1+\varepsilon)\mu\) points, so the slack stage topples nothing; on the reduction's grid (\(\delta=1/\lceil32/s\rceil\), \(s=L\sqrt{\log N/N}\), \(L\ge132\)) this holds with probability tending to one for every fixed \(\varepsilon\) with \(h(\varepsilon)>1089/L^2\), for instance \(\varepsilon\ge0.4\) at \(L=132\).

Proof. (a) For one stage with odometer \(v\), put \(u=v/\pi\); reversibility gives \(v(x)p(x,y)=u(x)c(x,y)\) and \(v(y)p(y,x)=u(y)c(x,y)\), so \(\theta(x,y)=c(x,y)(u(x)-u(y))\): this is step (b) of lem:balanced-sandpile-flow, which uses reversibility and not the balance of the thresholds (the reviewer's observation). The net flows of successive stages add, so the total is \(c\,\nabla(\sum_iu_i)\), a potential flow whose divergence is \(\eta-\eta'\); a potential flow is determined by its divergence on a connected graph (the weighted Laplacian's kernel is the constants), and the electrical flow is that potential flow. The slack-then-balanced pair ends at the background, so its flow is the electrical flow from \(\eta\) to the background. (b) For \(e_1=(2,0,-1,-1)\): site \(1\) has excess \(2\), \(D=\{4\}\) with deficit \(1<2\), so it sends \(1\) to \(4\) and splits the rest, \(\frac12\) to \(2\) and \(\frac12\) to \(4\); then site \(2\) sends its \(\frac12\) to \(3\) and site \(4\) its \(\frac12\) to \(3\): \(F(e_1)=(\frac12,\frac12,-\frac12,-\frac32)\). For \(e_2=(-1,-1,2,0)\): site \(3\) sends \(1\) to \(2\) and splits \(1\), \(\frac12\) to \(2\) and \(\frac12\) to \(4\); site \(2\) sends \(\frac12\) to \(1\), site \(4\) sends \(\frac12\) to \(1\): \(F(e_2)=(-\frac12,-\frac32,\frac12,\frac12)\). For \(e_1+e_2=(1,-1,1,-1)\): site \(1\) sends \(\frac12\) to each of \(2\), \(4\), site \(3\) likewise: \(F=(\frac12,-\frac12,\frac12,-\frac12)\), which differs from \(F(e_1)+F(e_2)=(0,-1,0,-1)\) by the circulation \((\frac12,\frac12,\frac12,\frac12)\). Each run ends in finitely many steps. The same values were computed in exact arithmetic by research/results/ultimate_matching_sandpile_rule_20261017/rule_additivity.py (output rule_additivity.json beside it). (c) \(n_Q\) is binomial \((N,\delta^2)\); the Chernoff bound gives \(\Pr(n_Q\ge(1+\varepsilon)\mu)\le\exp(-\mu h(\varepsilon))\), and a union over the \(M\) cells gives the first sentence. On the reduction's grid \(\delta\ge s/33\) for \(N\) large (as \(s\le1\)), so \(\mu\ge L^2\log N/1089\), and \(M\le(33/s)^2\le N\) once \(L^2\log N\ge1089\); the failure probability is at most \(N^{1-L^2h(\varepsilon)/1089}\to0\) when \(h(\varepsilon)>1089/L^2\); at \(L=132\), \(1089/L^2=0.0625\) and \(h(0.4)=0.07106\). \(\square\)

Hypotheses, each with its step. Reversibility of the one rule \(P\) used by every stage, with the same conductances: (a), through \(\theta=c\nabla u\) for each stage and the addition of the potentials; stages with different rules give a sum of potential flows for different conductances, which need not be one. Irreducibility: the potential flow is determined by its divergence. In (b), the rule's index order and tie rules: the computation, whose conclusion concerns this rule only. In (c), only the binomial law of each count (no independence across cells, as the union bound needs none), and \(h(\varepsilon)>1089/L^2\) for the probability to tend to one; (c) is not needed for the flow, which (a) gives for every slack. Conclusions: (a) deterministic, for every sequence of reversible same-rule stages; (b) for the deficit-first rule on the four-cycle; (c) for every grid and slack with the stated probability.

Baseline. Without (a), the pair's flow is known only as the electrical flow plus a divergence-free circulation, by the least-energy step of lem:balanced-sandpile-flow, for any two flows with the same divergence differ by one; (a) applies the same lemma's step (b) to each stage and shows the circulation is zero for every slack. Part (b) adds that a state-dependent splitting leaves the class of potential flows, which no statement about one reversible rule decides. Part (c) is an elementary fact about the counts, superseded for the flow by (a), kept as the statement that the slack stage is idle.

Degenerate cases. (a) with one stage: lem:balanced-sandpile-flow (b). With \(\varepsilon=0\): the slack stage is itself balanced. With every stage idle: the flow is zero and \(\eta=\eta'\). (b) with \(e_2=-e_1\): \(e_1+e_2=0\) and \(F(0)=0\), so additivity there asks \(F(-e_1)=-F(e_1)\), a different property; the counterexample uses another pair. The conclusion "not linear" holds for the deficit-first rule on the four-cycle itself. (c) with all \(N\) points in one cell: the bound \(M\exp(-\mu h)\) is then not small and (c) says nothing.

Nonvacuity. On the curve's parameters: (a) on the 4-neighbour graph of the reduction's cells with equal splitting, every sample and every slack; (c) at \(L=132\), \(\varepsilon=0.4\), where \(\mu\ge16\log N\), \(M\le N\) and the failure probability is at most \(N^{1-16\times0.07106}=N^{-0.137}\to0\). Plainest bound. (a) is deterministic and needs no bound; for one fixed cell in (c) the binomial tail is the whole content, and the plainest uniform bound, the union over the at most \(N\) cells, decides the uniform statement; (b) is a single computed instance.

The line's general claim. conj:conjugate-class-discrepancy on the curve: with probability tending to one every Lipschitz \(G\) with \(\int\sum_j\psi^*_{\alpha_j}(|\partial_jG|)\le2\) has \(\int G\,d(\mu_X-\mu_Y)\le\frac L2\sqrt{N\log N}\), \(\mu\) the cell-smeared measures on the reduction's grid; by cor:exponential-matching-discrepancy-reduction it gives the conjecture at every pair of the curve.

What the goal needs. The class bound in its smeared form at every pair of the curve, or a matching built directly. By lem:smeared-y-term (b) the smeared form and the class supremum of the \(X\)-term of cell averages differ by at most \(160e\sqrt N\), so the \(Y\)-term is settled; the period's bounds on the \(X\)-term are stated for grid functions, at \((4,4)\), on dyadic grids, and the pairs of the curve other than \((4,4)\) are anisotropic.

The six entries

  • Flow-coarea level bound (lem:flow-coarea-level-bound): in the dyadic flow's smearing, the class at gradients bounded by \((\log N)^K\) up to \((\log\log N)^{1/4}\), and levels \([y,Y]\) up to \(\min\{1+(\log Y)^{1/4},(\log N/\log y)^{1/4}\}\).
  • Discrete flow bound (lem:discrete-flow-bound): the same for grid functions on dyadic grids of side at least \(4\sqrt{\log N/N}\), and nested chains with at most \(m\) boundaries through an edge at \(C\sqrt{N\log N}(1+(\log(my))^{1/4})\).
  • Smeared \(Y\)-term (lem:smeared-y-term): the \(Y\)-term is \(O(\sqrt N)\) across the class, and the cell average's deviation is charged by the cellwise Lipschitz sum.
  • Cut-cell variance (lem:cut-cell-variance-bound): the fine part below the mesh at \(\sqrt{\log N}\) per unit of variation, single layers at every level \(y\ge2e^{16}\), and chains of at most \(N^{1/7}\) layers with \(\log K\le(\log N)^{2/3}(\log(y/2))^{1/3}\) at the conjectured order.
  • Guided chains (lem:guided-chain-bound): chains of any number of layers near guides from a family of at most \(N^c\) sets fixed before the points, at the conjectured order when the tube width is at most \(2^{-\ell_1}\exp((\log N)^{2/3}(\log(y/2))^{1/3})\).
  • Sandpile stages (lem:idle-slack-sandpile): every divisible sandpile of one reversible rule, in any number of stages, has the electrical flow; a state-dependent rule is nonlinear.

Falsification attempt. Against the class bound in its discrete form at \((4,4)\), with the chain the guided chains entry named as its next case: \(A_0\) a union of cells of perimeter \(P\) of order one, chosen after the points as a Leighton–Shor set, and the nested layers \(A_k=\bigcup_{j=k}^{K-1}(A_0+j\delta_0e_1)\) on a dyadic grid of side \(\delta_0\ge4\sqrt{\log N/N}\), at level \(y=(\log N)^2\). The instance must satisfy the hypotheses of the \((4,4)\) lemmas, \(y\ge2e^{16}=1.78\cdot10^7\), which \(y=(\log N)^2\) meets only for \(\log N\ge4220\) (the fifth review's instance at \(N=10^{12}\) did not, a defect this review's reviewer found there and in the first draft here); so \(\log N=5000\): \(y=2.5\cdot10^7\), \(\log(y/2)=16.34\), \(T=8(\log(y/2))^{-1/4}=3.98\). The chain is always mixed-level: the back boundary of the last translate lies on every layer, so the increments run from \(y\delta_0\) on the fronts to about \(Ky\delta_0\) on that back boundary, and \(K\) is at most \(T/(y\delta_0P)\), with \(\log K\) about \(\frac12\log N\) (about \(2478\) here). What the record gives on it: the level form of lem:discrete-flow-bound (c), increments in \([y,Ky]\), gives \(C\sqrt{N\log N}\min\{1+(\log(Ky))^{1/4},(\log N/\log(y/2))^{1/4}\}\), the second term \(4.18\) here, whatever \(K\) and however \(A_0\) depends on the points, and lem:fine-grid-leighton-shor (c) gives the same loss, \((\log N)^{3/4}(\log y)^{-1/4}=\sqrt{\log N}(\log N/\log y)^{1/4}\); lem:cut-cell-variance-bound (d) needs \(\log K\le\log N^{1/7}=714\) and \(\log K\le(\log N)^{2/3}(\log(y/2))^{1/3}=742\), and \(2478\) exceeds both; lem:guided-chain-bound (d) needs guides from a family fixed in advance. So, among the bounds evaluated here (lem:tube-localized-discrepancy and lem:band-family-discrepancy were not), the record bounds the translates chain as well as every level-\(y\) function whose increments reach \(Ky\) with \(\log(Ky)\) of order \(\log N\), with the factor \((\log N/\log y)^{1/4}\), and no better: the chain is not a harder instance than such a function. Against it as a counterexample: a translate \(A_0+j\delta_0e_1\) keeps \(A_0\)'s fit to the points only at scales above \(j\delta_0\), so, on the per-scale count of the fifth review's construction (ii), the layers' average factor is of order \((\log y)^{3/4}\), below the target's order: an untested heuristic, not a bound. Not decided.

Obstacle

The line is stuck on the factor \((\log N/\log y)^{1/4}\) for grid functions at levels \(y\) with \(\log y=o(\log N)\) whose increments reach \(Y\) with \(\log Y\) comparable to \(\log N\) (or chains whose boundaries pile up \(m\) deep with \(\log(my)\) comparable to \(\log N\)): lem:discrete-flow-bound (c) and lem:fine-grid-leighton-shor (c) lose it there (lem:flow-coarea-level-bound (d) is the same loss for Lipschitz functions), and the bounds that do not (lem:cut-cell-variance-bound (d), lem:guided-chain-bound (d)) need few layers or guides from a family of polynomial size fixed in advance, while the guides at the Leighton–Shor mesh number exponentially many in the perimeter in mesh units.

Through cor:exponential-matching-discrepancy-reduction the class bound in its smeared form implies the endpoint at every pair; through lem:smeared-y-term (b) the smeared form is the \(X\)-term of cell averages up to \(160e\sqrt N\); lem:fine-grid-leighton-shor (c), lem:cut-cell-variance-bound (d) and lem:guided-chain-bound (d) bound parts of the discrete class (grid functions at \((4,4)\)), which the continuous class reaches only through cell averages, and averaging does not keep the continuous class's level conditions; so what is proved downstream is the discrete \(X\)-term bound on parts of the discrete class at one pair, weaker than the goal. Cell flow duality and sufficiency

17 October 2026 · Working proof · Grid duality. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort set by the session).

Question. The queue drains, and its head, sandpile-odometer-flow, asks for a flow carrying the excess of \(X\) over the background whose per-point tails beat the dyadic flow's; its latest follow-up, in the sandpile stages entry, named the quartic-optimal flow and, first, "the asymptotics of the optimum's gain over the electrical flow". The sixth review posed instead, as this entry's lemma, the grid duality its stage-one reviewer observed and the Raviart–Thomas step its stage-two reviewer sketched (unverified there): whether the optimum's cost is the discrete class functional, so that the item's question is the discrete class bound. The missing implication is conj:conjugate-class-discrepancy; the test is a proof, and it ends the item if the equality holds.

Target form. The goal's form is the class bound for the cell-smeared \(\mu_X-\mu_Y\) on the reduction's grid; this entry works in the discrete form, the \(X\)-term of grid functions with the discrete conjugate cost, and shows that form sufficient for the goal by itself (part (c)), so the entry's form and the goal's sufficient form are linked by a proof, not by a convenience.

General statement. lem:grid-flow-duality: part (a) on every finite connected graph with even convex finite edge costs; part (b) on every square grid of \(k\times k\) cells; parts (c) and (d) at every pair \(\alpha\in[1,\infty]^2\) and every square grid of side \(\delta\) with \(1/\delta\) an integer, \(\delta\le s/32\) and \(N\delta^2\ge16\log N\), the reduction's grid among them when \(L\ge132\); since \(N\delta^2\le L^2\log N/1024\) on such a grid, the two conditions hold together only when \(L\ge128\), and (c) is vacuous below.

Cell flow duality

Setting. A finite connected graph with vertex set \(V\) and edge set \(E\), each edge oriented from a tail to a head; an edge flow \(\theta\in\mathbb R^E\) has net outflow \((\operatorname{out}\theta)_v=\sum_{e\text{ from }v}\theta_e-\sum_{e\text{ into }v}\theta_e\), and \(\Delta_eu=u_{\mathrm{head}}-u_{\mathrm{tail}}\) for \(u\in\mathbb R^V\). The cell grid: the unit square cut into \(k^2\) cells of side \(\delta=1/k\), edges between side-neighbours oriented in the increasing coordinate, the direction \(d(e)\in\{1,2\}\) of an edge the coordinate it crosses. \(X_1,\dots,X_N\) i.i.d. uniform, \(n_Q\) the count of a cell; \(Y\) evenly spread (rectangles \(R_j\) of area \(1/N\) tiling the square, \(Y_j\in R_j\subset B(Y_j,10/\sqrt N)\)); \(\psi_\alpha(t)=e^{t^\alpha}-1\), \(\psi_\infty(t)=N(t-1)_+\), \(\psi^*\) the conjugates, \(s=L\sqrt{\log N/N}\), as in cor:exponential-matching-discrepancy-reduction, whose grid \(\delta=1/\lceil32/s\rceil\) is one admissible grid when \(L\ge132\).

Statement. (a) If each \(\varphi_e\) is even, convex and finite, and \(\sum_v\rho_v=0\), then \(\min\{\sum_e\varphi_e(\theta_e):\operatorname{out}\theta=\rho\}=\max_u\big[\sum_vu_v\rho_v-\sum_e\varphi_e^*(\Delta_eu)\big]\), both attained. (b) On the cell grid, an edge flow \(\theta\) defines the field \(\Phi\) given on a cell \([a,a+\delta]\times[b,b+\delta]\) by \(\Phi_1(x,y)=\big(\theta_\ell(a+\delta-x)+\theta_r(x-a)\big)/\delta^2\) and \(\Phi_2(x,y)=\big(\theta_b(b+\delta-y)+\theta_t(y-b)\big)/\delta^2\), \(\theta_\ell,\theta_r,\theta_b,\theta_t\) the fluxes of its left, right, bottom and top edges in the increasing coordinate (zero on the outer boundary); \(\Phi\) is bounded, \(\int\nabla g\cdot\Phi\,dx=-\sum_Q\frac{(\operatorname{out}\theta)_Q}{\delta^2}\int_Qg\) for every Lipschitz \(g\), and for \(\Psi_1,\Psi_2\) convex nondecreasing on \([0,\infty)\) with \(\Psi_j(0)=0\) and every \(\lambda>0\), \(\int\big(\Psi_1(|\Phi_1|/\lambda)+\Psi_2(|\Phi_2|/\lambda)\big)dx\le\delta^2\sum_e\Psi_{d(e)}(|\theta_e|/(\delta\lambda))\). (c) Let \(\alpha\in[1,\infty]^2\), \(L>0\), and grids of side \(\delta=\delta_N\) with \(1/\delta\) an integer, \(\delta\le s/32\) and \(N\delta^2\ge16\log N\); let \(D^{\mathrm{disc}}_N\) be the supremum of \(\sum_QG_Q(n_Q-N\delta^2)\) over grid functions \(G\) with \(I_\delta(G)=\sum_e\delta^2\psi^*_{\alpha_{d(e)}}(|\Delta_eG|/\delta)\le2\). If \(P(D^{\mathrm{disc}}_N\le\frac L2\sqrt{N\log N})\to1\), then with probability tending to one there is a matching with \(\sum_i\exp[(|X^j_i-Y^j_{\pi(i)}|/s)^{\alpha_j}]\le2N\) for finite \(\alpha_j\) and \(\max_i|X^j_i-Y^j_{\pi(i)}|\le2s\) for \(\alpha_j=\infty\), the conclusion of cor:exponential-matching-discrepancy-reduction. (d) For every \(\lambda'>0\), with \(\Psi_j(t)=\psi_{\alpha_j}(t/s)\), \(\min\{\lambda'\delta^2\sum_e\Psi_{d(e)}(|\theta_e|/(\delta\lambda')):\operatorname{out}\theta_Q=N\delta^2-n_Q\}=\max_G\big[\frac1s\sum_QG_Q(n_Q-N\delta^2)-\lambda'I_\delta(G)\big]\).

Proof. (a) The map \(\operatorname{out}:\mathbb R^E\to\mathbb R^V\) has range \(\{\sum_v\rho_v=0\}\) on a connected graph (its transpose \(u\mapsto(-\Delta_eu)_e\) has kernel the constants), so \(\rho\) is in the range. With \(f(\theta)=\sum_e\varphi_e(\theta_e)\), finite and convex on all of \(\mathbb R^E\), and \(g\) the indicator of \(\{\rho\}\), finite-dimensional Fenchel–Rockafellar duality, whose qualification \(\rho\in\operatorname{out}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) holds since \(\operatorname{dom}f=\mathbb R^E\), gives \(\inf_\theta[f(\theta)+g(\operatorname{out}\theta)]=\max_u[-f^*(-\operatorname{out}^Tu)-g^*(u)]\), the maximum attained; here \(g^*(u)=\sum_vu_v\rho_v\), \(\sum_vu_v(\operatorname{out}\theta)_v=\sum_e\theta_e(u_{\mathrm{tail}}-u_{\mathrm{head}})\) so \(-\operatorname{out}^Tu=(\Delta_eu)_e\), and \(f^*(\xi)=\sum_e\varphi_e^*(\xi_e)\); the sign of \(u\) is immaterial by evenness of \(\varphi_e^*\). Attainment of the minimum: an even convex finite \(\varphi_e\) is either constant or grows at least linearly, \(\varphi_e(t)\ge c_e|t|-C_e\) with \(c_e>0\); with \(E'\) the edges of the second kind, \(f\) depends on \(\theta\) only through \(\theta_{E'}\) up to a constant, the projection of the affine set \(\{\operatorname{out}\theta=\rho\}\) to \(\mathbb R^{E'}\) is affine and closed, and \(f\) is coercive on it, so its infimum there is attained, at the projection of a feasible flow. (b) \(\Phi_1\) is affine in \(x\) on each cell with value \(\theta_e/\delta\) on each vertical edge \(e\) from both sides, so its normal component is continuous across inner vertical edges and zero on the outer ones; likewise \(\Phi_2\); so \(\Phi\) is bounded, \(\int\nabla g\cdot\Phi=-\sum_Q\int_Qg\operatorname{div}\Phi\) for Lipschitz \(g\) (integration by parts on each cell, the edge terms cancelling), and \(\operatorname{div}\Phi=(\theta_r-\theta_\ell+\theta_t-\theta_b)/\delta^2=(\operatorname{out}\theta)_Q/\delta^2\) on \(Q\). For the cost, on a cell \(|\Phi_1|\) at \(x=a+t\delta\) is \(|(1-t)\theta_\ell+t\theta_r|/\delta\le((1-t)|\theta_\ell|+t|\theta_r|)/\delta\), and \(\Psi_1\) is convex and nondecreasing, so \(\int_Q\Psi_1(|\Phi_1|/\lambda)\le\delta^2\int_0^1[(1-t)\Psi_1(|\theta_\ell|/(\delta\lambda))+t\Psi_1(|\theta_r|/(\delta\lambda))]dt=\frac{\delta^2}2[\Psi_1(|\theta_\ell|/(\delta\lambda))+\Psi_1(|\theta_r|/(\delta\lambda))]\); summing over the cells, each inner vertical edge appears in two cells with weight \(\frac12\) and each outer one contributes \(\Psi_1(0)=0\); likewise for \(\Phi_2\). (d) Apply (a) on the cell grid with \(\varphi_e(t)=\lambda'\delta^2\Psi_{d(e)}(|t|/(\delta\lambda'))\), even, convex and finite (for \(\alpha=\infty\), \(\psi_\infty(t)=N(t-1)_+\) is finite), and \(\rho_Q=N\delta^2-n_Q\), whose sum is \(Nk^2\delta^2-N=0\). Its conjugate is \(\varphi_e^*(v)=\sup_t[tv-\lambda'\delta^2\Psi(|t|/(\delta\lambda'))]=\lambda'\delta^2\sup_r[r\,|v|/\delta-\Psi(r)]=\lambda'\delta^2\Psi^*(|v|/\delta)\) (substituting \(t=\delta\lambda'r\)), and \(\Psi_j^*(x)=\psi^*_{\alpha_j}(sx)\); with \(G=-su\), \(\sum_Qu_Q\rho_Q=\frac1s\sum_QG_Q(n_Q-N\delta^2)\) and \(\sum_e\varphi_e^*(\Delta_eu)=\lambda'I_\delta(G)\). (c) Smearings: \(\nu_X=\sum_i\mathrm{Unif}(Q(X_i))\), supported within \(\ell^\infty\)-distance \(\delta\) of the points, with density \(n_Q/\delta^2\) on \(Q\); \(\nu_Y=\sum_j\mathrm{Unif}(R_j)\), supported within \(10/\sqrt N\), equal to \(N\) times Lebesgue measure since the \(R_j\) tile the square with area \(1/N\). Each \(n_Q\) is binomial with mean \(N\delta^2\ge16\log N\), so \(P(n_Q<N\delta^2/2)\le e^{-N\delta^2/8}\le N^{-2}\), and there are \(\delta^{-2}\le N/(16\log N)\) cells, so every \(n_Q\ge N\delta^2/2\) with probability at least \(1-1/N\); then both densities are at least \(\lambda=N/2\); with \(h=\frac14\), \(\lambda'=N/4\). Let \(\theta\) attain the minimum in (d) and \(\Phi\) its field by (b); \(\operatorname{out}\theta_Q=N\delta^2-n_Q\) gives \(\int\nabla g\cdot\Phi=\sum_Q\frac{n_Q-N\delta^2}{\delta^2}\int_Qg=\int g\,d(\nu_X-\nu_Y)\). By lem:flow-matching-bound (2) with \(C(z)=\sum_j\Psi_j(|z_j|)\), then (b) and (d), the minimal matching cost is at most \(\lambda'\int C(\Phi/\lambda')+E\le\lambda'\delta^2\sum_e\Psi_{d(e)}(|\theta_e|/(\delta\lambda'))+E=\max_G[\frac1s\sum_QG_Q(n_Q-N\delta^2)-\frac N4I_\delta(G)]+E\), \(E=hN\sum_j(\Psi_j(\delta/h)+\Psi_j(10/(h\sqrt N)))\). On the event \(D^{\mathrm{disc}}_N\le\frac L2\sqrt{N\log N}=\frac{sN}2\), the homogeneity step of cor:exponential-matching-discrepancy-reduction (for \(I_\delta(G)>2\), \(G'=\frac2{I_\delta(G)}G\) has \(I_\delta(G')\le2\) by convexity of \(\psi^*\) with \(\psi^*(0)=0\)) gives \(\frac1s\sum_QG_Q(n_Q-N\delta^2)-\frac N4I_\delta(G)\le\frac N2\) for every \(G\). For the error, \(4\delta\le s/8\), and \(40/\sqrt N=40s/(L\sqrt{\log N})\le s/8\) once \(\log N\ge(320/L)^2\), so for \(N\) large each \(\Psi_j(\cdot)\le\psi_{\alpha_j}(1/8)\le e^{1/8}-1<0.14\) and \(E\le\frac N4\cdot4\cdot0.14=0.14N\). So the minimal cost is below \(N\), and the corollary's conclusion step gives the matching. \(\square\)

Hypotheses, each with its step. Connectedness of the graph and \(\sum\rho=0\): the range of the divergence in (a). Finite costs: the constraint qualification in (a), whose domain is the whole space; for \(\psi_\infty\), finite as \(N(t-1)_+\). Evenness of \(\varphi_e\): the sign of \(u\) in (a); (b) applies \(\Psi_j\) to \(|\cdot|\) and needs none. No coercivity and no value at \(0\) are needed in (a): an even convex finite cost is constant or grows linearly, which gives attainment, and constants shift both sides. Convexity and monotonicity of \(\Psi_j\) with \(\Psi_j(0)=0\): the cell-by-cell bound in (b) and the outer edges' zero contribution. \(1/\delta\) an integer: the cells tile the square, so \(\sum\rho=0\) and the boundary terms vanish in (b). \(N\delta^2\ge16\log N\): the Chernoff count in (c) (so \(L\ge132\) enters only through it on the reduction's grid, where \(N\delta^2\ge L^2\log N/1089\)). \(\delta\le s/32\): \(\Psi_j(4\delta)\le\psi(1/8)\) in the error. \(N\) large: \(\log N\ge(320/L)^2\) in the error. \(L>0\) is stated, but \(\delta\le s/32\) and \(N\delta^2\ge16\log N\) together force \(L\ge128\), since \(N\delta^2\le L^2\log N/1024\). Evenly spread \(Y\): \(\nu_Y\) equal to \(N\) times Lebesgue measure in (c); for a general second sample the field of (b) carries \(\nu_X\) to \(N\,dx\) only, and the two-sample case follows from lem:two-sample-matching-transfer as in the corollary. Conclusions: (a) for every finite connected graph; (b) for every cell grid and every such \(\Psi_j\); (c), (d) at every pair in \([1,\infty]^2\), the curve's pairs included, on every grid meeting the three conditions.

Baseline. Without (a), the Young step (lem:discrete-flow-bound (a)'s, or lem:flow-matching-bound (2)'s Fenchel–Young inequality) gives weak duality: every flow's cost bounds the penalized discrete functional above; (a) adds the equality, the best flow's cost being exactly that functional. Without (b) and (c), the record makes the discrete class bound sufficient only through the sample-point pyramids entry's reduction (a computation of that entry, not part of a registered statement: the smeared \(X\)-term is at most the supremum over grid functions with \(\sum\delta^2\psi^*(|D_jg|/2)\le2\)) and lem:smeared-y-term (b) (the \(Y\)-term within \(160e\sqrt N\)), with cor:exponential-matching-discrepancy-reduction; a grid function \(g\) of that halved class has \(g/2\) in the discrete class, so its supremum is at most \(2D^{\mathrm{disc}}_N\), and \(160e\sqrt N\) is \(o(\sqrt{N\log N})\): the record gives (c) with \(L\) replaced by a constant multiple and for \(N\) large, and (c) gives it with neither the factor nor the \(Y\)-term.

Degenerate cases. \(\rho=0\): both sides of (a) are the constant \(\sum_e\varphi_e(0)\) (\(\theta=0\), \(u=0\)). One vertex: no edges, \(\rho=0\), both sides \(0\). A graph that is not connected: (a) fails when \(\rho\) does not sum to zero on each component, a case its hypothesis excludes. \(\theta=0\) in (b): \(\Phi=0\), cost \(0\). \(k=1\): no inner edges, \(\Phi=0\), and (d) reads \(0=\max_G\frac1s G_Q(n_Q-N)=0\) since \(n_Q=N\). \(\alpha=(\infty,\infty)\): \(\psi^*_\infty(x)=x\) for \(x\le N\), so the discrete class is a total-variation class with increments \(|\Delta_eG|\le N\delta\) (\(\psi^*_\infty\) being finite only up to \(N\)), and (c) gives the maximum-displacement conclusion in both coordinates.

Nonvacuity. A witness that exercises (c), off the curve: \(\alpha=(2,2)\), \(L\ge\max(256,\frac92L_0)\) with \(L_0\) the constant of thm:dyadic-flow-square-exponential, and the dyadic grid of side \(\delta\in[s/64,s/32]\). Then \(\delta\ge s/64=\frac L{64}\sqrt{\log N/N}\ge4\sqrt{\log N/N}\), \(N\delta^2\ge L^2\log N/4096\ge16\log N\) (equality at \(L=256\)), and \(\delta\le s/32\); lem:discrete-flow-bound (a), on that dyadic grid, gives with probability tending to one \(|\sum_QG_Q(n_Q-N\delta^2)|\le\frac34L_0\sqrt{N\log N}(1+I_\delta(G))\le\frac94L_0\sqrt{N\log N}\le\frac L2\sqrt{N\log N}\) for every \(G\) with \(I_\delta(G)\le2\), which is (c)'s premise; so (c) gives the matching at \((2,2)\), the conclusion of thm:dyadic-flow-square-exponential for \(L\ge\max(256,\frac92L_0)\) only, not for every \(L\ge L_0\), and not as an independent proof: lem:discrete-flow-bound (a) is built from that theorem's own dyadic flow, so the witness re-routes the same flow through (b), (d) and (c), and what it exercises is (c)'s implication. On the curve's parameters, (a), (b) and (d) hold for every sample on the reduction's grid, and (c)'s premise is the open discrete form of conj:conjugate-class-discrepancy. Plainest bound. For one fixed grid function the discrete functional is one binomial sum, decided by its variance; the plainest uniform bound, the variance bound with a union over the unions of cells, is lem:fine-grid-leighton-shor (b), which charges \((\log N)^{3/4}\) per unit of variation on dyadic grids of side between \(\kappa\sqrt{\log N/N}\) and \(2^{-\ell_1}\), above the conjectured order by \((\log N)^{1/4}\); the uniform statement at the conjectured order is the open problem. For (a) the plainest bound is weak duality, which (a) improves to equality; the numerical check (research/results/ultimate_matching_grid_duality_20261017/duality_check.json) finds the two sides of (a) equal to within \(5.4\cdot10^{-7}\) relative on nine instances of \(2\times2\) to \(4\times4\) grids, the field cost of (b) below the edge cost on every one, a wrong conjugate scaling giving a gap of at least \(0.31\), and the quadratic control equal to the weighted electrical energy to within \(2\cdot10^{-13}\); a first version of its primal, minimized with SLSQP under the constraint, stopped above the minimum, which the control caught, and was replaced by a minimization over the circulations.

Architecture test

Architecture test. Not decided. The sixth review's retained test, the gap-charged bound for nested chains, was neither proved nor refuted; neither of its outcomes occurred. What this entry gives the test: by (c), its object, the discrete \(X\)-term of grid functions, is now sufficient for the goal by itself, so a proof of the test's bound for all level-\(y\) chains bears on the goal with no continuous class or \(Y\)-term in between, and by (d) a chain violating it is, up to constants in \(L\), an obstruction to every flow on the cells.

New mathematics. lem:grid-flow-duality: on a finite connected graph the minimal edge cost of a flow with given net outflow equals the maximum of the dual vertex functional, both attained; on the cell grid the lowest-order Raviart–Thomas field of an edge flow carries the cell-uniform smearing to the uniform one at a field cost at most the edge cost; so the discrete \(X\)-term class bound on grid functions, on any grid with \(1/\delta\) an integer, \(\delta\le s/32\) and \(N\delta^2\ge16\log N\), implies the ultimate matching conjecture's conclusion at every pair (part (c)), and the minimal edge cost over flows carrying the cell counts to the background equals the penalized discrete class functional exactly (part (d)).

At the goal's own parameters, at every pair of the curve on the reduction's grid, the sufficient statement is now the discrete one, \(P(D^{\mathrm{disc}}_N\le\frac L2\sqrt{N\log N})\to1\), and every candidate flow on the cells, sandpile or other, is judged by (d) against the penalized discrete functional, hence against that bound up to constants in \(L\) (a penalized maximum at most \(cN\) gives \(D^{\mathrm{disc}}_N\le(c+\frac12)sN\), and \(D^{\mathrm{disc}}_N\le\frac{sN}2\) gives a penalized maximum at most \(\frac N2\)); curve's parameters. Not covered. Straight-cut forced flux is cheap

17 October 2026 · Working proof · Two-choice routing. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort set by the session).

Where we stand. Unchanged: A queue item's entry: its lemma bounds forced cut totals and changes no statement of Where we stand.

Question. The queue drains, and its head, two-choice-routing, asks to "route each unit of dyadic excess along the less loaded of two candidate paths, keeping the divergence, and test whether the per-point loads lose their Gaussian tails as two choices do for balls into bins". In balls into bins two choices lower the maximum load under a fixed total; the question here is what, in a flow carrying the cell counts to the background, a routing rule cannot change, and whether that fixed part is already an obstruction. The missing implication is conj:conjugate-class-discrepancy through its primal form, lem:grid-flow-duality (d); the test is a proof of what every flow is forced to carry across straight cuts, which ends the item's first reading if that forced part is cheap.

Target form. The goal's form is the class bound for the cell-smeared measures; by lem:grid-flow-duality (c) and (d) it is, up to constants, the cost of the cheapest flow on the cells; this entry bounds below, and then above, the part of any flow's cost that its divergence forces across straight cuts of rectangles of cells.

General statement. lem:straight-cut-forced-flux: parts (a) and (b) for every set \(S\) of cells of every cell grid, every subset \(A\subset S\), every flow local to \(S\) and every convex nondecreasing \(\Psi\) with \(\Psi(0)=0\); part (c) on every grid of side \(\delta\) (\(1/\delta\) an integer) with \(N\delta^2\ge16\log N\), for every \(L>0\), every rectangle of cells and every straight cut of it.

Straight-cut forced flux

Setting. The cell grid of side \(\delta=1/k\) of lem:grid-flow-duality, with \(\rho_Q=N\delta^2-n_Q\) (the opposite sign to that record's "carrying \(n_Q\) to \(N\delta^2\)", harmless since every cost here is even). For a set \(S\) of cells, \(\bar\rho_S\) is the mean of \(\rho\) over \(S\); a flow \(\theta\) is local to \(S\) if it vanishes on every edge with exactly one end in \(S\) and \((\operatorname{out}\theta)_Q=\rho_Q-\bar\rho_S\) for \(Q\in S\). Since \(\sum_Q\rho_Q=Nk^2\delta^2-N=0\), every flow on the grid carrying \(\rho\) is local to the whole square. For \(A\subset S\), the cut \(\partial_SA\) is the set of edges between \(A\) and \(S\setminus A\), \(m=|\partial_SA|\), and \(E_S(A)=\sum_{Q\in A}(\rho_Q-\bar\rho_S)\). A straight cut of a rectangle \(S\) of cells (sides \(a\) and \(b\), multiples of \(\delta\)) is \(A\) the cells of \(S\) on one side of an inner grid line parallel to the side \(b\); then \(m=b/\delta\). \(\psi_4(t)=e^{t^4}-1\), \(s=L\sqrt{\log N/N}\), \(\lambda'=N/4\).

Statement. (a) Every flow local to \(S\) has net flux \(\sum_{e\in\partial_SA}\theta_e=E_S(A)\) out of \(A\), for every \(A\subset S\). (b) Hence for \(\Psi\) convex nondecreasing with \(\Psi(0)=0\) and \(\lambda>0\), \(\sum_{e\in\partial_SA}\Psi(|\theta_e|/\lambda)\ge m\,\Psi\big(|E_S(A)|/(m\lambda)\big)\), with equality for the flow spreading \(E_S(A)\) evenly over the cut when such a flow exists. (c) On every grid with \(N\delta^2\ge16\log N\), with probability at least \(1-2N^{-1.2}\), every rectangle \(S\) of cells (sides \(a,b\)) and every straight cut \(A\) of it parallel to the side \(b\) have \(|E_S(A)|\le2\sqrt{8Nab\log N}\); so at \(\Psi=\psi_4(\cdot/s)\), \(\lambda=\delta\lambda'\), the argument \(|E_S(A)|/(m\delta\lambda's)\) of (b) is at most \(8\sqrt8\sqrt{a/b}/L\), for every \(L>0\); and for any family of disjoint square blocks, all their straight cuts in both directions together force a cost \(\lambda'\delta^2\sum m\,\psi_4(|E_S(A)|/(m\delta\lambda's))\le\frac N2\psi_4(8\sqrt8/L)\), which is \(4.3\cdot10^{-4}N\) at \(L=132\). The family may be the whole square alone, so this bounds the straight-cut forced cost of every flow carrying the counts to the background.

Proof. (a) Sum the outflow over the cells of \(A\): an edge with both ends in \(A\) cancels, an edge with one end in \(S\) and one outside carries \(0\) by locality, and the remaining edges are those of \(\partial_SA\), oriented out of \(A\); so \(\sum_{e\in\partial_SA}\theta_e=\sum_{Q\in A}(\rho_Q-\bar\rho_S)=E_S(A)\). (b) By (a), \(\sum_{e\in\partial_SA}|\theta_e|\ge|E_S(A)|\); \(\Psi(|\cdot|/\lambda)\) is convex, so Jensen's inequality over the \(m\) edges gives \(\frac1m\sum\Psi(|\theta_e|/\lambda)\ge\Psi(\frac1m\sum|\theta_e|/\lambda)\), and \(\Psi\) nondecreasing gives \(\ge\Psi(|E_S(A)|/(m\lambda))\); the even spreading attains it. (c) With \(d(R)=n(R)-N|R|\) for a set \(R\) of cells, \(|\cdot|\) the area, \(E_S(A)=-d(A)+\frac{|A|}{|S|}d(S)\). For an axis rectangle \(R\) of cells, \(n(R)\) is a sum of \(N\) independent indicators (the points are independent) with variance \(\sigma^2\le N|R|\); Bernstein's inequality with \(t=\sqrt{8N|R|\log N}\) gives \(P(|d(R)|\ge t)\le2\exp\big(-\frac{t^2}{2(\sigma^2+t/3)}\big)\le2\exp\big(-\frac{4\log N}{1+\sqrt{8\log N/(N|R|)}/3}\big)\), and \(N|R|\ge N\delta^2\ge16\log N\) makes the denominator at most \(1+\sqrt{1/2}/3<1.24\), so the probability is at most \(2N^{-3.2}\). There are \((k(k+1)/2)^2\le k^4\le N^2\) axis rectangles of cells (\(k^2\le N/(16\log N)\)), and a union bound over them gives the event, of probability at least \(1-2N^{-1.2}\), on which every one has \(|d(R)|\le\sqrt{8N|R|\log N}\). A straight cut \(A\) and \(S\) are axis rectangles with \(|A|\le|S|=ab\), so \(|E_S(A)|\le2\sqrt{8Nab\log N}\), and \(|E_S(A)|/(m\delta\lambda's)\le2\sqrt{8Nab\log N}\cdot4/(bNs)=8\sqrt8\sqrt{a/b}\sqrt{\log N}/(\sqrt Ns)=8\sqrt8\sqrt{a/b}/L\). A square block of \(j\times j\) cells has \(j-1\) straight cuts per direction, each of \(j\) edges, and disjoint blocks have \(\sum_S j_S(j_S-1)\le k^2\) such edges per direction; each costs at most \(\lambda'\delta^2\psi_4(8\sqrt8/L)\), so the total is at most \(\frac N4\cdot\frac1{k^2}\cdot2k^2\psi_4(8\sqrt8/L)=\frac N2\psi_4(8\sqrt8/L)\); at \(L=132\), \(8\sqrt8/L=0.1714\) and \(\psi_4(0.1714)=8.6\cdot10^{-4}\). \(\square\)

Hypotheses, each with its step. Locality (zero on edges with one end in \(S\), outflow \(\rho-\bar\rho_S\) on \(S\)): (a), the boundary terms; for a flow not local to \(S\) the flux out of \(A\) is \(E_S(A)\) plus what leaves \(A\) through the boundary of \(S\), not fixed. Convexity and monotonicity of \(\Psi\) with \(\Psi(0)=0\): Jensen and the monotone step of (b). In (c): \(N\delta^2\ge16\log N\) for Bernstein's denominator at every rectangle of at least one cell (no variance floor and no area restriction); the independence of the \(N\) points for Bernstein; the count of rectangles, at most \(N^2\), for the union; that \(1/\delta\) is an integer is the definition of the grid, and the count holds for every \(k\times k\) grid; rectangles are needed only so that \(A\) and \(S\) lie in the counted family, square blocks only for the family total, where \(a=b\); \(L\) enters only through \(s\), and every \(L>0\) is allowed.

Baseline. The plainest bound on what a flow carries across a cut is the cut's own count: the net flux equals the excess on one side, for flows that do not leave the region, which (a) states, and (b) is Jensen's inequality on it. What the lemma adds is (c): at the reduction's scale, at every rectangle at once, the forced part across straight cuts is cheap for flows local to the rectangle, at most \(\frac N2\psi_4(8\sqrt8/L)\) for flows local to every block of a disjoint family of square blocks with all their cuts, and so, through the whole square, across full grid lines for every flow.

Degenerate cases. \(A=\emptyset\) or \(A=S\): \(E_S(A)=0\) and the cut has no edges. A block of one cell: no inner cut. A block with \(\rho\) constant on it: \(E_S(A)=0\) for every \(A\), the zero flow is local and costs \(0\). The whole square: every flow carrying \(\rho\) is local to it, and (a) is the flux identity across full grid lines and around every set of cells. A thin rectangle with \(a/b\) large: the argument bound \(8\sqrt8\sqrt{a/b}/L\) grows, as it must, a long strip's excess crossing a short cut.

Nonvacuity. On the curve's parameters, at \((4,4)\) with \(L=132\) on the reduction's grid of side \(1/\lceil32/s\rceil\) (\(N\delta^2\ge L^2\log N/1089=16\log N\)): the dyadic flow of thm:dyadic-flow-square-exponential carries \(\rho\) on the cells (up to the sign) and is local to the whole square, so (c) bounds its forced straight-cut cost at \(4.3\cdot10^{-4}N\); on a grid with \(k=2^J\) a power of \(2\) and \(N4^{-J}\ge16\log N\), a grid other than the reduction's (whose side \(1/\lceil32/s\rceil\) need not make dyadic squares unions of cells), the sum of the dyadic flow's components at a dyadic square \(S\) and at the squares below it, restricted to \(S\), is local to \(S\), the witness on which (a) is used for a block smaller than the square.Plainest bound. For one fixed rectangle and cut the forced argument is one binomial deviation, decided by Bernstein's inequality on its variance; the plainest uniform bound, that inequality with the union over the at most \(N^2\) axis rectangles, is the proof of (c), which decides it. The record's rectangle bound, lem:tube-localized-discrepancy (a) on the event of lem:mesh-function-discrepancy, gives a union \(A\) of cells of a dyadic mesh \(|d(A)|\le L\sqrt N\,\Phi\,(\mathrm{perimeter}(A)+4W\cdot\#\{W\text{-cells containing a cell of }A\})\) with \(\Phi=(2(j-k)+5)^{3/4}+\sqrt{\log N}\), which for a square of side \(r\) at \(W=r\) (perimeter \(4r\), at most four \(W\)-cells) is at most \(20L\sqrt N\,r\,\Phi\) with \(j-k=\log_2(r2^j)\); since \(\Phi\ge\sqrt{\log N}\) it is never below (c)'s \(\sqrt{8N\log N}\,r\) by more than a constant factor, and it exceeds it by the factor \((2\log_2(r2^j)+5)^{3/4}/\sqrt{\log N}\), unbounded for squares with \(\log_2(r2^j)\gg(\log N)^{2/3}\); with lem:loglog-mesh-deviation, \(\sqrt{\log N}\) becomes \(\sqrt{j+\log\log N}\), of the same order at meshes with \(j\) of order \(\log N\). Those lemmas hold only for meshes \(2^{-j}\) with \(j\le\ell_1\), \(2^{-\ell_1}\ge(\log N)^{3/4}/\sqrt N\), while the reduction's cells, of side about \(s/32=O(\sqrt{\log N/N})\), are finer and not dyadic; so the record bounds these rectangles' deviations on dyadic meshes no finer than \(2^{-\ell_1}\), up to constants for small rectangles and with the extra factor for large ones, and not on the reduction's grid at all; the union-bound Bernstein bound of (c) is the plainest uniform bound there.

Architecture test

Architecture test. Not decided. The sixth review's retained test, the gap-charged bound for nested chains, was neither proved nor refuted; this entry bears on its primal side only: by (c) the forced flux across full grid lines is cheap for every flow, and across the straight cuts of rectangles for flows local to them, so an obstruction to a cheap flow, if there is one, lies in how the flux is distributed along the cuts and among the other edges, not in the cuts' totals; thm:dyadic-flow-obstruction's obstruction is of that kind, per point.

Follow-up. Continuing. The item's words allow three readings. First, what a two-choice routing cannot change: (a)–(c) answer it, the straight-cut totals being fixed and cheap across full grid lines for every flow, and across block cuts for flows local to the blocks. Second, a two-choice rule as the choice of a circulation added to a fixed flow: not examined here; lem:grid-flow-duality (d) bounds every such choice below by the penalized functional, which restates the open problem rather than examining the rule, and ex:greedy-circulation-tails tested a greedy circulation, not a two-choice one. Third, the item's test, a less-loaded rule run at reachable sizes: not run, the next attempt. Next attempt, a lemma before any run: the water-filling reduction across all \(J\) levels. Its argument, from the reviewer's second pass and unverified: a less-loaded rule on a finer cut sends each unit to the edge whose total load (the coarser levels' load plus the units already placed) is lowest, so wherever the finer forced flux suffices to level the cut it drives every edge's total toward the cut's average total, the coarser components' integral along the segment plus \(E_S(A)\); that integral is fixed for the dyadic components and free only for components that are not, and both are linear in the count deviations, so the rule's per-edge totals are near-Gaussian like the dyadic flow's. To be proved: that over all levels the rule's per-point value differs from a linear function of the counts by a term whose fourth moment is \(o\) of the dyadic flow's, so its per-point shape is near-Gaussian; that the rule then fails above exponent \(2\) needs one more step, a per-point variance of order \(N\log N\) at a positive fraction of points for the levelled linear function, which thm:dyadic-flow-obstruction's proof gets from the dyadic flow's own weights and which does not follow here, the levelling replacing coarse per-point loads by segment averages of possibly smaller variance. Prediction. The rule's per-position standardized kurtosis stays at a constant offset from the dyadic flow's at \(J=6,\dots,9\), with no trend in \(J\) (a constant offset is allowed: ex:greedy-circulation-tails found a greedy circulation lower by about \(0.2\)–\(0.3\), kurtosis \(2.71\)–\(2.89\) against \(2.88\)–\(3.19\), without trend); refuted if the gap grows with \(J\), the balls-into-bins effect. That the levelling fails at a positive fraction of cuts, which would make such a gap possible, is an untested hypothesis: the fine forced flux \(|E_S(A)|\) and the spread of the coarse loads along the segment are both of order \(\sqrt N\,r\), so neither dominates by size alone. Two levels alone cannot show a gap that grows with the number of levels, so the test runs over all levels, per point. Smallest case. One cut of \(m\) edges and no coarser load: sending the units of \(E_S(A)\) one at a time to the less loaded edge leaves loads differing by at most one unit, so each edge carries \(|E_S(A)|/m\) up to one unit, the even spreading that attains (b); on one cut the rule gives the optimum and the per-edge load has the tail of \(E_S(A)\), so no gain is possible within a cut, by (b). Own statements. Part (b) decides the single cut, as just shown, and with (a) gives the water-filling step on one cut: the levelled total on a cut is its average total, the coarser segment integral plus \(E_S(A)\); part (c) bounds the forced totals and says nothing about the coarser components' redistribution along a segment or about where the finer flux is too small to level; thm:dyadic-flow-obstruction decides the dyadic flow, whose per-point values are Gaussian, and not a rule that chooses by the coarser load; none decides the reduction over all levels.Plainest bound. Each level's even spreading has per-edge load \(|E_S(A)|/m\) with the tail of one binomial deviation, and the levels' loads at an edge add to at most the sum of their absolute values; the attempt asks whether the rule's choice cancels them beyond a linear function of the counts, which no recorded bound decides. Sequential rules reproduce the dyadic flow

17 October 2026 · [status written after the review] · Two-choice routing. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort set by the session).

Where we stand. Unchanged: A queue item's entry: its lemma concerns local routing rules and changes no statement of Where we stand.

Question. The queue head, two-choice-routing, continued from the straight-cut forced flux entry, whose next attempt was "the water-filling reduction across all \(J\) levels": whether a less-loaded crossing rule changes the dyadic flow's per-point values beyond a linear function of the counts, with the Prediction that its per-position kurtosis stays at a constant offset from the dyadic flow's with no trend in \(J\). The missing implication is still conj:conjugate-class-discrepancy through its primal form; the test is whether the rules the item names give a flow other than the dyadic one, and if so whether its tails change.

Target form. The goal's form is the class bound for the cell-smeared measures, by lem:grid-flow-duality up to constants the cheapest flow's cost; this entry decides, for local routing rules applied square by square in the dyadic flow's order of steps, which flow they produce.

Owed attempt. The previous entry's next attempt, the water-filling reduction, was made: in the run's model the levelled field is the dyadic flow itself, exactly, at every level (lem:sequential-rules-dyadic (b) below), so its per-point values are those of the dyadic flow, with the per-point variance and obstruction of thm:dyadic-flow-obstruction, and the variance step that attempt lacked is that theorem. The Prediction holds, trivially: the gap is \(0\) at every size, fixed by the structure before the run.

General statement. lem:sequential-rules-dyadic: for every \(J\), every count configuration, and every rule applied square by square, level by level from the coarsest, the vertical move of a square before its horizontal moves, that chooses each move's profile from the running field by a crossing map sending a constant crossing load to the constant profile, or by minimizing over the square a sum of strictly convex costs of each coordinate, the points symmetric about the mid-lines; the two kinds may be mixed across steps, squares and levels, the proof working step by step.

Sequential rules reproduce the dyadic flow

Setting. The dyadic flow of the adaptive circulation entry's model (the square flows of the dyadic flow bound entry): on a square of level \(i\) and side \(\rho_i=2^{-i}\), with child excesses \(e_{a,b}\) (\(a\) the horizontal and \(b\) the vertical half), \(E_b=e_{0,b}+e_{1,b}\), \(d_b=(e_{0,b}-e_{1,b})/2\), relative position \(t\) and \(\mathrm{tent}(t)=2\min(t,1-t)\), its coordinate \(2\) is \(v_i=(-E_0/\rho_i)\,\mathrm{tent}(t_2)\) and its coordinate \(1\), on the half \(b\), \(k_i=(-2d_b/\rho_i)\,\mathrm{tent}(t_1)\) (the adaptive circulation entry's script writes \(v\) piecewise; \(E_1=-E_0\), since the excesses sum to zero, makes it this). A sequential rule treats each square \(S\) of level \(j\) in two steps. Vertical step: \(v\) is replaced by \(\varphi(t_1)\,\mathrm{tent}(t_2)\) with \(\bar\varphi=-E_0/\rho_j\) fixed, compensated in coordinate \(1\) by \(-\mathrm{tent}'(t_2)\Phi(t_1)\), \(\Phi'=\varphi-\bar\varphi\), \(\Phi(0)=\Phi(1)=0\). Horizontal step, after it: in each half, \(k\) is replaced by \(\varphi_b(t_2)\,\mathrm{tent}(t_1)\) with mean \(-2d_b/\rho_j\), compensated in coordinate \(2\) by \(-\mathrm{tent}'(t_1)\Psi_b(t_2)\), \(\Psi_b\) vanishing at both ends of the half. Each profile is chosen from the running field (coarser levels, and for the horizontal step also \(S\)'s vertical step), either (i) by a crossing map that reads the crossing coordinate's load along the crossing line and sends a constant load to the constant profile (water-filling, \(\varphi=\bar\varphi-(A_2-\bar A_2)\), the continuum limit of sending each unit across at the less loaded edge, is one), or (ii) by minimizing \(\sum_xC_1(F_1(x))+C_2(F_2(x))\) over the square's points, \(F\) the running field with the step added and \(C_1,C_2\) strictly convex. Points: the square's continuum, or the centres of an even \(m\times m\) grid, symmetric about both mid-lines.

Statement. (a) For every square \(S\) of level \(j\) and every \(i<j\), on all of \(S\) the dyadic flow's level-\(i\) coordinate \(2\) is a function of \(t_2\) alone and its level-\(i\) coordinate \(1\) a function of \(t_1\) alone. (b) Hence every sequential rule of kind (i) or (ii), or mixing the two across steps, squares and levels, produces the dyadic flow exactly. A jointly convex cost \(C(F_1,F_2)\) is not covered: at the paired points both coordinates change at once.

Proof. (a) \(S\) lies inside one square \(T\) of level \(i\) and inside one child of \(T\), since the levels are nested (also when \(S\) is a child of \(T\)), hence inside one half of \(T\) in each direction. On \(T\), \(v_i\) depends on \(t_2\) alone; on each half \(b\) of \(T\), \(k_i\) depends on \(t_1\) alone, and \(S\) lies in one such half. (b) By induction on \(j\); the case \(j=0\) has no coarser field. Let levels \(i<j\) be the dyadic flow's, so on \(S\) the coarser field is \((c_1(t_1),c_2(t_2))\) by (a). Vertical step. For (i), the load \(c_2\) along the mid-line is constant, so \(\varphi=\bar\varphi\) and \(\Phi=0\). For (ii), the coordinate-\(2\) cost is \(\sum_{t_2}\sum_{t_1}C_2(c_2(t_2)+\varphi(t_1)\mathrm{tent}(t_2))\), which for each \(t_2\) is at least its value at \(\varphi\equiv\bar\varphi\) by Jensen's inequality over \(t_1\), the mean of \(\varphi\) being fixed; the coordinate-\(1\) cost pairs \((t_1,t_2)\) with \((t_1,1-t_2)\), where \(\mathrm{tent}'\) changes sign, so it is \(\sum C_1(c_1(t_1)-2\Phi(t_1))+C_1(c_1(t_1)+2\Phi(t_1))\ge\sum2C_1(c_1(t_1))\), its value at \(\Phi=0\); both minima are reached at \(\varphi\equiv\bar\varphi\), uniquely by strict convexity of \(C_2\). So the vertical step is \(v_j\), with no coordinate-\(1\) part. Horizontal step: the running field on \(S\) is now \((c_1(t_1),c_2(t_2)+v_j(t_2))\), and the same argument with the coordinates exchanged, in each half, gives \(\varphi_b\equiv-2d_b/\rho_j\) and \(\Psi_b=0\): the step is \(k_j\). So level \(j\) is the dyadic flow's. \(\square\)

Hypotheses, each with its step. The nesting of dyadic squares: (a). The separable profiles of the dyadic flow (\(v_i\) a function of \(t_2\), \(k_i\) on each half a function of \(t_1\)): (a). The order of the two steps of a square, the vertical first and each chosen from the running field: (b), whose horizontal step uses that the vertical step added nothing to coordinate \(1\); a rule choosing both moves of a square together is outside it, and the Smallest case of the next attempt shows it leaves the dyadic profile. For (i), only that a constant load gives the constant profile; for (ii), convexity of \(C_1,C_2\) and strict convexity of \(C_2\) (of \(C_1\) for the horizontal step) for uniqueness, and the symmetry of the points about the mid-lines for the pairing. The statement holds for every count configuration, with no probability.

Degenerate cases. \(J=1\): one level, no coarser field; both kinds pick the constant profile. Counts all equal: every excess is \(0\), both flows vanish. A rule mapping a constant load to a nonconstant profile (a fixed tilt): outside (i), and it gives another flow, through its compensation. A merely convex \(C\) (such as a linear cost): the dyadic profile is a minimizer, not necessarily the one chosen.

Nonvacuity. The run at \(J=6,\dots,9\), \(N=16\cdot4^J\), eight seeds each (research/results/ultimate_matching_water_filling_20261017/results.json): the water-filling rule, a rule of kind (i), gave per-coordinate variance ratios to the dyadic flow of \(1.000\) and kurtosis gaps of \(0.000\) at every size, the identity (b) states. A member of kind (ii), checked by hand through the proof: \(C_1=C_2=u^4\) on the even grid of the run, the cost the next attempt uses; on each square the coarser field is \((c_1(t_1),c_2(t_2))\), Jensen for \(u^4\) gives the constant profile and the pairing gives \(\Phi=0\), and \(u^4\) is strictly convex, so the choice is the dyadic one. Plainest bound. On one square with no coarser field, the previous entry's Smallest case, a less-loaded rule spreads the crossing evenly, the dyadic profile; the smallest nontrivial case, two levels, is (a) at \(j=1\), which already decides kind (i), and was not taken in the previous entry, whose Smallest case had no coarser load.

Baseline. The construction that needs no idea is the dyadic flow itself; the lemma says these rules give nothing more, for a structural reason: the dyadic flow's coarser load in each coordinate is, on every finer square, a function of that coordinate alone.

The run

Run. research/results/ultimate_matching_water_filling_20261017/water_filling_test.py, its expectations committed before the run; the per-seed times in results.json sum to \(10.6\) s over \(32\) runs, made in parallel. Control 1, the rule with its levelling switched off against the earlier script's dyadic flow: relative difference \(0.0\). Control 2, global averages: difference \(0.0\). Control 3, offered as showing the levelling act, was tautological: the mid-line total right after a step is constant by construction for any rows taken, so it could not fail on any input (the reviewer's finding), and on this model the coarser spread it divides by was \(0\) everywhere, which is (a). Prediction: gap growth from \(J=6\) to \(9\) of \(0.0\) in both coordinates against the band \(0.15\), seed spread \(0.0\), both flows being equal on every seed. The dyadic flow's own per-position kurtosis was \(2.88\)–\(3.11\) in coordinate \(1\) and \(2.96\)–\(3.06\) in coordinate \(2\). The run decided nothing that (b) did not already fix; it is a check of the implementation, and says nothing about rules outside (b).

Architecture test

Architecture test. Not decided. The sixth review's retained test, the gap-charged bound for nested chains, was neither proved nor refuted; this entry shows only that a class of local routing rules reproduces the dyadic flow, whose obstruction is recorded.

Record search. tools/search-claims.py "dyadic flow coarser field constant along mid-line finer square separable profile tent levelling fixed point" returned lem:guided-chain-bound, lem:cut-cell-variance-bound, thm:dyadic-flow-obstruction, ex:greedy-circulation-tails and lem:two-mesh-partition-discrepancy; the reviewer's searches "greedy quartic profile choice per square both coordinates circulation dyadic flow" and "hierarchical flow nested squares separable field constant along line" returned these and lem:grid-flow-duality, lem:discrete-flow-bound and thm:dyadic-flow-square-exponential; none states (a) or (b).

Record comparison. From the record's side: the dyadic flow's square formulas are the dyadic flow bound entry's, written as the adaptive circulation entry's script writes them; thm:dyadic-flow-obstruction's proof uses their scale-invariant coefficient weights for the per-point variance, not the separability on finer squares, which is (a); ex:greedy-circulation-tails added a pyramid circulation per square, chosen by the quartic cost of both coordinates with the square's whole dyadic field, both moves included, in place: the closest recorded analogue of the simultaneous rule, outside the crossing family and chosen with both moves present; it changed the flow (kurtosis lower by \(0.2\)–\(0.3\), without trend), and that its being outside (b) is the reason is judgement, since whether it would change the flow if applied after the vertical step alone was never checked. The reviewer also found the pyramid outside the crossing family: crossing changes are curls of \(\Phi(t_1)\mathrm{tent}(t_2)+\mathrm{tent}(t_1)\Psi_b(t_2)\), and matching the pyramid on both mid-lines leaves \(\mathrm{tent}(t_1)\mathrm{tent}(t_2)/2\), which is \(1/8\) at \((1/4,1/4)\) where the pyramid \(\min(t_1,1-t_1,t_2,1-t_2)\) is \(1/4\) (the two values computed here; the reduction is the reviewer's). So (a) and (b) are new and elementary, and the run checks (b)'s implementation.

New mathematics. lem:sequential-rules-dyadic: in the dyadic flow every coarser level's field is, on every finer square, a function of \(t_2\) in coordinate \(2\) and of \(t_1\) in coordinate \(1\), so every rule that treats each square's vertical and then horizontal move from the running field, by a crossing map sending a constant load to the constant profile (water-filling and less-loaded crossing among them) or by minimizing over the square a sum of strictly convex costs of each coordinate (points symmetric about the mid-lines), produces the dyadic flow exactly, for every count configuration; a jointly convex cost of both coordinates is not covered.
