Two-graph chain duality

17 October 2026 · Working proof, reviewed; strict form of the both-high instance · Mixed levels. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort set by the session).

Chosen. The queue head is two-choice-routing; mixed-level-counts bears on ultimate-matching directly (a refutation of the mixed counts refutes the conjecture), and its third entry in a row, within the spell of four, comes first because the previous entry left its both-high instance with a named attempt.

Question. The column crossing obstruction left the both-high instance, \((4,4)\), \(t_1=\log N\), \(t_2=\sqrt{\log N}\), as a repair whose repaired pairs must carry the strip discrepancy through pairs inside both boxes, and asked whether alternating cycles can do it. The missing implication is the mixed counts there. This entry asks what exactly decides the least number of second-coordinate exceptions over matchings that keep every pair within \(D_1\) horizontally, and answers it by a duality.

Target form. The goal's own form, a matching, at two of its levels, in the strict form that allows no first-coordinate exception (the condition allows two at \(t_1=\log N\)).

Owed attempt. The previous entry named "the cycle repair of the windowed mixed counts entry ... decide whether the alternating cycles can be kept short while doing so", first by testing its untested placement hypothesis. The placement test was made: the per-level construction takes, in each cell, "from each sample its \(k_Q\) points of \(Q\) with the smallest labels" (per-level counts), so its leftovers are uniform in their cells and the hypothesis holds for that construction as recorded; a repair must therefore move good pairs. The cycle bound was replaced, not made: the alternating cycles of a min-cost matching are the primal side of a linear program whose dual is the chain value below, and this entry states that dual exactly; the cycle lengths were not bounded. The duality came first because short cycles are one sufficient route to the count, while the chain value is the count itself, so its form decides which bound a cycle argument must reach, and its length-one part was provable at once. That attempt, named by the windowed entry and left unmade by the column crossing entry and this one, is dropped as an owed attempt: the next attempt asks the chain bound directly, and the cycle composition survives only as the reviewer's unverified primal suggestion below. The earlier named attempts: the low-level entry's "a test-set argument that tolerates \(2Ne^{-t_2}\) second-coordinate exceptions" has, in the strict form, its exact form in the lemma: the best such lower bound is a chain's value, and the best chain value is the least exception count; the windowed entry's composition of \(\pi_2\) and \(\pi_{\max}\) along alternating cycles is a primal upper bound on that count, not evaluated, carried in the next attempt's primal side. The item's earlier entries, read in this session: the low-level mixed counts, whose follow-up says "bounded box ratio and a high second level remain", and the windowed mixed counts, whose follow-up says "a scheme of cells whose leftovers may all violate fails"; this entry's duality is exact for every scheme in the strict form, those included.

General statement. lem:two-graph-chain-duality, for every finite bipartite graph \(H\) on \(X\cup Y\) with \(|X|=|Y|\) and a perfect matching and every cost on its edges with values in \(\{0,1,2,\dots\}\), the two-graph case being the \(0/1\) cost; and its corollary cor:short-chains-per-level, for every pair on or above the curve and levels \(t_2\le t_1\) with \(t_2+\log2\le\log N\).

Two-graph chain duality

Lemma. Let \(H\) be a bipartite graph on \(X\cup Y\), \(|X|=|Y|=N\), with a perfect matching, and \(c\) a cost on its edges with values in \(\{0,1,2,\dots\}\); put \(G_k=\{e\in H:c_e\le k\}\) for \(k\ge0\), and let \(k^*\) be the least cost \(\sum_{e\in\pi}c_e\) of a perfect matching \(\pi\) of \(H\). Call a chain two families \((S_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z}\) of subsets of \(X\) and \((T_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z}\) of \(Y\), both nonincreasing in \(j\), equal to \(X\) and \(Y\) for \(j\) small and empty for \(j\) large, with \(N_{G_k}(S_{j+k})\subseteq T_j\) for every \(j\) and every \(k\ge0\); its value is \(\sum_j(|S_j|-|T_j|)\) and its length the number of \(j\) with \(\varnothing\ne S_j\ne X\). Then \(k^*\) is the largest value of a chain. In particular, for a graph \(G\) and \(c=1\) on the edges of \(H\) outside \(G\) and \(0\) on \(G\cap H\), the conditions are \(N_{G\cap H}(S_j)\subseteq T_j\) and \(N_H(S_{j+1})\subseteq T_j\), and \(k^*\) is the least number of edges outside \(G\) in a perfect matching of \(H\). For real costs \(c\ge0\) the same holds with families \((S_r)\), \((T_r)\) indexed by \(r\in\mathbb R\), conditions \(N_{G_k}(S_{r+k})\subseteq T_r\) for all real \(r\) and \(k\ge0\) (\(G_k\) the edges of cost at most \(k\)), and value \(\int_{\mathbb R}(|S_r|-|T_r|)\,dr\).

Proof. Lower bound: for a chain and a perfect matching \(\pi\) of \(H\), put \(u(x)=\max\{j:x\in S_j\}\) and \(w(y)=\max\{j:y\in T_j\}\), finite by the conditions at the ends. For an edge \(xy\) of \(\pi\), of cost \(k=c_{xy}\), it is an edge of \(G_k\) and \(x\in S_{u(x)}\), so \(y\in N_{G_k}(S_{u(x)})\subseteq T_{u(x)-k}\) and \(w(y)\ge u(x)-c_{xy}\). Summing over the \(N\) edges of \(\pi\), \(\sum_xu(x)-\sum_yw(y)\le\sum_{e\in\pi}c_e\). Layer cake: for an integer \(m\) below every value of \(u\) and \(w\), \(u(x)-m=\sum_{j>m}1[x\in S_j]\) and likewise for \(w\), so, as \(|X|=|Y|\), \(\sum_xu-\sum_yw=\sum_{j>m}(|S_j|-|T_j|)\), which is the chain's value since \(|S_j|=|T_j|=N\) for \(j\le m\). So every chain's value is at most \(k^*\). Upper bound: \(k^*\) is the minimum of \(\sum_ec_ez_e\) over \(z\ge0\) covering every vertex of \(X\cup Y\) once along edges of \(H\), whose constraint matrix, the incidence matrix of a bipartite graph, is totally unimodular, so the minimum \(k^*\) is attained at an integral point; the dual, \(\max\sum_xu_x-\sum_yw_y\) subject to \(u_x-w_y\le c_{xy}\) on the edges of \(H\), has optimal value \(k^*\), and since its constraint matrix is the transpose, also totally unimodular, and \(c\) is integral, every nonempty face of its polyhedron, the optimal face included, contains an integer point. Take such \(u\), \(w\), and \(S_j=\{x:u_x\ge j\}\), \(T_j=\{y:w_y\ge j\}\): an edge \(xy\) of \(G_k\) with \(x\in S_{j+k}\) gives \(w_y\ge u_x-c_{xy}\ge j+k-k=j\), so \(N_{G_k}(S_{j+k})\subseteq T_j\); finitely many integer values make the families nonincreasing with the right ends, and by the layer cake their value is \(\sum u-\sum w=k^*\). Real costs: with \(u(x)=\sup\{r:x\in S_r\}\) and \(w(y)=\sup\{r:y\in T_r\}\), for an edge \(xy\) of \(\pi\) of cost \(c\) and every \(r<u(x)\), \(x\in S_r\), so \(y\in N_{G_c}(S_r)\subseteq T_{r-c}\) and \(w(y)\ge r-c\); the supremum over \(r\) gives \(w(y)\ge u(x)-c_{xy}\), with no attainment needed; the layer cake \(\sum_xu-\sum_yw=\int(|S_r|-|T_r|)\,dr\) holds for any nonincreasing families, \(\{r:x\in S_r\}\) being an interval whose endpoint has measure zero. Upper bound: the primal minimum is attained at a perfect matching by the integrality of the bipartite perfect-matching polytope, for real costs too, so the dual optimum, a real one, has value \(k^*\); its level sets \(\{u\ge r\}\), \(\{w\ge r\}\) satisfy the conditions as above; only the integrality of the dual is dropped. \(\square\)

Corollary. Let \(\alpha_1,\alpha_2\in(0,\infty]\), \(\beta_j=1/\alpha_j\), with \(\beta_1+\beta_2\ge1/2\), \(L\ge L_0(1+\log2)^{\max(\beta_1,\beta_2)}\), \(L_0\) the universal constant of thm:per-level-count-matchings, \(s_1=\sqrt{\log N/N}\), levels \(1\le t_2\le t_1\le\log N\) with \(t_2+\log2\le\log N\), \(D_j=Ls_1t_j^{\beta_j}\), \(H=\{|X^1_i-Y^1_k|\le D_1\}\) and \(G=H\cap\{|X^2_i-Y^2_k|\le D_2\}\), for \(X\), \(Y\) independent uniform samples of size \(N\) in \([0,1]^2\). With probability tending to one, if no vertex of \(Y\) is isolated in \(H\), every chain of length at most one, for the \(0/1\) cost of the lemma, has value at most \(2Ne^{-t_2}\); so if \(H\) has a perfect matching and \(k^*>2Ne^{-t_2}\), a chain of length at least two shows it.

Proof. A matching in \(G\): the per-level matching at level \(t'=t_2+\log2\in[1,\log N]\) has at most \(2Ne^{-t'}=Ne^{-t_2}\) pairs beyond \(L_0s_1t'^{\beta_j}\) in some coordinate; its other pairs are edges of \(G\), since \(L_0t'^{\beta_j}\le L_0(1+\log2)^{\beta_j}t_2^{\beta_j}\le Lt_j^{\beta_j}\) (\(t'\le(1+\log2)t_2\) as \(t_2\ge1\), and \(t_2\le t_1\)); so \(G\) has a matching \(M_G\) leaving at most \(M=Ne^{-t_2}\) vertices of each side uncovered, as many on each side. The chain: with \(u\), \(w\) its level indices as in the lemma's proof, its value is \(\sum_xu(x)-\sum_yw(y)\). Length zero: \(S_j=X\) exactly for \(j\le m_0\); then \(u\equiv m_0\), and \(T_{m_0-1}\supseteq N_H(S_{m_0})=N_H(X)=Y\) (no vertex of \(Y\) is isolated in \(H\)), so \(w\ge m_0-1\). Length one: the index \(m\) with \(\varnothing\ne S_m\ne X\); then \(u\le m\), and \(T_{m-2}\supseteq N_H(S_{m-1})=Y\), so \(w\ge m-2\). Along each edge \(xy\) of \(M_G\), \(w(y)\ge u(x)\) (lemma's proof, cost \(0\)); so the value is at most \(\sum_{x\text{ uncovered}}u(x)-\sum_{y\text{ uncovered}}w(y)\le2M=2Ne^{-t_2}\) in both cases, the two sums having equally many terms. The last clause is the lemma. \(\square\)

Hypotheses, each with its step. Lemma: costs only on the edges of \(H\), so that the graphs \(G_k\) lie in \(H\): the lower bound needs each edge of \(\pi\) in the \(G_k\) of its cost, the upper bound needs every edge of \(G_k\) to be a constraint of the dual; for a graph \(G\) not inside \(H\) the special case reads \(G\cap H\). \(|X|=|Y|\): the layer cake. \(H\) with a perfect matching: the primal's feasibility; without it both sides of "some perfect matching of \(H\) has cost at most \(b\) if and only if every chain has value at most \(b\)" are false, the chain values being unbounded. Bipartiteness: the integrality of the perfect-matching polytope, so that the primal minimum is a perfect matching, for every cost; and, for integer costs, the total unimodularity that gives an integral dual and integer-indexed chains; for real costs only that integrality of the dual is dropped, the chains being indexed by the reals. Corollary: \(\beta_1+\beta_2\ge1/2\) and \(L_0\), for the per-level counts; \(L\ge L_0(1+\log2)^{\max\beta_j}\), \(t_2\le t_1\) and \(t_2+\log2\le\log N\), for the level-\((t_2+\log2)\) box inside \(G\); the samples' law only through that theorem; no vertex of \(Y\) isolated in \(H\), in the step \(N_H(X)=Y\); a perfect matching of \(H\) only for the last clause, through the lemma. No other condition on the exponents.

Degenerate cases. Lemma: \(c\equiv0\) (\(G=H\)): \(k^*=0\), and every chain has value at most \(0\), since \(|S_j|\le|N_H(S_j)|\le|T_j|\) by Hall in \(H\). \(c\equiv1\) (\(G=\varnothing\)): \(k^*=N\), attained by \(S_j=X\) for \(j\le1\), \(T_j=Y\) for \(j\le0\), \(T_1=\varnothing\), \(S_j=\varnothing\) for \(j\ge2\). \(H\) without a perfect matching: excluded; the minimum is over an empty set. \(N=1\): the smallest case, by hand: one edge of \(H\setminus G\) gives \(k^*=1\) and the chain \(S_j=X\) for \(j\le1\), \(T_j=Y\) for \(j\le0\), \(T_1=\varnothing\), of value \(1\). Corollary: a chain of length zero has value at most \(Ne^{-t_2}\), the uncovered \(Y\)-vertices with \(w=m_0-1\); a chain of length one whose \(S_m\) is a single point counts the \(Y\)-vertices outside \(N_H(S_m)\) that have no \(G\)-neighbour, the case a first draft of this proof missed (it bounded the levels below \(m\) by \(0\)), and they are among the uncovered vertices of \(M_G\); \(t_2=t_1\): the per-level matching at level \(t_1+\log2\), inside \(G\) by the condition on \(L\); \(L\) below \(L_0\): outside the statement, the per-level matching then not inside \(G\).

Nonvacuity. On the curve's parameters: \((4,4)\), \(t_1=\log N\), \(t_2=\sqrt{\log N}\), \(D_1=L(\log N)^{3/4}/\sqrt N\), \(D_2=L\sqrt{\log N/N}\,(\log N)^{1/8}\), \(L\ge L_0(1+\log2)^{1/4}\). \(H\) has a perfect matching with probability tending to one: matching the samples in the order of their first coordinates moves each first coordinate by \(O_p(1/\sqrt N)\), below \(D_1\). The corollary's step, the uncovered vertices of the level-\((t_2+\log2)\) matching weighted by the potentials' range, is used, and its \(G\) box holds about \(ND_1D_2=L^2(\log N)^{11/8}\) points of each sample (\(121922\,L^2\) at \(\log N=5000\); research/results/ultimate_matching_chain_duality_20261017/instance.txt). Plainest bound. König on \(G\) alone: \(k^*\ge\max_S(|S|-|N_G(S)|)\), a lower bound only; the plainest upper bound is \(k^*\le N\), and the Leighton–Shor matching of thm:maximum-displacement-curve-threshold, inside \(H\) for \(L\ge K\), bounds \(k^*\) by its pairs beyond \(D_2\), on which the record has no tail bound.

Baseline. König's deficiency for \(G\) alone, which the per-level counts bound; the lemma adds the coupling with \(H\), as the steps \(N_{G_k}(S_{j+k})\subseteq T_j\) between levels, and makes the bound exact.

Architecture test

Architecture test. Not decided. The seventh review's retained test, the gap-charged bound for nested chains of the class function, was not run. The chains here are level sets of the dual potentials of an integer assignment cost, of the same form as the layers of a class function (level sets of a dual potential) but for another cost; no implication between the two is derived.

"per-level cells leftovers chosen near boundary position aware exits Leighton Shor inside cells" returned thm:per-level-count-matchings and ex:simultaneous-rule-tails. Record comparison. From the record's side: lem:grid-flow-duality is Fenchel–Rockafellar duality for convex edge costs of flows on the cell grid, the class side of the conjugate cost; this lemma is the integer assignment duality on the samples' own bipartite graph, Egerváry's weighted form of König's theorem read through level sets, not new as a duality. lem:per-level-gluing-fails concerns nested graphs \(\Gamma_k=\{|x-y|\le e^{k-1}\}\) weighted by \(w_k=e^k\); its matching cost \(\sum_kw_k|M\setminus\Gamma_k|\) is the lemma's real cost \(c_e=\sum_kw_k1[e\notin\Gamma_k]\), finite since the weights over \(k\le K\) sum, on the complete graph, so its least value is the largest real-indexed chain value, while its weighted deficiency sum is not derived here as a chain's value. thm:per-level-count-matchings is used in the corollary only through its statement. New mathematics. lem:two-graph-chain-duality: for a bipartite \(H\) with a perfect matching and an integer cost on its edges (a real cost with real-indexed chains), the least cost of a perfect matching is the largest value \(\sum_j(|S_j|-|T_j|)\) of a nested chain with \(N_{G_k}(S_{j+k})\subseteq T_j\), \(G_k\) the edges of cost at most \(k\); for two graphs, \(N_{G\cap H}(S_j)\subseteq T_j\) and \(N_H(S_{j+1})\subseteq T_j\). cor:short-chains-per-level: on and above the curve, at levels \(t_2\le t_1\) with \(t_2+\log2\le\log N\) and \(L\ge L_0(1+\log2)^{\max\beta_j}\), with probability tending to one, if no vertex of \(Y\) is isolated in \(H\), chains of length at most one have value at most \(2Ne^{-t_2}\).

Exponential-length chain value bound

17 October 2026 · Working proof, reviewed; strict form of the both-high instance · Mixed levels. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort set by the session).

Chosen. The queue head is two-choice-routing; mixed-level-counts bears on ultimate-matching directly (a refutation of the mixed counts refutes the conjecture), and its fourth entry in the spell, the last before its boundary, comes first because the previous entry named the length-two chains as its next attempt.

Question. The two-graph chain duality made the strict both-high question exact: some perfect matching of \(H\) (pairs within \(D_1\) horizontally) has at most \(2Ne^{-t_2}\) pairs beyond \(D_2\) if and only if every chain has value at most \(2Ne^{-t_2}\); it bounded chains of length at most one, and its potential-range argument gave \((\ell+1)Ne^{-t_2}\) for length \(\ell\) at the level \(t_2+\log2\). The missing implication is the bound for every chain. This entry runs that argument at a free level and adds an isolated-point step.

Target form. The goal's own form, a matching, at two of its levels, in the strict form that allows no first-coordinate exception.

Owed attempt. The previous entry named "bound the value of every chain at the both-high instance by \(CNe^{-t_2}\), or exhibit one above \(2Ne^{-t_2}\)", first for chains of length two. Made for chains of length up to \(e^{t'-t_2}\), for a chosen level \(t'\) whose box lies in \(G\) (below); longer chains are not bounded. The item's earlier entries, read in this session: the low-level mixed counts ("bounded box ratio and a high second level remain"), the windowed mixed counts ("a scheme of cells whose leftovers may all violate fails"), the column crossing obstruction ("the per-level cells, whose good pairs do not cross their boundaries") and the two-graph chain duality ("now exactly the bound \(2Ne^{-t_2}\) on chain values").

General statement. thm:bounded-length-chains, for every pair on or above the curve, every \(L>0\), levels \(1\le t_2\le t_1\le\log N\) and every level \(t'\in[1,\log N]\) with \(L_0t'^{\beta_j}\le Lt_j^{\beta_j}\) for both \(j\).

Bounded-length chains

Theorem. Let \(\alpha_1,\alpha_2\in(0,\infty]\), \(\beta_j=1/\alpha_j\), \(\beta_1+\beta_2\ge1/2\), \(L_0\) the universal constant of thm:per-level-count-matchings, \(L>0\), \(s_1=\sqrt{\log N/N}\), levels \(1\le t_2\le t_1\le\log N\), \(D_j=Ls_1t_j^{\beta_j}\), \(H=\{|X^1_i-Y^1_k|\le D_1\}\), \(G=H\cap\{|X^2_i-Y^2_k|\le D_2\}\), \(X\), \(Y\) independent uniform samples of size \(N\) in \([0,1]^2\), and \(t'=t'_N\in[1,\log N]\) with \(L_0t'^{\beta_j}\le Lt_j^{\beta_j}\) for \(j=1,2\). With probability tending to one, every chain of lem:two-graph-chain-duality for the \(0/1\) cost (\(1\) on \(H\setminus G\)) of length \(\ell\) has value at most \((\ell+1)\cdot2Ne^{-t'}\), and at most \(\ell\cdot2Ne^{-t'}\) if moreover \(N\min(D_1,1)\min(D_2,1)\ge(1+\delta)\log N\) for a fixed \(\delta>0\). In particular every chain of length \(\ell\le e^{t'-t_2}\) has value at most \(2Ne^{-t_2}\) under the second condition, and every one of length \(\ell\le e^{t'-t_2}-1\) under the first alone.

Proof. A matching in \(G\): the per-level matching at level \(t'\) has at most \(M=2Ne^{-t'}\) pairs beyond \(L_0s_1t'^{\beta_j}\) in some coordinate; its other pairs lie in \(G\), as \(L_0s_1t'^{\beta_j}\le D_j\); being a bijection, it leaves, after its other pairs are dropped, equally many, \(k\le M\), vertices of each side uncovered; call the rest \(M_G\). The chain: with \(m\) its first proper index, \(S_j=X\) for \(j<m\) and \(S_j=\varnothing\) for \(j\ge m+\ell\); its level indices \(u\), \(w\) (lemma's proof) have \(u\le m+\ell-1\), and \(T_{m-2}\supseteq N_H(S_{m-1})=N_H(X)\), which is \(Y\) when no point of \(Y\) is isolated in \(H\), so \(w\ge m-2\). Its value is \(\sum_xu(x)-\sum_yw(y)\); along each edge \(xy\) of \(M_G\), of cost \(0\), \(w(y)\ge u(x)\); so the value is at most \(\sum_{x\text{ uncovered}}u(x)-\sum_{y\text{ uncovered}}w(y)\le k(\ell+1)\). Isolated points: a point \(y\) of \(Y\) has no \(G\)-neighbour only if no point of \(X\) lies in \(\{|x^1-y^1|\le D_1,|x^2-y^2|\le D_2\}\cap[0,1]^2\), whose area is at least \(\min(D_1,1)\min(D_2,1)\) (each one-sided interval meets \([0,1]\) in length at least \(\min(D_j,1)\)); given \(Y\), this has probability at most \(\exp(-N\min(D_1,1)\min(D_2,1))\le N^{-(1+\delta)}\) under the second condition, and a union over the \(N\) points of \(Y\), using only the independence of the \(X\)-points, leaves \(N^{-\delta}\to0\). On that event \(N_G(X)=Y\), so \(T_{m-1}\supseteq N_G(S_{m-1})=Y\), \(w\ge m-1\), and the bound is \(k\ell\). The same union with \(H\) in place of \(G\) gives no isolated point of \(H\) under the first condition alone, the area being at least \(\min(D_1,1)\), and \(ND_1\ge L\sqrt{N\log N}\to\infty\) faster than \(\log N\). Length zero: value at most \(k\) under the first condition and \(0\) under the second. The last sentence: \(\ell\cdot2Ne^{-t'}\le2Ne^{-t_2}\) when \(\ell\le e^{t'-t_2}\). \(\square\)

Hypotheses, each with its step. \(\beta_1+\beta_2\ge1/2\), \(L_0\) and \(t'\in[1,\log N]\): the per-level counts at level \(t'\); \(L_0t'^{\beta_j}\le Lt_j^{\beta_j}\): the level-\(t'\) box inside \(G\), for each \(j\) separately; \(N\min(D_1,1)\min(D_2,1)\ge(1+\delta)\log N\): no isolated \(Y\)-point in \(G\), by the union bound over the \(N\) points, given \(Y\), using only the independence of the \(X\)-points; it holds, for instance, whenever \(D_j\le1\) and \(L^2t_1^{\beta_1}t_2^{\beta_2}\ge1+\delta\). \(t_2\le t_1\) is not used by the proof, only by the choice of \(t'\) through the box condition. The chain's length enters only through the range of its level indices. The bound holds for every chain simultaneously, on events that involve no chain, for the one level \(t'\) chosen.

Degenerate cases. Theorem: \(t'=t_2\) (possible when \(L\ge L_0\) and \(t_2\le t_1\)): chains of length at most one have value at most \(2Ne^{-t_2}\) under the second condition, at level \(t_2\) itself, where the previous corollary used \(t_2+\log2\) and two lengths' worth of range; \(\ell=0\): value \(0\) under the second condition; isolated points (the second condition failing): the lowest level need not hold all of \(Y\), and the range is \(\ell+1\), the previous entry's bound with \(t'\) free; \(t'>\log N\): outside the per-level theorem's levels.

Nonvacuity. On the curve's parameters: \((4,4)\), \(t_1=\log N\), \(t_2=\sqrt{\log N}\), \(t'=2t_2\), and every \(L\ge\max(1.19L_0,0.21)\) (\(2^{1/4}=1.189\), the box condition for \(j=2\); for \(j=1\) it needs \(L\ge L_0\), implied, as \(t'\le t_1\)): \(t'=141.4\le\log N=5000\), chains up to length \(e^{70.7}\); the isolation condition reads \(L^2t_1^{1/4}t_2^{1/4}=24.4L^2\ge1+\delta\), so \(L\ge0.21\) suffices for small \(\delta\), and at \(L=1.19\) the isolation exponent of \(N\) is \(-33.5\) (research/results/ultimate_matching_bounded_chains_20261017/instance.txt); the isolated-point step is used. Plainest bound. The previous entry's own argument with the level free, which is this theorem's first bound: \((\ell+1)\cdot2Ne^{-t'}\), so every chain of length up to \(e^{t'-t_2}-1\) has value at most \(2Ne^{-t_2}\); at the corollary's fixed level \(t_2+\log2\) it gives \(3Ne^{-t_2}\) at length two, and level \(t_2+\log3\) already settles length two.

Baseline. cor:short-chains-per-level's argument with its level left free, the first bound of the theorem: choosing the level by the chain's length is that argument, not a new step. The theorem adds the isolated-point step, which replaces \(\ell+1\) by \(\ell\): a factor \(\ell/(\ell+1)\), one more length \(e^{t'-t_2}\) at each level, and at length one the removal of the corollary's shift to \(t_2+\log2\).

Follow-up. Continuing. The item's readings: the mixed counts at every pair of levels, proved at low second levels; at the both-high instance, in the strict form, the bound on every chain's value, now proved for chains of length up to \(e^{t'-t_2}\); in the condition's form not reduced. A chain of length \(\ell\) whose proper levels repeat one set \(S\): for \(j\) from \(m\) to \(m+\ell-2\), \(T_j\supseteq N_H(S_{j+1})=N_H(S)\), so each such term is at most \(|S|-|N_H(S)|\le0\), by Hall in \(H\), which has a perfect matching (the lemma's hypothesis); the chain's value is then at most that of its length-one shortening at the last level, so an optimal chain gains nothing by repeating a set, and a long optimal chain must change its sets at most levels. Prevention. The class is a comparison with a recorded result evaluated at the parameter values its statement fixes rather than at the range its proof allows; the Plainest bound rule names "the record's oldest applicable lemma" but not the free parameters of its proof, which AGENTS.md's rule on free parameters asks only of a new statement. That rule now covers a cited result's proof as well (AGENTS.md, order of work, commit of 17 October 2026): a recorded bound used as a baseline is run with each of its proof's free parameters at its whole range. Meta. This entry's mistakes share a way of working: reading a recorded result through its statement as written, its levels and its relations fixed, rather than through what its proof and the lemma's two directions give; it shows in every Plainest bound and Record comparison, where a result's statement is the easy thing to quote. Its change is in the Spin prompt's self-review step (PROMPTS.md, commit of 17 October 2026): a recorded result an entry compares itself with is reread through its proof, and each relation the entry states is derived from that proof and any duality in the record. For the stand-in review's right objections (2) to (5): the way of working behind them is treating a gate's paragraph or a reply's sentence as the end of a duty, so that a push blocker is mentioned rather than filed, a retry is sent rather than its refusal quoted, a queued item is cited rather than the stage changed, and a Meta repeats its Prevention; it shows wherever a written form is taken for the act it reports. The change is in AGENTS.md's order of work, whose rule that a required paragraph is checked for what it establishes in the case at hand now covers replies: a reply's sentence about a blocker, a retry or a prevention reports the act done, with its file or commit, or names it undone.

Exceedance slopes at J = 5, 6

17 October 2026 · Finite check, reviewed; J = 7 not run · Routing rules. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort set by the session).

Where we stand. Unchanged: a finite check at J = 5, 6; Where we stand states no routing measurement, and none of its statements changes

Question. The item two-choice-routing asks whether a routing rule can give per-point flow values lighter-tailed than the dyadic flow's (near-Gaussian at the sizes measured, by Control 1 below), as the open statement conj:conjugate-class-discrepancy needs of a flow at exponents above \(2\) (thm:dyadic-flow-obstruction excludes the dyadic flow there). The simultaneous rule exceedances entry measured the simultaneous rule's per-point tail at \(3.3\) standard deviations as \(0.25\)–\(0.36\) of the dyadic flow's at \(J=6,7\), and left open whether that lighter shape is fixed or drifts back toward the Gaussian as \(J\) grows. The test: the slope in \(t\) of the log-ratio of the two flows' exceedance fractions, at \(J=5\) and \(J=7\), with one estimator at every size and the spread from many splits of the seeds. What would end the test: the \(J=7\) slope against the \(J=5\) one, within or beyond twice their combined spread.

Target form. A flow's per-point values, the primal side of the class bound; not the goal's own form, a matching, but its flow bound (thm:dyadic-flow-square-exponential's route).

Owed attempt. The previous entry on the item named "the reviewer's first suggestion, the fixed-estimator curve, made to decide between a fixed-shape lighter law and one returning to the dyadic flow's": made in part. The run finished \(J=5\) and \(J=6\); Claude Code stopped it during \(J=7\), after \(277\) s, because the machine was critically low on memory while the session was idle, the job's own budget not exceeded. The restart was filed in user_requests and withdrawn the same day, once the measured spreads showed that \(J=7\) at \(512\) seeds could not decide the question (Power, below). The item's earlier entries, read through their statements and follow-ups: "Straight-cut forced flux is cheap", whose follow-up begins "what a two-choice routing cannot change: (a)–(c) answer it"; "Sequential rules reproduce the dyadic flow", whose follow-up says "a rule that chooses a square's two moves together, not covered by (b), and the next attempt"; "Simultaneous rule lowers pooled kurtosis", whose follow-up says "the rule itself lowers the pooled kurtosis by about \(0.4\) at the sizes run, with its trend undecided"; and the simultaneous rule exceedances entry.

General statement. No all-parameter claim is proved here: the entry registers the finite check ex:exceedance-curve-slopes, bearing on conj:conjugate-class-discrepancy through the flow route.

The run

Script. research/results/ultimate_matching_exceedance_curve_20261017/curve_test.py, committed with its expectations, controls and Prediction before the run (commit "Exceedance curve script for two-choice-routing, before its run"); a plumbing run at \(J=3,4\) with \(32\) seeds ran end to end first. The flows are the simultaneous rule entry's, imported unchanged, on a grid of \(G=2^{J+1}\) positions per side, \(4^{J+1}\) per seed; at each \(J\), \(512\) seeds, each position centred and standardized across all the seeds for each flow, exceedance fractions pooled over seeds and positions at \(t=2.6,3.0,3.3,3.6\), the log-ratio rule over dyadic fitted as a line in \(t\), and the spread of each slope as half the standard deviation of the half-slope difference over \(200\) random half-splits (first-order; the halves share the standardization, so they are slightly dependent). Output beside the script: partial_J5_J6.txt (the run), partial_summary.txt (its slopes and ratios), gaussian_slopes.txt (each flow against the Gaussian and the counts, written by summarize_partial.py, which reads the grid from the rule's run()), power_seeds.txt (the spreads against the change to be seen).

Results. Slopes of the log-ratio rule over dyadic, with their spreads: coordinate \(1\), \(-1.281\pm0.298\) at \(J=5\) and \(-1.348\pm0.225\) at \(J=6\); coordinate \(2\), \(-0.772\pm0.214\) and \(-0.482\pm0.271\); each change within twice the combined spread (\(0.747\), \(0.690\)). The ratio at \(3.3\): \(0.248\) and \(0.239\) in coordinate \(1\), \(0.329\) and \(0.361\) in coordinate \(2\), in line with the previous entry's \(0.25\)–\(0.36\) at \(J=6,7\). Against the Gaussian instead of the dyadic flow (gaussian_slopes.txt, without spreads): the rule's slopes are \(-1.297\) and \(-1.471\) in coordinate \(1\) and \(-0.479\) and \(-0.377\) in coordinate \(2\); the dyadic flow's own are \(-0.016\) and \(-0.123\) in coordinate \(1\) and \(+0.293\) and \(+0.105\) in coordinate \(2\). So most of coordinate \(2\)'s change in the ratio slope, \(0.29\), is the dyadic flow's own: its fractions over the Gaussian rise with \(t\) at \(J=5\) (\(1.03\), \(1.10\), \(1.15\), \(1.42\)), a trend in \(t\) resting on \(944\) dyadic exceedances at \(3.6\), not on a small count; against the Gaussian the rule's coordinate-\(2\) slope changes by \(0.10\). Control 1: the dyadic fractions within a factor \(1.42\) of the Gaussian, inside the committed \(1.5\). Positive control: the planted law \(\mathrm{sign}(D)|D|^{0.8}\) has slopes \(-2.828\pm0.396\) and \(-2.624\pm0.608\) in coordinate \(1\) and \(-2.882\pm0.395\) and \(-2.492\pm0.630\) in coordinate \(2\), negative and equal within twice the combined spread; being a fixed transform of the dyadic values, it shows that a fixed lighter shape reads as a negative slope and could not have failed on a drift; at \(J=5\), \(t=3.6\) it rests on \(10\) and \(12\) exceedances. The Prediction, on \(J=5\) against \(J=7\): not decided, \(J=7\) not run.

Power. The script's committed decisiveness line estimated a slope standard error near \(0.096\) from Poisson counts with independent positions; the measured spreads are \(0.21\)–\(0.30\), two to three times larger, the positions of one seed being correlated. Twice the \(J=5\) spread alone, \(0.596\) and \(0.428\) (power_seeds.txt), already exceeds a drift of order \(1/J\) on coordinate \(1\) (about \(0.29\)), so whatever the \(J=7\) spread, \(J=7\) at \(512\) seeds cannot decide such a drift, still less one of order \(1/\sqrt J\) (\(0.12\)–\(0.15\)); the restart was withdrawn. The limit is the seed count: the spread falls like \(1/\sqrt S\), and with the \(J=7\) spread taken equal to the \(J=6\) one a bound of \(0.29\) needs about \(5.7\) to \(6.6\) times as many seeds, \(2900\) to \(3400\) (power_seeds.txt).

What it does not show. Two sizes give a difference, not a trend; the ratio slopes mix the rule's tail with the dyadic flow's departure from the Gaussian at finite \(J\), largest in coordinate \(2\) at \(J=5\); the thresholds reach \(3.6\) standard deviations, far below the \(\sqrt{\log N}\) scale the conjugate class tests; why the rule's tail is lighter in coordinate \(1\) than in coordinate \(2\), by a factor near \(3\) in the slope against the Gaussian, is not examined, though lem:equalized-flow-separable, which makes the coordinate-\(1\) part of the rule's family the transposed dyadic flow, bears on it.

Nonvacuity. The Prediction as committed could fail where its bound, twice the combined spread, is smaller than the change: at \(J=5\) against \(J=6\) the bounds were \(0.69\) and \(0.75\) and the changes \(0.29\) and \(0.07\); at \(J=7\) a coordinate-\(2\) ratio slope above \(-0.772+2\sqrt{0.214^2+s_7^2}\) would refute it, \(-0.11\) for a \(J=7\) spread \(s_7=0.25\) and \(-0.19\) for \(s_7=0.20\). Plainest bound. For Gaussian per-point values the slope against the Gaussian is \(0\) at every \(J\); the rule's stays near \(-1.3\) to \(-1.5\) in coordinate \(1\) and \(-0.4\) to \(-0.5\) in coordinate \(2\).

Architecture test

Architecture test. Not decided. The seventh review's retained test, the gap-charged bound for nested chains of the class function, was not run.

Record comparison. ex:simultaneous-rule-exceedances measured the ratio at two thresholds at \(J=6,7\) from one split; this run adds \(J=5\), four thresholds, the slope and its spread over many splits, with per-position centring; its \(J=6\) ratios agree. ex:simultaneous-rule-tails measured this rule's pooled kurtosis at \(J=6,7,8\), \(0.36\)–\(0.44\) below the dyadic flow's, its trend undecided, the same drift question by another statistic. ex:greedy-circulation-tails measured another rule's kurtosis at \(J=6\)–\(10\) and does not bear on this rule. thm:dyadic-flow-obstruction proves a lower bound for the dyadic flow, that for each fixed \(L\), with probability tending to one, \(\int\psi_\alpha(4|\Phi_k|/(L\sqrt{N\log N}))\) exceeds every constant for each \(\alpha>2\), from a per-point variance of order \(N\log N\) and a block lower tail; it does not state the per-point law Gaussian, and Control 1 compares the dyadic fractions with the Gaussian ones as a measured baseline at these sizes, not as the theorem's consequence.

New mathematics. ex:exceedance-curve-slopes: at \(J=5,6\), over \(512\) seeds each, the simultaneous rule's per-point exceedance fractions over \(t=2.6\)–\(3.6\) fall below the Gaussian ones with log-slope about \(-1.3\) to \(-1.5\) in coordinate \(1\) and \(-0.4\) to \(-0.5\) in coordinate \(2\); the slopes of its ratio to the dyadic flow change between the sizes by less than twice their split spreads (\(0.21\)–\(0.30\) each), and the dyadic flow's own departure from the Gaussian, up to a factor \(1.42\), accounts for most of the coordinate-\(2\) change; at these spreads \(J=7\) at \(512\) seeds could not decide a drift of order \(1/J\), which would need about six times the seeds if the \(J=7\) spread equals the \(J=6\) one, and was not run.

Goal progress. Unchanged: a finite check at small \(J\). Bearing. None at the goal's own parameters: the slopes are measured at \(J\le6\) and at most \(3.6\) standard deviations, while the class bound at exponent \(4\) concerns tails at \(\sqrt{\log N}\) standard deviations as \(N\to\infty\); what the cycle could have given is a constant slope from \(J=5\) to \(J=7\), evidence that the rule's lighter tail is a fixed shape and the rule a candidate flow beyond the dyadic obstruction, and its measured spreads show that \(512\) seeds cannot give it at \(J=7\).

Follow-up

Follow-up. Continuing. The item's readings: what a routing cannot change, answered (lem:straight-cut-forced-flux); sequential rules, the dyadic flow (lem:sequential-rules-dyadic); the simultaneous rule, lighter-tailed per point at \(J=5,6,7\) by a factor \(3\) to \(4\) at \(3.3\) standard deviations, its drift with \(J\) out of reach of tail counts at \(512\) seeds; the discrete two-choice rule with integer units, not examined. Smallest case. Run, at \(J=2\), \(N=256\), \(14000\) seeds (per_level_smallest.py, run without its expectations committed first and testing no statement; per_level_J2.json beside it): the per-level increments, each standardized per position across seeds, have pooled excess kurtosis \(0.024\) and \(0.051\) (coordinate \(1\)) and \(-0.035\) and \(0.000\) (coordinate \(2\)) for the dyadic flow at levels \(0\) and \(1\), and \(-0.514\) and \(-0.301\), \(-0.564\) and \(-0.308\) for the rule; the two levels' increments are uncorrelated at each position for both flows (mean correlation below \(0.01\) in absolute value); at each position the full field's excess is compared with the value independent levels would give there, \(\sum_j\kappa_j(x)v_j(x)^2/(\sum_jv_j(x))^2\) from that position's level variances and excesses, and the difference averaged over the \(64\) positions, with its spread over \(20\) random half-splits: for the rule the full excess averages \(-0.479\) and \(-0.492\) against \(-0.278\) and \(-0.294\), a gap of \(-0.202\pm0.010\) and \(-0.198\pm0.009\); for the dyadic flow the gap is \(-0.000\pm0.009\) and \(-0.009\pm0.010\), its control. (A first, pooled form of the independent-levels value, pooled excesses with position-averaged variances, gave a factor near \(2\) for both flows alike and was replaced on the reviewer's third pass.) So at \(J=2\) the rule's levels are uncorrelated but not independent: beyond what independent levels give, their joint fourth-order dependence lowers the full field's excess by about \(0.20\), where the dyadic flow's lowers it by at most \(0.01\); the levels' small correlation (about \(-0.006\)) shifts \((\sum_jv_j)^2\) by about \(1\%\) and the excess by about \(0.003\) of that gap (the reviewer's fourth check). Nontrivial because: at \(J=2\) the rule's level-\(1\) step reads the level-\(0\) field and chooses each square's crossing profiles to minimize the quartic load of the running field, so the cross-level dependence the attempt measures is already present, while \(J=1\) has one level and no such dependence. Own statements. The plainest bound below says that a per-level shortfall bounded below, alone, cannot keep the full field non-Gaussian, so the reviewer's suggestion as worded is not decisive; what can is the cross-level part seen at \(J=2\), and ex:simultaneous-rule-tails' pooled gap of about \(0.4\) at \(J=6\)–\(8\), of the order of the \(J=2\) full shortfall rather than of a value falling like \(1/J\), is consistent with it without testing it (pooled, not per-position, standardization). Against it stands the unverified argument recorded in the straight-cut entry's reviewer's suggestions, that "the rule's per-edge totals are near-Gaussian like the dyadic flow's", with its step "to be proved": the next attempt measures the quantity that argument predicts small. ex:simultaneous-rule-exceedances gives this rule's tail ratios at \(3.3\) standard deviations at \(J=6,7\) (\(0.245\) and \(0.309\) in coordinate \(1\), \(0.364\) and \(0.330\) in coordinate \(2\)), tails and not cumulants by level distance, so it decides nothing of the attempt; it is the tail-side reading the attempt's outcome must agree with. ex:greedy-circulation-tails concerns another rule, the dyadic flow plus a greedy circulation per square, whose kurtosis after division by the dyadic flow's analytic per-position standard deviation is \(2.71\)–\(2.89\) against \(2.88\)–\(3.19\), "lower at every size with no trend in \(J\)" over \(J=6\)–\(10\): it does not concern the simultaneous rule's levels and decides nothing here, and it is a second rule on which the same cumulant-by-distance measurement can run. Next attempt: at \(J=3\) to \(6\), per position, the joint fourth cumulants \(\kappa(X_i,X_i,X_j,X_j)\) and \(\kappa(X_i,X_i,X_i,X_j)\) of the level increments as functions of \(|i-j|\), normalized by \((\sum_jv_j)^2\), with the exact control that all of them together sum to the full field's fourth cumulant (the reviewer's third pass, unverified until run). The full gap against independent levels is not itself decisive: cross terms only between nearby levels, with comparable variances, add \(O(J)\) terms of size \(O(1/J^2)\), so they too vanish like \(1/J\); a full excess bounded away from \(0\) needs fourth-order dependence that does not decay with \(|i-j|\), or variance concentrated in a few levels, and the cumulants by distance say which. Artefacts to rule out there: pooling positions of unequal variance (avoided per position), the finest levels' fixed local optimization, the seeds' noise on an excess (about \(\sqrt{24/S}\) per position), and the Newton step's convergence, unchecked in these runs. Plainest bound. For increments independent across levels with variances \(v_j\) and excess kurtoses \(\kappa_j\), the sum's excess is \(\sum_j\kappa_jv_j^2/(\sum_jv_j)^2\), at most \(\max_j|\kappa_j|\max_jv_j/\sum_jv_j\) in absolute value, of order \(1/J\) when the \(v_j\) are comparable; the dyadic flow's increments are functions of nested cell counts, not independent, and their near-zero correlation at \(J=2\) is measured, not proved. Record search. "exceedance slope log ratio thresholds per position tails lighter than Gaussian sizes drift dyadic flow rule".

Process assessment. The first launch was written from memory: it named a phase category the timing tool does not have and gave no kernel reason, which compute.sh asks of a Python run allowed more than \(120\) s; both refusals came before any work, and the relaunch used the reason the earlier run of the same flows (session um-exceed) had recorded. The launcher's refusals are the check for the launch, and they stopped both faults before any work ran. For the ratio read as one part's change, and for the power estimate: a rule in COMPUTATION_RULES.md's numerical-verification section (a ratio is read after each part beside its baseline; a committed decisiveness estimate is set beside the measured spread before a next size is called decisive), a rule because no text check can judge whether a ratio was decomposed. For the typed constant: the rule that every quoted number is read by a script, which the typed constant broke inside a script, now says that a summarizing script reads the computation's constants from the generating code or its output (COMPUTATION_RULES.md, persistence section), and summarize_partial.py does so, refusing to run if it cannot find the grid line.

Meta. The way of working behind all three is filling in a quantity from my picture of the computation (a flag, a ratio's meaning, a grid size) when the computation's own record is at hand; it shows wherever a number is restated rather than reread. Flows keeping dyadic square means fail

17 October 2026 · Working proofs, reviewed, and one finite check · Routing rules. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort set by the session).

Question. The item two-choice-routing asks whether a routing rule can give per-point flow values lighter-tailed than the dyadic flow's, as conj:conjugate-class-discrepancy needs of a flow at exponents above \(2\) through the flow bound. The missing implication: which property of a level-by-level flow decides its cost \(\int\psi_\alpha(4|\Phi_k|/(L\sqrt{N\log N}))\) at \(\alpha>2\). At \((4,4)\) the integral is decided where \(|\Phi_k|/\sqrt{N\log N}\) is of order \(\sqrt{\log N}\), a large deviation of a sum of about \(\log N\) level increments; there the per-point tail is set by the conditional law of the increments, not by a kurtosis, which measures the central scale. This entry proves that the cost diverges for every flow whose level steps keep the dyadic square means, whatever its rule, and, more generally, for every adapted local field that keeps a conditional push along its running sum. What ends the test: the proofs.

Target form. A flow's per-point values, the primal side of the class bound (the flow bound of thm:dyadic-flow-square-exponential's route, which lem:grid-flow-duality makes equivalent up to constants to the discrete class); not the goal's own form, a matching.

Owed attempt. The previous entry named "the joint fourth cumulants \(\kappa(X_i,X_i,X_j,X_j)\) and \(\kappa(X_i,X_i,X_i,X_j)\) of the level increments as functions of \(|i-j|\)" at \(J=3\) to \(6\): not made; another came first, for a reason found in this cycle: a fourth cumulant measures the per-point law at the central scale, while the cost at \(\alpha>2\) is decided at \(\sqrt{\log N}\) standard deviations (Question), so the cumulants could not decide the item at the goal's exponent; the theorem below decides it for every rule that keeps the square means. The item's earlier entries, read in this cycle's session through their follow-ups: "Straight-cut forced flux is cheap" ("what a two-choice routing cannot change: (a)–(c) answer it"), "Sequential rules reproduce the dyadic flow" ("the item's rule as a sequential rule, crossing or cost-greedy, answered here, the dyadic flow"), "Simultaneous rule lowers pooled kurtosis" ("sequential rules, the dyadic flow (lem:sequential-rules-dyadic); the simultaneous rule, here"), "Rule's per-point tails lighter at 3.3σ" ("the simultaneous rule, whose per-point tail at \(3.3\) standard deviations is lighter than Gaussian") and "Exceedance slopes at J = 5, 6" ("its drift with \(J\) out of reach of tail counts at \(512\) seeds").

General statement. thm:square-mean-flow-obstruction: every local level-by-level field whose level-\(j\) step has, on every level-\(j\) square, the mean the dyadic step has there (which every flow whose level steps stay inside the dyadic squares with zero normal flux has) costs more than every constant at every exponent above \(2\), for every \(L\), with probability tending to one. lem:conditional-push-obstruction is the pointwise form: a conditional push along the running sum, at every fine level and on a set of points of measure \(N^{-\gamma}\), forces the same.

Setting

\(X_1,\dots,X_N\) i.i.d. uniform on \([0,1]^2\); \(\mathcal F_j\) the \(\sigma\)-field of the counts of all dyadic squares of level at most \(j\); \(n_S\) the count of a square \(S\); \(S_j(x)\) the level-\(j\) square containing \(x\); \(\rho_j=2^{-j}\). A level-by-level field is \(\Phi=\sum_{j<J}\Phi_j\), each \(\Phi_j\) a jointly measurable, locally integrable random field on \([0,1]^2\times\Omega\) with values in \(\mathbb R^2\), \(\mathcal F_{j+1}\)-measurable; it need not be a flow. It is local if for every \(i\le j<J\) and every level-\(i\) square \(T\), \(\Phi_j\) on \(T\) is a function of \(\mathcal F_i\) and the points in \(T\). The depth satisfies \(\kappa\log N\le N4^{-J}\le K\log N\), \(0<\kappa\le K\) fixed. A square \(Q\) of level \(i\) is good if \(n_Q\ge N4^{-i}/2\), and \(B_j(x)\in\mathcal F_j\) is the event that \(S_i(x)\) is good for every \(i\le j\). For \(\alpha\in(2,\infty)\), \(\psi_\alpha(u)=e^{u^\alpha}-1\); \(\psi_\infty(u)=N(u-1)_+\); \(m=\lfloor\theta\log_2N\rfloor\), \(j_1=J-m\), \(u_N=4mh/(L\sqrt{N\log N})\) for a push size \(h\).

Exceptional counts (used twice). A level-\(i\) count is binomial with mean \(N4^{-i}\ge\kappa\log N\); by Chernoff's bound it is below half its mean with probability at most \(e^{-N4^{-i}/8}\), and \(\sum_{i\le J}e^{-N4^{-i}/8}\le\sum_{r\ge0}e^{-4^r\kappa\log N/8}\le2N^{-\kappa/8}\) for large \(N\). So for every \(x\), \(P(B_J(x)^c)\le2N^{-\kappa/8}\), and the expected total area of bad squares of each level is at most the same sum's term for that level.

Square-mean flow obstruction

Statement. Let \(k\in\{1,2\}\), \(0<\theta<\min(1/1542,\kappa/6160)\) fixed, and \(\Phi\) a level-by-level field local at level \(j_1=J-\lfloor\theta\log_2N\rfloor\) (for every level-\(j_1\) square \(T\) and \(j\ge j_1\), \(\Phi_j\) on \(T\) is a function of \(\mathcal F_{j_1}\) and the points in \(T\)), and suppose that for every \(j_1\le j<J\) and every level-\(j\) square \(S\), \[\int_S\Phi_{j,k}\,dx=\frac{\rho_j}2\,\epsilon_S\,E_k(S),\qquad E_k(S)=n_{S,k}^{\rm low}-\frac{n_S}2,\] where \(n^{\rm low}_{S,k}\) counts the points of \(S\) in its lower half in coordinate \(k\) (bottom half for \(k=2\), left half for \(k=1\)) and \(\epsilon_S\in\{-1,1\}\) is \(\mathcal F_j\)-measurable (a fixed sign convention, or one varying with the level or the square); the coarser steps \(\Phi_j\), \(j<j_1\), are unrestricted beyond measurability. Then for every \(L>0\), \(\alpha\in(2,\infty]\) and \(M\), with probability tending to one, \(I_k=\int\psi_\alpha(4|\Phi_k|/(L\sqrt{N\log N}))\,dx\ge M\). The condition holds for every \(\Phi_j\) supported in the level-\(j\) squares with zero normal flux on their boundaries and divergence \(\epsilon'(\nu_{j+1}-\nu_j)\) on each, \(\nu_i=\sum_Q(n_Q/|Q|)1_Q\) over the level-\(i\) squares (weakly: \(\int_S\Phi_j\cdot\nabla g=-\epsilon'\int_Sg(\nu_{j+1}-\nu_j)\) for \(g\in C^1(\bar S)\)).

Proof. The mean condition. For such \(\Phi_j\), take \(g=x_k-c_k(S)\), \(c(S)\) the centre: \(\nu_j\) is constant on \(S\) and \(\int_Sg=0\), and on each child \(S'\), \(\nu_{j+1}=n_{S'}/|S'|\) and \(\int_{S'}g=\pm\frac{\rho_j}4|S'|\), minus for the two lower children; so \(\int_S\Phi_{j,k}=-\epsilon'\frac{\rho_j}4(n^{\rm up}-n^{\rm low})=\epsilon'\frac{\rho_j}2E_k(S)\), since \(n^{\rm up}-n^{\rm low}=-2E_k(S)\).

A walk on square means. For a level-\(j\) square \(S\) let \(U_j(S)=|S|^{-1}\int_SR_j\), \(R_j=\sum_{i<j}\Phi_{i,k}\), which is \(\mathcal F_j\)-measurable, and \(\xi_S=|S|^{-1}\int_S\Phi_{j,k}=\epsilon_S E_k(S)/(2\rho_j)\) for \(j\ge j_1\). For each child \(S'\) let \(\delta_{S'}=U_{j+1}(S')-U_j(S)-\xi_S\), which is \(\mathcal F_{j+1}\)-measurable. The four children have equal area, so the mean over \(S\) of \(R_j+\Phi_{j,k}\) is the average of its means over the children, and \(\sum_{S'}\delta_{S'}=0\). With \(\sigma_S=\operatorname{sign}U_j(S)\) (\(+1\) at \(0\)), let \(S'_*\) be the first child, in a fixed order, with \(\sigma_S\delta_{S'}\ge0\). Then \(|U_{j+1}(S'_*)|\ge\sigma_S(U_j(S)+\xi_S+\delta_{S'_*})\ge|U_j(S)|+\sigma_S\xi_S\).

The push of a square mean. Given \(\mathcal F_j\), the \(n_S\) points of \(S\) are i.i.d. uniform in \(S\), and \(E_k(S)=\sum_{z\in S}(1\{z\text{ lower}\}-\frac12)\) is a sum of i.i.d. terms of mean \(0\), variance \(\frac14\) and size \(\frac12\), standard deviation \(s=\sqrt{n_S}/2\). If \(S\) is good, \(s\ge\rho_j\sqrt{N/8}\); lem:block-lower-tail at \(x=1\), applied to the terms multiplied by \(\epsilon_S\sigma_S\) (\(\mathcal F_j\)-measurable), needs \(128\le n_S\) and \(\frac14\le s^2/256\), that is \(n_S\ge256\), true for large \(N\) since \(n_S\ge\kappa\log N/2\); it gives \(P(\sigma_S\xi_S\ge h\mid\mathcal F_j)\ge p_0:=64^{-128}=2^{-768}\) with \(h=\sqrt{N/32}\le s/(2\rho_j)\).

A chain of squares. Let \(\mathcal A_{j_1}\) be the set of level-\(j_1\) squares \(T\) all of whose ancestors and \(T\) itself are good, and \(\mathcal A_{j+1}=\{S'_*(S):S\in\mathcal A_j,\ \sigma_S\xi_S\ge h,\ S'_*(S)\text{ good}\}\). By induction, \(|U_j(S)|\ge(j-j_1)h\) for \(S\in\mathcal A_j\). With \(W_j=\sum_{S\in\mathcal A_j}|S|\), \(\mathbb E[W_{j+1}\mid\mathcal F_j]\ge\sum_{S\in\mathcal A_j}\frac{|S|}4\big(p_0-P(\text{some child of }S\text{ bad}\mid\mathcal F_j)\big)\ge\frac{p_0}4W_j-Y_j\), \(Y_j\) the conditional expected area of bad level-\((j+1)\) squares. Iterating, with \(p_0/4\le1\), \(\mathbb E[W_J\mid\mathcal F_{j_1}]\ge(p_0/4)^mW_{j_1}-Y\), \(Y=\sum_j\mathbb E[Y_j\mid\mathcal F_{j_1}]\), and \(\mathbb EY\le2N^{-\kappa/8}\) by the exceptional counts. Let \(\mu=(p_0/4)^m\ge N^{-\theta\log_2(4/p_0)}\). By Markov, \(P(Y\ge\mu/4)\le8N^{\theta\log_2(4/p_0)-\kappa/8}\) and \(P(W_{j_1}<1/2)\le4N^{-\kappa/8}\); so \(\mathbb E[W_J\mid\mathcal F_{j_1}]\ge\mu/4\) with probability tending to one when \(\theta\log_2(4/p_0)<\kappa/8\).

Many squares. \(W_J=\sum_TW_J(T)\) over the level-\(j_1\) squares \(T\), \(W_J(T)\in[0,|T|]\) the area of the chain inside \(T\). It is a function of \(\mathcal F_{j_1}\) and the points of \(T\): the chain inside \(T\) uses \(U_j\), \(\xi\) and \(\delta\) on squares inside \(T\), that is \(\Phi_i\) on \(T\) for \(i\ge j_1\) (a function of \(\mathcal F_{j_1}\) and the points of \(T\) by locality) and \(\Phi_i\) for \(i<j_1\) (\(\mathcal F_{j_1}\)-measurable). Given \(\mathcal F_{j_1}\) the point sets of distinct \(T\) are independent, so the \(W_J(T)\) are, with conditional variance at most \(\sum_T|T|^2/4=4^{-j_1}/4\le N^{2\theta}K\log N/(4N)\). By Chebyshev, \(P(W_J<\mu/8\mid\mathcal F_{j_1})\le16K\log N\,N^{2\theta-1+2\theta\log_2(4/p_0)}\), which tends to \(0\) when \(2\theta\log_2(4/p_0)<1-2\theta\).

Cost by convexity. For a level-\(J\) square \(Q\in\mathcal A_J\), \(U_J(Q)\) is the mean of \(\Phi_k\) over \(Q\) and \(|U_J(Q)|\ge mh\). The function \(z\mapsto\psi_\alpha(4|z|/(L\sqrt{N\log N}))\) is convex (a convex nondecreasing function of \(|z|\)), so by Jensen's inequality \(\int_Q\psi_\alpha(\cdots|\Phi_k|)\ge|Q|\psi_\alpha(u_N)\), and \(I_k\ge W_J\psi_\alpha(u_N)\ge\frac\mu8\psi_\alpha(u_N)\). With \(h=\sqrt{N/32}\) and \(m\ge\frac12\theta\log N\) for large \(N\), \(u_N\ge\frac{\theta}{\sqrt2L}\sqrt{\log N}\). For finite \(\alpha>2\), \(u_N^\alpha\) grows like \((\log N)^{\alpha/2}\), faster than \(\theta\log_2(4/p_0)\log N\), so \(I_k\to\infty\); for \(\alpha=\infty\), \(u_N\ge2\) for large \(N\) and \(I_k\ge N^{1-\theta\log_2(4/p_0)}/8\to\infty\). The choice of \(\theta\). \(\log_2(4/p_0)=770\); any \(\theta<\min(1/1542,\kappa/6160)\) meets both conditions, and one exists for every \(\kappa>0\). \(\square\)

Hypotheses, each with its step. The mean condition: the push of a square mean, and only there; it is all the theorem asks of the rule, and zero normal flux with the prescribed divergence is one way to have it (the integration by parts uses only the test function \(x_k-c_k\)). Equal-area children: \(\sum\delta_{S'}=0\). \(\mathcal F_{j+1}\)-measurability: \(U_j(S)\), \(\sigma_S\in\mathcal F_j\) and the chain's choices in \(\mathcal F_{j+1}\). Locality, at level \(j_1\) only: many squares. The depth bounds: exceptional counts (\(\kappa\)) and \(4^{-j_1}\) (\(K\)). \(\alpha>2\): the cost step. Not used: that \(\Phi\) is a flow (only the means of its steps), any bound on \(\Phi_j\), and any property of the rule inside the squares; the conclusion holds in the coordinate \(k\) for which the mean condition holds.

Degenerate cases. thm:square-mean-flow-obstruction: \(\alpha=2\): \(u_N^2\) is of order \(\theta^2\log N/L^2\) against \(\mu=N^{-770\theta}\), so the cost step depends on \(L\), consistently with thm:dyadic-flow-square-exponential, which bounds the dyadic flow's cost at exponent \(2\) for \(L\ge260\). A field with steps of mean zero on every square, such as \(\Phi\equiv0\), violates the mean condition (\(E_k(S)\) is not zero), as it must. A partition adapted to the points, cut where the two halves hold equal counts, has \(E_k=0\) for its own cells and is not a dyadic square step: the theorem does not apply to it.

Nonvacuity. The simultaneous rule at every pair of the curve, in its model quoted from research/results/ultimate_matching_simultaneous_rule_20261017/simultaneous_rule_test.py: on a level-\(j\) square, "coordinate 2 gets (phibar + psi(t1)) tent(t2) - tent'(t1) Psi(t2)", "coordinate 1 gets (phibar1_b + chi(t2)) tent(t1) - tent'(t2) Phi(t1) on half b", with "psi of zero mean over t1, chi of zero mean over each half, Phi(t1) = int_0^t1 psi, Psi(t2) = int over the half of chi"; at \(t_2\in\{0,1\}\) coordinate \(2\) is \(0\) (\(\operatorname{tent}=0\), \(\Psi=0\) at a half's ends), and at \(t_1\in\{0,1\}\) coordinate \(1\) is \(0\) (\(\Phi(0)=\Phi(1)=0\)), so each step has zero normal flux on its square. Its mean, computed directly from the quoted model: over the square, coordinate \(2\) integrates to \(\bar\varphi\int\operatorname{tent}(t_2)+\int\psi(t_1)\,dt_1\int\operatorname{tent}(t_2)\,dt_2-\int\operatorname{tent}'(t_1)\,dt_1\int\Psi(t_2)\,dt_2\), where the second term vanishes because \(\psi\) has mean zero and the third because \(\int_0^1\operatorname{tent}'=\operatorname{tent}(1)-\operatorname{tent}(0)=0\); so the mean is the dyadic step's, \(\bar\varphi\int\operatorname{tent}\), the same for every choice of \(\psi,\chi\); for coordinate \(1\), the term \(\chi(t_2)\operatorname{tent}(t_1)\) vanishes by \(\chi\)'s zero mean on each half, and the term \(-\operatorname{tent}'(t_2)\Phi(t_1)\), with \(\operatorname{tent}'\) taken over the whole interval (\(+2\) on the lower half, \(-2\) on the upper) and \(\Phi(t_1)=\int_0^{t_1}\psi\) the same on both halves, integrates to opposite values on the two halves and cancels over the whole square, though not on each half; the theorem uses only the whole square's mean. The rule is deterministic (Newton's method from a fixed start), so each step is a function of the counts, \(\mathcal F_{j+1}\)-measurable, and it is local (each square's step depends on the running field there and the square's child counts). With \(\kappa=L_0^2/4096\) at its depth \(L_0=260\), \(\kappa\approx16.5\), \(\theta=6\cdot10^{-4}\) meets both conditions (\(\theta<1/1542\approx6.49\cdot10^{-4}\) and \(770\theta=0.462<\kappa/8\approx2.06\)). thm:dyadic-flow-obstruction, about the linear dyadic flow alone, does not cover this rule. Plainest bound. One level's forced mean: \(|\xi_S|\) is of order \(\sqrt N\), an argument of order \(1/\sqrt{\log N}\), nothing; lem:straight-cut-forced-flux (c) says the cost forced across straight cuts, level by level, is at most \((N/2)\psi_4(8\sqrt8/L)\); the theorem adds the alignment of the forced means of \(m\) nested squares along a chain, which no single level's bound sees.

Baseline. thm:dyadic-flow-obstruction for the one linear flow; the theorem needs no linearity and no hypothesis on the rule beyond the means, so it covers the dyadic flow (it refines that theorem, at worse constants), every sequential rule (lem:sequential-rules-dyadic), the simultaneous rule, and any deterministic rule, local at level \(j_1\), that routes inside the dyadic squares, two-choice rules among them, steered or not.

Conditional push obstruction

Statement. Let \(\Phi\) be a level-by-level field, \(k\in\{1,2\}\), \(p\in(0,1]\), \(\theta>0\) and \(\gamma\ge0\) with \(a:=\theta\log_2(1/p)+\gamma\), \(2a<1-2\theta\) and \(\theta\log_2(1/p)<\kappa/8\). Suppose that for all large \(N\), \(\Phi\) is local at level \(j_1=J-m\) (for every level-\(j_1\) square \(T\) and \(j\ge j_1\), \(\Phi_j\) on \(T\) is a function of \(\mathcal F_{j_1}\) and the points in \(T\)), and there are \(h=h_N>0\) and a Borel set \(G_N\) with \(\lambda(G_N)\ge N^{-\gamma}\) such that for every \(x\in G_N\) and \(j_1\le j<J\), with \(R_j=\sum_{i<j}\Phi_{i,k}(x)\) and \(\sigma_j=\operatorname{sign}R_j\) (\(+1\) at \(0\)), \[P\big(\sigma_j\Phi_{j,k}(x)\ge h\ \big|\ \mathcal F_j\big)\ge p\quad\text{on }B_j(x).\] If \(\alpha\in(2,\infty)\) and \(u_N^\alpha-a\log N\to\infty\), or \(\alpha=\infty\) and \(u_N\ge2\) for large \(N\), then for every \(M\), with probability tending to one, \(I_k\ge M\). With \(h=c\sqrt N\) this holds at every \(L>0\) and every \(\alpha\in(2,\infty]\).

Proof. A run of pushes. Fix \(x\in G_N\). \(R_j\) and \(\sigma_j\) are \(\mathcal F_j\)-measurable, and \(E_j=\{\sigma_j\Phi_{j,k}(x)\ge h\}\in\mathcal F_{j+1}\) has \(P(E_j\mid\mathcal F_j)\ge p\) on \(B_j(x)\). On \(E_j\), \(|R_{j+1}|\ge\sigma_j(R_j+\Phi_{j,k}(x))=|R_j|+\sigma_j\Phi_{j,k}(x)\ge|R_j|+h\), so on \(\bigcap_{j_1\le j<J}E_j\), \(|\Phi_k(x)|\ge mh\). With \(H_{j_1}=B_{j_1}(x)\), \(H_{j+1}=H_j\cap E_j\cap B_{j+1}(x)\): \(P(H_{j+1}\mid\mathcal F_{j_1})\ge p\,P(H_j\mid\mathcal F_{j_1})-P(B_j(x)\setminus B_{j+1}(x)\mid\mathcal F_{j_1})\), since \(H_j\in\mathcal F_j\), \(H_j\subseteq B_j(x)\). Iterating, \(P(|\Phi_k(x)|\ge mh\mid\mathcal F_{j_1})\ge p^m1_{B_{j_1}(x)}-P(B_{j_1}(x)\setminus B_J(x)\mid\mathcal F_{j_1})\). Exceptional counts, as above: with \(\mu=p^m\lambda(G_N)\ge N^{-a}\), \(Y=\int_{G_N}P(B_{j_1}(x)\setminus B_J(x)\mid\mathcal F_{j_1})dx\) and \(Z=\int_{G_N}1_{B_{j_1}(x)^c}dx\) have means at most \(2N^{-\kappa/8}\lambda(G_N)\), and \(P(Y\ge\mu/4)\le8N^{\theta\log_2(1/p)-\kappa/8}\), \(P(Z\ge\lambda(G_N)/2)\le4N^{-\kappa/8}\). Many points. \(D=\{x:|\Phi_k(x)|\ge mh\}\) has \(\mathbb E[\lambda(D)\mid\mathcal F_{j_1}]\ge p^m(\lambda(G_N)-Z)-Y\ge\mu/4\) outside those events; the \(\lambda(D\cap T)\) over the level-\(j_1\) squares are conditionally independent by locality, with variance at most \(4^{-j_1}/4\); Chebyshev gives \(P(\lambda(D)<\mu/8\mid\mathcal F_{j_1})\le16K\log N\,N^{2\theta-1+2a}\to0\). Cost. On \(D\) the argument is at least \(u_N\): \(I_k\ge\frac{N^{-a}}8(e^{u_N^\alpha}-1)\to\infty\) for finite \(\alpha\), and \(I_k\ge N^{1-a}/8\to\infty\) for \(\alpha=\infty\) (\(a<1/2\)). For \(h=c\sqrt N\), \(u_N\ge(2c\theta/L)\sqrt{\log N}\) for large \(N\), as \(m\ge\frac12\theta\log N\). \(\square\)

Hypotheses, each with its step. The push along the running sign only, which is the form the run uses (a push in both signs, assumed in this entry's first draft, is stronger and forces \(p\le1/2\)); \(\mathcal F_{j+1}\)-measurability: the run; the push only on \(B_j(x)\) and \(\theta\log_2(1/p)<\kappa/8\): exceptional counts; locality at level \(j_1\) and \(2a<1-2\theta\) (which implies \(\theta<1/2\)): many points; \(\lambda(G_N)\ge N^{-\gamma}\): the mean; the growth of \(u_N\): the cost. Not used: that \(\Phi\) is a flow. The proof uses \(\mathcal F_j\) only for measurability and for the conditional independence of the level-\(j_1\) squares, so a filtration \(\mathcal G_j\supseteq\mathcal F_j\) that keeps that independence (a randomized rule's own coins, split by square) serves in its place; this extension is not written out.

Degenerate cases. lem:conditional-push-obstruction: \(p=1\), a push along the running sum that is certain, is a real case under this form and gives \(a=\gamma\). \(\Phi\equiv0\) violates the push for every \(h>0\). \(\alpha=2\) is excluded as for the theorem. A push of size \(h=o(\sqrt N(\log N)^{1/\alpha-1/2})\) makes \(u_N^\alpha\) at most of order \(\log N\), and the lemma says nothing.

Nonvacuity. At every pair of the curve: the dyadic flow \(\Phi^0\) of thm:dyadic-flow-square-exponential at depth \(L_0=260\) (\(\kappa\approx16.5\)) plus \(\sum_j\Psi_j\), each \(\Psi_j\) divergence-free and supported in the level-\(j\) squares with \(|\Psi_{j,k}|\le h/2\), for instance the curl of \(\epsilon_S(h/2)\rho_j\varphi((x-x_S)/\rho_j)\) with \(|\nabla\varphi|\le1\) and \(\varphi\) vanishing near the square's boundary, and \(\epsilon_S\in\{-1,0,1\}\) chosen from \(\mathcal F_{j_1}\) and the counts inside the level-\(j_1\) square containing \(S\), so that the sum is local at level \(j_1\); coordinate \(2\), \(h=\sqrt{N/512}\). Given \(\mathcal F_j\) on \(B_j(x)\), \(\Phi^0_{j,2}(x)=\sum_z(\beta_{c(z)}-\bar\beta)\) over the \(n\ge N4^{-j}/2\) points of \(S_j(x)\), terms of mean \(0\), size at most \(2/\rho_j\) and variance \(w_2(t)/\rho_j^2\), \(w_2(t)=\min(t_2,1-t_2)^2\) (the coefficient lemma of the dyadic flow obstruction entry); for \(t_2\in[1/8,7/8]\) the standard deviation \(s\ge\sqrt{N/128}=2h\), and lem:block-lower-tail at \(x=1\) on the terms times \(\sigma_j\) (needing \(n\ge65536\)) gives \(P(\sigma_j\Phi^0_{j,2}(x)\ge2h\mid\mathcal F_j)\ge2^{-768}\), whence \(\sigma_j\Phi_{j,2}(x)\ge2h-h/2\ge h\). So \(p=2^{-768}\), \(G_N=\{x:t_2(T_j(x))\in[1/8,7/8],\ j_1\le j<J\}\), \(\lambda(G_N)=(3/4)^m\), \(\gamma=\theta\log_2(4/3)\); at \(\theta=6\cdot10^{-4}\), \(2a=0.922<0.9988\) and \(768\theta=0.461<2.06\). A circulation does not change square means, so the theorem covers this flow too; the lemma's use is for fields the mean condition does not cover. Plainest bound. The triangle inequality with thm:dyadic-flow-obstruction's set: there \(|\Phi^0_2|\ge\tau\sqrt N\log N/12\approx0.0009\sqrt N\log N\) (\(\tau^2=1/8640\)), while \(\sum_j|\Psi_{j,2}|\le Jh/2\approx0.016\sqrt N\log N\), so it decides nothing.

Refinement at every depth. For the dyadic flow of depth constant \(L_0\), \(\kappa=L_0^2/4096\), and the witness argument holds with any \(\theta<\min(6.49\cdot10^{-4},\kappa/6144)\); so the lemma, and the theorem, imply thm:dyadic-flow-obstruction's conclusion at every \(L_0\) and every \(L\), and separate the depth constant from the cost constant, which that theorem ties together.

The simultaneous rule's pushes

Script. research/results/ultimate_matching_conditional_push_20261017/push_test.py, committed with its control, Prediction and baseline before the run (commit "Conditional push script for two-choice-routing, before its run"); a plumbing run at \(J=2,4\) ran first. For each level \(j\ge1\), position and flow it estimates over the seeds \(\text{same}=P(\operatorname{sign}(R_j)\Phi_j\ge0.5\,\text{sd}_j)\) and \(\text{opposite}=P(-\operatorname{sign}(R_j)\Phi_j\ge0.5\,\text{sd}_j)\), averaged over positions, with the minimum of same over positions. The first run, \(J=2,3,4\), stopped at its \(60\) s allowance after \(J=2\) (\(4000\) seeds) and \(J=3\) (\(4000\)); \(J=4\) (\(1400\) seeds) ran alone after; outputs push_J2_J3_output.txt and push_results_J4.json, summary push_summary.txt, beside the script.

Results. All figures from push_summary.txt, written by a script from the two outputs. Dyadic flow (control): same and opposite agree within \(0.006\) at every level and size (largest difference \(0.0058\)), between \(0.291\) and \(0.330\), near \(P(Z\ge0.5)=0.31\). Rule: same \(0.320\)–\(0.333\), opposite \(0.300\)–\(0.321\); the minimum of same over positions, the figure the lemma's form uses, is \(0.270\) to \(0.310\) for the rule against \(0.263\) to \(0.312\) for the dyadic flow. The Prediction (same at least half of opposite at every level and \(J\le4\)) holds; it tests steering, which the lemma's corrected form does not need. The excess of same over opposite, \(0.0068\) to \(0.0227\), exceeds the control's \(0.0058\) in most cells, the smallest (\(J=4\), coordinate \(1\), level \(1\)) by \(0.001\), with position averages sharing seeds: the rule leans along the running field slightly in most cells and against it in none.

What it does not show. The lemma's hypothesis is a conditional lower bound at every point of \(G_N\) at the fine levels; the measurement averages over seeds at \(J\le4\). For this rule the question is settled by the theorem instead, through the mean condition, so the measurement is now a consistency check: a rule the theorem covers was expected to keep a push.

Nonvacuity (check). The flows run are those of the rule's model at the curve's scale \(\sqrt{N\log N}\), at \(J\le4\). The Prediction could fail: a rule steering fresh flux strongly against the running field would show same below half of opposite; the dyadic control shows the estimator reads symmetric pushes as equal within \(0.006\). Plainest bound. For a flow whose increments are independent of the coarser field and symmetric, same equals opposite.

Eighth review: boundary fluxes locate escape

17 October 2026 · Goal-level route review, reviewed in two stages; no statement registered · Eighth route review. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort set by the session).

Where we stand. Unchanged: a review registering no statement; its finding, that the square-mean obstruction does not reach flows crossing dyadic boundaries, stands in the clause the previous entry wrote

Where we stand. Six research entries since the seventh review: two on the mixed-level counts' strict both-high form (chain duality, bounded chains), two before them on its windows and crossings (windowed mixed counts, column crossing), and two on two-choice-routing (exceedance slopes, square means). The last proves thm:square-mean-flow-obstruction: no level-by-level field, local at the fine levels and measurable in the counts, whose fine steps keep the dyadic square means meets the flow bound's cost above exponent \(2\).

Open statements. ultimate-matching (the full target) and conjugate-class-discrepancy (sufficient) open; shor-exponential and grid-discrepancy open and untouched in the period. The line's open-item count is \(4\), as at the review twelve research entries back, so this review is goal-level.

The line's general claim. conj:conjugate-class-discrepancy on the curve in its discrete form: by lem:grid-flow-duality (c) the discrete \(X\)-term class bound on grids with \(\delta\le s/32\) and \(N\delta^2\ge16\log N\) gives the conclusion of cor:exponential-matching-discrepancy-reduction, and by its (d) the class supremum is a minimal edge flow cost.

What the goal needs. That discrete bound at every pair of the curve, or a matching built directly; equivalently, an edge flow carrying the cell counts to the background at cost of order \(N\), with one universal \(L\).

The six entries

Windowed mixed counts (thm:windowed-mixed-counts): mixed levels hold at low second levels in column windows at bounded box ratios, extending the low-level counts; bearing on mixed-level-counts, the strict both-high case untouched. Column crossing (lem:column-crossing-count, thm:column-crossing-obstruction): at \(t_1=\log N\), \(t_2=\sqrt{\log N}\) the first-coordinate repair must carry the strip discrepancy across fine columns by pairs inside both boxes, at least \(\varepsilon_N\sqrt N/(8(D_1+w))\) of them. Chain duality (lem:two-graph-chain-duality, cor:short-chains-per-level): the strict both-high form holds iff every chain of a nested-set dual has value at most \(2Ne^{-t_2}\); chains of length at most one do. Bounded chains (thm:bounded-length-chains): chains of length up to \(e^{t'-t_2}\) do, at a free level \(t'\); whether an optimal chain can be longer is open. Exceedance slopes (ex:exceedance-curve-slopes): the simultaneous rule's per-point tails at \(J=5,6\) are lighter than Gaussian at central scales, its drift with \(J\) undecidable at \(512\) seeds. Square means (thm:square-mean-flow-obstruction, lem:conditional-push-obstruction, ex:rule-conditional-pushes): every local level-by-level field keeping the dyadic square means at the fine levels fails above exponent \(2\) at every \(L\), which covers the simultaneous rule and every rule routing inside the dyadic squares; the exceedance slopes' lighter central tails do not reach the scale \(\sqrt{\log N}\) standard deviations, where the cost is decided.

Falsification attempt. Does thm:square-mean-flow-obstruction reach the cheapest flow, the class bound itself through lem:grid-flow-duality (d)? For any flow \(\Phi\) with the prescribed divergence and any dyadic square \(S\), \(\int_S\Phi_k=-\int_S(x_k-c_k)\operatorname{div}\Phi+\int_{\partial S}(x_k-c_k)\,\Phi\cdot n\): the first term is fixed by the counts, the second is free whenever flux crosses \(\partial S\). The theorem's walk needs the second term to vanish at the fine levels; the cheapest flow is under no such constraint. So the attempt fails: the obstruction does not reach the class bound, and it locates where a cheap flow must differ from every hierarchical one, in the boundary fluxes across fine dyadic squares, which must cancel the aligned forced means along chains of nested squares. A second attempt, on the adapted partition (each cell cut where its halves hold equal counts): the walk returns in the cuts' positions. A cell of side \(\rho\) with \(n\approx N\rho^2\) points has its median cut offset from the middle by about \(\rho|E|/n\approx1/(2\sqrt N)\), \(E\) the lower half's binomial excess, and rescaling the halves moves a point at relative position \(t\) by \(2\min(t,1-t)\) times that offset, both halves in one direction, to first order the dyadic flow's tent profile. Given the coarser cuts and counts, the cell's points are i.i.d. uniform, so reflecting the cell about its midline keeps their law and flips the offset's sign, while the running displacement is fixed by the coarser cuts: the offset's conditional law is symmetric about \(0\), and no restoring drift can arise in the equal-count partition (the stage-two reviewer's argument, checked here). So the obstruction should transfer to the median partition; the next entry writes that lemma.

Assessment of this line. The period closed a class on the primal side and narrowed one on the dual side, and supplied no upper-bound mechanism. Primal: thm:square-mean-flow-obstruction excludes, for the flow bound above exponent \(2\), every local level-by-level field measurable in the counts whose fine steps keep the dyadic square means; the falsification attempt finds the same walk, with a symmetric conditional law, in the cut positions of the equal-count partition, so that partition appears to fall to it too (a hand computation, to be proved). Hierarchical partitions whose cuts are chosen against the running displacement, carrying count imbalances to the children, are not covered by either and are where the restoring drift could live. Dual: the strict both-high form of the mixed counts is a chain-value statement, true for chains up to length \(e^{\lambda t_2}\), open beyond. The evidence therefore points away from hierarchical constructions that cut at equal counts or keep the square means: a cheap flow, if one exists, steers the running field back across dyadic boundaries, as the blind stage's restoring-drift architecture proposes independently. The line is not refuted, and its core statement keeps all its evidence (the forced order, the class lower bounds, the partial dual bounds).

Obstacle

On the primal side the line is stuck at a mechanism no construction has: at \((4,4)\) the running field's square means, which every step keeping the dyadic square means forces to walk with pushes of order \(\sqrt N\) per fine level (the walk in the proof of thm:square-mean-flow-obstruction, which uses the mean condition and the measurability of the signs; locality enters only the concentration over the level-\(j_1\) squares), must be returned toward zero by fluxes across the boundaries of fine dyadic squares, whose weighted integrals \(\int_{\partial S}(x_k-c_k)\Phi\cdot n\) cancel aligned forced means along chains of nested squares (the falsification attempt's identity); no construction does this and no bound shows the cross-boundary cost affordable. On the dual side it is stuck where the seventh review put it: class functions with gradients over many levels, here in the form of chains longer than \(e^{\lambda\sqrt{\log N}}\) in the strict both-high instance.

  • shor-exponential: unchanged; no cycle.
  • grid-discrepancy: unchanged; no cycle.

The blind stage proposes a further open statement, the diagonal pairs \((\alpha,\alpha)\), \(2<\alpha<4\), above the curve: every flow obstruction of the record applies there already, and the conjecture at \((4,4)\) implies it with a larger constant: at scale \(Ms\), with \(c=M^{-\alpha}\le1\) and \(u\) a displacement in units of \(s\), \((u/M)^\alpha=cu^\alpha\le c(1+u^4)\) for \(\alpha\le4\), so \(\sum_ie^{(u_i/M)^\alpha}\le e^c\sum_i(e^{u_i^4})^c\le e^cN^{1-c}(\sum_ie^{u_i^4})^c\le e^c2^cN\) by Hölder, at most \(2N\) once \(c\le\ln2/(1+\ln2)\) (the stage-two reviewer's argument, checked here; the pointwise step needs \(\alpha\le4\)); the statement is recorded below as a reviewer's suggestion, not adopted as an open statement.

Architecture review

Necessary target. The weakest endpoint: at every pair of the curve, with probability tending to one, one matching with \(\sum_i\exp[(|X^j_i-Y^j_{\pi(i)}|/s)^{\alpha_j}]\le2N\) for both \(j\), \(s=L\sqrt{\log N/N}\), \(L\) universal; evenly spread \(Y\) suffice by lem:two-sample-matching-transfer. Downstream. Through lem:grid-flow-duality (c) the discrete class bound gives that endpoint at every pair with \(\alpha\in[1,\infty]^2\); through its (d) the bound is a minimal edge flow cost; thm:square-mean-flow-obstruction and thm:dyadic-flow-obstruction show that level-by-level fields measurable in the counts, local at the fine levels and keeping the dyadic square means there, cannot certify it above exponent \(2\); thm:dyadic-flow-square-exponential gives the endpoint at \((2,2)\), off the curve; weaker than the goal.

Extra requirements. The route demands one flow where the goal needs one matching; lem:grid-flow-duality (d) makes the class bound and the cheapest flow one problem, and lem:segment-flow-cost (a good matching of tube density at most \(KN\) gives a segment flux of bounded flow cost) gives a good flow from a good matching of bounded tube density, so the flow demand is justified up to tube density.
